# Rupert, Ab-
## BOT OF DEUTZ <note>Latin: "Tuitiensis." Rupert was an influential Benedictine monk and theologian from the monastery of Deutz, near Cologne, Germany.</note>
### OF THE COMMENTARIES,
### ON THE REVELATION OF JOHN <note>original: "Ioannis Apocalypsin"</note>

## 22 BOOKS. <note>While Rupert's commentary on the Apocalypse is traditionally organized into 12 books, the Roman numerals here indicate 22, possibly reflecting a different division of the text in this specific edition.</note>

<insert>From the library of <unclear>Master Charles Coupigny</unclear> <unclear>arny</unclear> <unclear>Morbier</unclear></insert> <note>These are handwritten provenance notes, showing the book was once owned by an individual named Charles Coupigny.</note>

### PARIS

->At the shop of Pierre Regnault, under the sign of<-
->the Three Crowns, on the Rue Saint-Jacques.<- <note>In the 16th century, printers used "signs" (like Three Crowns) to identify their shops before the use of street numbers. The Rue Saint-Jacques was the center of the Parisian book trade.</note>

**To those journeying here on earth, Christ is a star; to the blessed in heaven, he is the sun.** <note>original: "peregrinātibus... beatis in cælo." The text contrasts the 'wayfarers' of this life with those who have reached their heavenly home. The OCR 'fol' is a transcription of 'sol' (sun).</note>
**At the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, Christians were in Pella under Agrippa.** 194. <note>Referencing the historical tradition that early Christians fled Jerusalem for the city of Pella before the Roman siege in 70 AD.</note>
**Christians fleeing into the wilderness—that is, possessing nothing of their own.** 347. <note>A spiritual interpretation of 'the wilderness' as a state of voluntary poverty or asceticism.</note>
**The prophets and teachers of the Law are likened to cups.** 410. <note>original: "cyathis." Small vessels used for pouring or drinking.</note>
**Cups under the Law, Bowls under the Gospel.** 420. <note>original: "cyathi sub lege, Phialæ sub Euāgelio." A comparison of the liturgical vessels used in the Old Covenant versus the New.</note>
**The harps of the saints are their bodies, mortified for the sake of Christ.** 155. <note>original: "cithare sanctorum... corpora... mortificata." The music of the harp represents the disciplined, holy life of a believer.</note>
**The great city belongs to the devil, and its buildings are vices.** 298.
**The city of the whole world is divided into three parts through the preaching of the Gospel.** 443.
**The city of the devil does not have a single head, as the city of God does.** 447.
**The city of the saints: holy in its merits, Jerusalem by name, and new in its condition.** Section 35. <note>original: "habitu noua." Refers to the 'New Jerusalem' appearing in a new form or state.</note>
**The greatest dissimilarity between these two cities.** Section 35. <note>Likely referring to the City of God and the City of Man/Devil.</note>
**Of the great cry ascending, one is of sin, the other of good work.** 223. <note>In scripture, both 'the cry of Sodom' (sin) and the 'cry of the poor' (righteousness) are said to ascend to God.</note>
**The loud cry is the passion of Christ, through which Babylon fell.** 475. <note>original: "clamor fortis." Interprets the loud voice in Revelation as the power of Christ’s suffering on the cross.</note>
**The city is laid out as a square because there is the highest harmony of all things there.** Section 50. <note>original: "ciuitas in quadro posita." Refers to the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:16.</note>
**The glory of Christ in the flesh with the Father is like the light of seven days.** 50. <note>original: "claritas christi... sicut lux septem diem." A reference to Isaiah 30:26, signifying perfected light.</note>
**A person cannot see the glory of God unless they stand at the right hand of Christ.** 51.
**The glory of God in the heavenly Jerusalem, both in the body and in the soul.** Section 42.
**What the key of David is.** 101. <note>A reference to Revelation 3:7 regarding Christ's authority.</note>
**What the marriage supper of the Lamb and his wife is.** 490.
**The eye-salve with which the eyes are to be anointed is humility.** 111. <note>original: "collyrium." Refers to Revelation 3:18, where the 'blind' church is told to buy eye-salve to see.</note>
**General councils swallow up the river of the dragon—that is, the dogmas of heretics.** 343. <note>Interpreting Revelation 12:16, where the earth helps the woman by swallowing the flood sent by the dragon.</note>
**The horn of the Macedonian kingdom divided into four kingdoms.** 322. <note>A reference to the prophecies in the Book of Daniel regarding Alexander the Great.</note>
**Horns like those of a lamb are the deceptions of magic.** 372. <note>Refers to the false prophet in Revelation 13:11, who looks like a lamb but speaks like a dragon.</note>
**Christ is crowned through each of our virtues.** 22.

Page 1

# The Prologue of RU-
## PERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE
### Apocalypse of John the Apostle, addressed to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'V' containing intricate vine and leaf patterns, with a small human face positioned at the bottom junction of the letter looking upwards.</image-desc>
AS YOU ALSO PERCEIVE, O venerable Frederick, Archbishop of the people of Cologne, and as the clear example of truth in the Scriptures teaches, a spirit of piety is necessary for all who strive toward the true land of promise, so that they may be meek. For "Blessed are the meek," says the Lord himself, "for they shall inherit the earth." <note>original: "Beati nanque mites (ait ipse dominus) quoniam ipsi possidebūt terrā." This is a quotation from the Beatitudes in Matthew 5:5.</note>

<margin>Matthew 5</margin>
By excluding the harsh <note>original: "immites." In this context, it refers to those who are stubborn or resistant to divine truth, the opposite of the "meek" (mites).</note> from blessedness, He shows they shall not inherit the earth. This applies to both groups: those who are meek and therefore will possess the land, and those who are harsh and therefore will not. A well-known and famous example of this is expressed in those spies whom Moses, at the Lord's command, sent to inspect the land of Canaan.

<margin>Numbers 18 <note>Though the margin notes chapter 18, the narrative described is found in Numbers 13–14.</note></margin>

<margin>The occasion for writing.</margin>
this book, the *Apocalypse of John the Apostle*? To explore this part through diligent meditation, I was greatly stirred by the pleasantness of your conversations. For a man illustrious in religion and devoted to sacred letters, Lord Cuno, Abbot of the monastery of Siegburg <note>Siegburg was a prominent Benedictine abbey near Cologne, where Cuno served as abbot from 1105 to 1126.</note>, was urging me, proposing certain chapters of this book, first privately and then in your hearing. His intention was that it might be discovered by you as well that I (as he himself believed) might be able to usefully contribute something beyond what the ancient fathers felt or said in explaining this book. He acted out of the excessive kindness of his mind, through which he had long ago begun to think more highly of my smallness than the capability of my talent allows. Indeed, both before and after those same discussions, he insisted that I undertake this work; nor did he cease his persuasion until at last he prevailed as he wished.

<margin>
Jerome’s praise of the book of the Apocalypse.
</margin>
What sequence of Holy Scripture, I ask, is either more beautiful on its surface or richer in meaning than this Apocalypse? For (as has been said before us) it has as many mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta." Even this is an understatement, and all praise is inferior to the merit of the volume. Multiple layers of understanding lie hidden in every single word. Therefore, so that we may possess this land, let us follow the example of the faithful explorers who were meek.

# Prologue

...let us be humble in spirit, whoever we are that enter this land <note>original: "hanc terram"</note>—that is, this scripture—and let us believe that a deeper majesty of divine meanings lies hidden where we still understand the least. For if the Lord is favorable, he will lead us into it and hand over a soil flowing with milk and honey, so that we may find hidden within it the riches of salvation: the treasures of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge, piety, and the fear of the Lord. But someone will say: "Enough has already been found and written by others who were nevertheless better, holier, and more learned than you. It is unlawful and rash to add anything to those things said by the renowned and Catholic fathers, and so to cause disgust in readers by increasing the sheer number of commentaries." To this I say: The exceedingly spacious field of the holy Scriptures is common to all who confess Christ, and the license to treat them cannot rightfully be denied to anyone, provided that, while keeping the faith safe, one says or writes what they perceive. For who would rightly be indignant that, on the same property, after one or two wells that the preceding fathers dug, the succeeding sons should dig more through their own labor? Finally, Isaac also dug other wells besides those which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, which the Philistines had once blocked up after he died. For 

<columns>2</columns>

after he dug those again and called them by the same names his father had used before, the Scripture continues and says: *They dug in the valley and found living water.* <note>Referencing Genesis 26, where Isaac re-opens the wells of Abraham; Rupert uses this to justify "re-digging" into the depths of scripture even if others have done so before.</note> Likewise they dug another. And so on. Moving forward, he dug another well. Therefore, according to this rule, let them also grant us the right—after those wells which they dug, that is, after those treatises our fathers and predecessors composed—to dig other wells with the plowshare of our own intellect, provided that we too can find living water, which harms no one who drinks it and creates no scandal or error for the reader. But now, relying on the grace of God and the patronage of your authority, I shall enter upon the proposed work, judging it good to place my hope only in the Lord God: so that I may receive my reward <note>original: "mercedem"</note> not here, but in the future.

## The Apocalypse of John the Apostle,
### The First Book of Commentaries.

*Apocalypsis* <note>original: "αποκάλυψις"</note>, the Greek title of the book, used because of the dignity of the mysteries and meanings.
</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A'. Within the framework of the letter, two figures are depicted: on the left, a man holding a book, and on the right, another man looking upward toward the apex of the letter where a celestial light or manifestation appears.</image-desc>
**T**HE REVELATION OF JESUS CHRIST. <note>original: "APOCALYPSIS IESV CHRISTI"</note> Since the entire series of this book was written in Greek and flowed from a Greek source into the stream of the Latin language, its title alone has beautifully remained untouched, so that among the Latins it is called *Apocalypsis* <note>The Greek term for "unveiling" or "revelation."</note>. This name could have been translated as "revelation," but it was kept in the original, clearly because of the excellence of the things or mysteries that this scripture contains. In the same way, *Alleluia* and *Amen*, which are Hebrew words, have remained in Greek and Latin letters because of the dignity of their meanings. Likewise, the term *Gospel* <note>original: "Euangelium"</note> has been preserved from the Greek in Latin manuscripts—the language in which all the Evangelists wrote, except for Matthew.

<margin>
Psalm 44. <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 45:7.</note>
Jesus.
</margin>

Therefore, "Apocalypse" means an excellent revelation, full of majesty to be adored in its meanings. "Of Jesus Christ," he says, which means the "Anointed Savior," just as it is written in the Psalm: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.*

<margin>
Matthew 1.
Christ.
</margin>

And indeed, many have shared the name "Jesus" <note>The name Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua.</note>, but this person holds the true meaning of this name. The angel added this reason when he said: *And you shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he himself,* the angel said, *shall save his people from their sins.*

<margin>
Colossians 2.
</margin>

Likewise, there have been many "Christs"—that is, many who were "anointed"—but this man is anointed above all others, inasmuch as in him *dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily*; those others, however, were or are sharers or participants in him.

## Which God gave him to make known to his ser-
## vants what must happen soon.

<margin>1 Corinthians 4; Romans 8.</margin>
For what does our nature possess that it has not received in the person of the only-begotten Son? <note>Rupert is arguing that Jesus, in his human nature, received these gifts from God, emphasizing the union of human and divine.</note> Furthermore, what did he not receive, or what was not given to him in exchange for his obedience even unto death, even death on a cross? God left nothing that was not subject to him, as the Psalmist says: *You have put all things under his feet.*

<margin>Psalm 8; Matthew, last chapter, section a.</margin>
But he also says of himself, now that his obedience is fulfilled: *All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.* In this very book he also says: *I was dead, and behold I am alive forever and ever, and I have the keys of death and of hell.* <note>original: "claues mortis & inferni"</note> Truly, these things were spoken concerning his power over all things.

<margin>The power of revealing thus given to Christ.</margin>
That power of which we now speak—namely, the power of revealing heavenly mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> to his servants—his humanity received as a gift. This is signified elsewhere in this book, where the Lamb <note>A title for Jesus in the Apocalypse, representing his sacrifice.</note> took and opened the sealed book from the right hand of the one sitting on the throne. Regarding this same power, the Spirit says to the churches: *These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens.* Therefore, regarding the humanity of Jesus Christ, there is nothing that has not been given or that he has not received; but regarding his divinity, no power was given that he did not already possess.

<margin>A figure of speech <note>original: "tropus"</note>. 2 Timothy 4.</margin>
Therefore, let the text say: *Which <note>original: "quam"</note> God gave him to make known to his servants.* It would indeed be clearer if he had said *by which* <note>original: "qua"</note>. But this way of speaking often occurs in the Scriptures. It is like the phrase: *I have fought the good fight* <note>original: "Bonum certamen certaui"</note>, used instead of "I have fought *with* a good fight." To which servants should he make this known? Surely to those whom he now calls "friends" because of this very manifestation. He spoke this way at the opening of the sealed book—that is, at the moment of his Passion—by which he made the Scriptures understandable by fulfilling them.

<margin>John 15.</margin>
*I will no longer call you servants, but my friends, because everything I have heard from my Father, I have made known to you.* But what he says next—*what must happen soon*—is not to be understood as if this Apocalypse contains only those things which were still in the future, and not those which were already happening then, or those which had occurred before. For later it is said to John: *Write therefore the things which...*

<margin>John 20</margin>

And those things which belonged to Jesus Christ—that is, things performed visibly according to the "form of a servant" <note>A reference to Philippians 2:7, meaning Christ's human nature.</note> or the appearance of a man—he was able to see; but the Word itself, to which he nonetheless bore witness, he could not see with his physical eyes. He argues that John "saw" the human actions and signs of Jesus, which serve as the "testimony" to the invisible "Word of God."</note>

## **Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written in it. For the time is near.**

<margin>John’s exclamation resulting from the vision granted to him.</margin>
Conscious within himself of what and what kind of things he saw—what punishments of the wicked and what rewards of the righteous this Revelation of Jesus Christ made clear to him—John appropriately exclaims with a great voice and vehement intensity that such a person is truly blessed, saying: "He who [hears] those things which are written here—for instance, the seven wonderful trumpets thundering in this prophecy—or if he knows how to read, he who reads and observes them, and vigilantly prepares himself for that voice of the archangel, the trumpet of God, the final trumpet <note>Rupert links the trumpets of the Apocalypse to the "last trumpet" mentioned in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and 1 Corinthians 15:52.</note> that shall sound on the Day of Judgment." In this same way, the lawgiver Moses, when he looked forward from a distance—being, of course, much more ancient than John—toward the blessedness of the saints, and preached it partly through enigmas <note>original: *ænigmata*; referring to the symbolic or veiled language of the Old Testament</note>, suddenly exclaimed:

<margin>Deuteronomy 33</margin>
**Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved [by the Lord]?** <note>Deuteronomy 33:29</note> For so great and so horrific is the damnation of the wicked, and so great and so desirable is the glorification of the righteous, that the spectator rightly cries out; and by crying out, the Spirit signifies what the tongue cannot explain through mere speech. This is especially true because the time is near, and it is uncertain when it will arrive or when the final trumpet will sound; it cannot be foreseen. Indeed, when he speaks the "words of this prophecy," we ought to understand or expect every kind of prophecy here—that is, of the three times: the past, the present, and the future. For as has been said before us and is true, there are three times of prophecy: namely, past, present, and future.

<margin>

Isaiah 7.
Genesis 1.
1 Corinthians 14.

Prophecy concerning the present is that which the Apostle Paul describes: *But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among*

<header>### On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse</header>

...God is truly present. Therefore, when it is said, "the secrets of his heart are made manifest," <note>Rupert is quoting 1 Corinthians 14:24–25, where Paul describes how prophecy reveals the hidden thoughts of an unbeliever, leading them to acknowledge God's presence.</note> it is certainly shown that in this manner the spirit of prophecy does not merely predict what is to come, but reveals what already exists.

<margin>Prophecy, strictly speaking, concerns the future</margin>
But it must be understood that in two time periods prophecy loses its literal meaning. <note>The word "prophecy" comes from the Greek *propheteia*, meaning "speaking beforehand" or "foretelling."</note> Since prophecy is defined by its name as foretelling future events, when it speaks of the past or the present, it loses the logic of its name; for it is not "prophesying" what is to come, but is either recalling things that have already happened or describing things that are currently happening.

<margin>The threefold state of the Church</margin>
This prophecy is woven from all these times—or rather, it concerns all these times: namely, the past, the present, and the future. Through this Apocalypse, Jesus Christ revealed to his beloved [John] what the state of the Church had been, what it was at that time, and what it would be in the future. As the reader—or the blessed listener—can recognize from the wonderful sequence of the text itself, provided by that same Jesus Christ. Therefore, with the promised hope of blessedness, let us enter into the reading of this prophecy under the guidance of Jesus Christ. And as we read, let us likewise "hear": reading the literal text outwardly, while hearing the mysteries inwardly. <margin>Matthew 11</margin> These are the mysteries which the Father reveals to "little ones" <note>Rupert refers to the "spiritually humble" rather than children; see Matthew 11:25.</note> while hiding them from the wise and the prudent of this world—to those who apply that "ear" which this very prophecy so often requires when it says: *He who has an ear to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.*

<margin>The Introduction</margin>
For the things that have been said so far were spoken to persuade us to have or to seek such an ear—namely, one that is attentive, teachable, and well-disposed. <note>Rupert is applying classical Roman rhetoric here. In a formal introduction (an *exordium*), a speaker tried to make the audience *attentus* (attentive), *docilis* (teachable), and *benevolus* (well-disposed/friendly).</note> Secular scholars of rhetoric work with no small effort to achieve this in their own introductions. For by saying, *The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place,* <margin>Attentive. Teachable.</margin> he demands the **attention** of the listener, as one who promises to speak of great matters that will soon come to pass. Indeed, he intends to make the listener **teachable** by saying, *And he signified it.* <note>Revelation 1:1. The word "signified" (Latin: *significavit*) implies that the truth is communicated through signs and symbols rather than plain speech.</note> By this, he hints that heavenly mysteries must be sought beneath the figures of names or images.

<margin>Well-disposed</margin>
He desires the listener to be **well-disposed** (friendly to the message) when he speaks of his own person, as the one *who bore witness to the word of God, and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, and to all things that he saw.* He certainly draws much [authority] from...

<summary>Rupert explains that while "prophecy" usually means foretelling the future, the Apocalypse also reveals the past and present state of the Church. He uses classical rhetorical categories to show how the book's opening prepares the reader to be attentive and receptive to divine mysteries.</summary>

->**John to the seven churches which are in Asia: grace to you and peace.**<-

All the faithful throughout the nations gladly receive this greeting of grace and peace from the mouth of John as if it were truly sent to us, freely and truthfully professing that we are of the seven churches and we are in Asia. 

<margin>Asia signifies the proud world. Psalm 92.</margin>
Indeed, "Asia" is interpreted as "elation" <note>Rupert uses an allegorical etymology common in the Middle Ages, linking the name "Asia" to the Latin *elatio*, meaning pride or a swelling up, like a wave.</note> and it signifies this proud world, raising itself up and carrying itself along like the waves of the sea, as it is sung in the Psalm: *Wonderful are the surges of the sea, wonderful is the Lord on high.* <note>original: "Mirabiles elationes maris, mirabilis in altis dominus." This is Psalm 92:4 in the Vulgate, or Psalm 93:4 in modern Bibles.</note> This is to say: wonderful are the persecutions of the world, but much more wonderful is the Lord in suppressing those same persecutions. 

<margin>The seven churches in Asia.</margin>
In this kind of "Asia" there are seven churches—that is, the one and only Catholic Church, ordered and adorned by the holy sevenfold Spirit. Therefore, whatever grace and peace is wished here for the seven churches in Asia, we who worship Christ among all nations rightly claim for ourselves. This is true even if this apostle and Evangelist, humble in spirit, chose not to impose his authority upon the whole world, naming only that small part of the world—that is, Asia Minor—in which he had labored. 

These are the "seven women" <note>Rupert is drawing an allegory from Isaiah 4:1, where seven women take hold of one man.</note> who—in an Asia where the heads of the daughters of Zion have now been shaved <note>Rupert alludes to Isaiah 3:17–24, describing the humiliation of Jerusalem, which leads into the imagery of the seven women.</note>—take hold of one man, saying: *We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach.* 

<margin>Allegory of the seven women for the one man in Isaiah 4. Psalm 22. Against the Jews. Joshua 14.</margin>
It is as if all the families of the nations, while worshiping him, were to say: "Look at that nation [Israel] which you led out of Egypt when they had no land. You destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan <note>Refers to Joshua 14:1, where seven nations were conquered to give Israel their inheritance.</note> and distributed their land to them by lot. Look at the kind of reward they have paid back to you: casting you outside the gate of the city and crucifying you. At least now, turn toward us. We do not ask that you give us the regions of others as a reward..."

# xiiii Commentary of Rupert, Book 1.

...sary <note>original: "quit," completing "inquit" (he says)</note> says, "who was, and who is, and who is to come." To some it has seemed that these words ought to be understood as being about the person of the Son, especially because he said at the end, "and who is to come." Since the Son himself is the one who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and since [they argue] no mention is made here of the person of the Father, but only of the Son and the Holy Spirit—the Son twice, in fact: both in what he said first, "from him who was, and who is, and who is to come," and in what he said later, "and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness," etc. But the Holy Spirit is mentioned only once, in that he says, "and from the seven spirits who are in the presence of his throne." But the aforementioned Apostle Paul often occurs to us, saying and distinguishing so many times: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ."

<margin>John 20</margin>
Indeed, the Father of Christ is our Father, just as he says: "I ascend to my Father and your Father," <note>John 20:17</note> and so he was, and is, and is to come. Only this which is said at the end—"and who is to come"—seems to compel one to understand these words as spoken of the person of the Son, because the angels said concerning this person:

<margin>Acts 1</margin>
"He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven." <note>Acts 1:11</note> But truly, the Father is also without doubt "to come," that is, he is to manifest himself to the faithful, who now see him through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
There is only this difference: the Son will come in the "form of a servant" <note>The human nature of Christ; Philippians 2:7</note> in such a way that not only the good may see that same form, but also the wicked, just as it is written below: "And every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him." <note>Revelation 1:7</note> The Father, however, will come—that is, will appear—in such a way that none but the good alone may see the glory of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If one requires the testimony of the Scriptures to rightly believe that the Father "comes" or is "to come" in that manner: behold, it is written thus in Daniel: "And I watched until thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days took his seat."

<margin>Daniel 7</margin>
<margin>The Ancient of Days</margin>
Likewise: "And behold, that horn made war against the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days should come and give judgment to the saints of the Most High, and the time arrived, and the saints obtained the kingdom." <note>Daniel 7:21-22</note> Who can doubt that in the "Ancient of Days" who comes, the person of the Father is expressed? For concerning the person of the Son, it is written in the same place: I was watching...

->xv<-
->On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse<-

...therefore <note>original: "ergo," continuing the thought from the previous page</note> in a vision of the night, "and behold, the son of man was coming in the clouds of heaven, and he reached even to the Ancient of Days." <note>A reference to Daniel 7:13.</note> Therefore, nothing prevents us from understanding "him who was, and who is, and who is to come" as God the Father; indeed, it is very beautiful, worthy, and venerable. Thus, as there follows the mention of "the seven spirits who are in the presence of his throne" and "Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness," a glorious confession of the entire Trinity may be believed to be proclaimed. 

The Father **was**, I say—that is, he remained immutable <note>unchanging</note> in himself before he established these mutable things. And he also **is**—that is, he remains immutable while he rules these same things as they run their changing course. He is nonetheless **to come**—that is, he will appear as the immutable one when this corruptible hope of changing things has passed away. Furthermore, concerning the evil beast <note>the Antichrist</note>, who strives with the purpose of this adversary, it is written much further down: "And the beast which I saw, was, and is not." <note>Revelation 17:8</note>

<margin>2 Timothy 3</margin>
Therefore, let them receive consolation in that grace: both John himself, relegated to exile, and all those who, wishing to live piously in Christ, suffer persecution. <note>2 Timothy 3:12</note> For it shall come to pass that regarding every persecution, or the one who persecutes, one may say: "he was, and is not." But concerning him for whose sake they suffer, it is always said: "He who both was, and is, and shall never cease to be."

### And from the seven spirits who are in the presence of his throne.

<margin>Isaiah 11</margin>
"From the seven spirits," that is, from the sevenfold <term>spirit<gloss>Rupert identifies the seven spirits as the Holy Spirit, expressing himself through seven distinct gifts</gloss></term>. In saying this, he looks back to the face of the earlier scripture <note>the Old Testament</note>, where it is written: "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him." <note>Isaiah 11:2-3</note> 

And here he undoubtedly looked back opportunely to the face of that scripture, especially because he of whom the prophet spoke—the "flower that ascended from the root of Jesse," <note>original: "flos qui ascendit de radice Iesse"</note> the "lamb of God," <note>original: "agnus dei"</note> and also the "strong lion" <note>original: "leo fortis"</note>—signified both the strength and clarity of those same seven spirits resting upon him. These are seen in his seven horns, and seven eyes, and in the seven lamps burning before the throne of God, and in so many sevenfold <note>original: "septemplā," likely completing as "septemplatīs" or "septemplaciter" (sevenfold signs)</note> signs of mysteries...

->xvii<-

### On Revelation Chapter 1

...of peace. Truly he has rightly placed this person <note>referring to Jesus Christ</note> now in the last, that is, the third place, because he is about to say more about Him here, and in the following sections He is seen in various figures; He speaks much and indeed almost everything. For even the seven spirits speak in order to the individual churches—as we will consider more carefully in the proper place—and it is said through each or concerning each, "let him who has an ear, hear what the Spirit says to the churches." But this very thing that the Spirit speaks, He speaks in the person of Christ, who says to this or that church, or rather "write to the angel of the church." Therefore, as befits the matter, this same person is adorned and commended with praises, so that in all things He speaks in this scripture, as in the others, faith may be placed in Him without hesitation. 

**He is**, he says, **the faithful witness**; and immediately he adds, **the firstborn of the dead**. He adds still further, **and the prince of the kings of the earth**. And even more abundantly:

> Who loved us, he says, and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to his God and Father. To him be glory and power forever and ever, amen. Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn because of him, even so, amen. I am Alpha and Omega <note>original: "α & ω"; the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, signifying Christ as the beginning and the end of all things</note>, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who was, and who is, and who is to come, the Almighty.

<margin>The majesty of the broadest meanings in a few syllables.</margin>

In this way, as was already said above, the beloved apostle <note>John the Evangelist</note> confesses the universal <note>original: "catholicam"</note> faith of Jesus Christ with a gracious mouth; and at the same time, he prays for the grace of the same faith for the churches. While he does both most beautifully, he seems to do one thing in a wonderful way: namely, making the prayer for grace and peace alone. Each word proceeds with the greatest dignity; each contains, in a few syllables, the majesty of the broadest meanings.

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 1

<margin>John 18</margin> Truly a witness, which in Greek is called <term>martys <note>original: μάρτυς; the root of the English word "martyr," meaning one who bears witness even unto death</note></term>, because he was both born to testify to the truth and died for the testimony of the truth, just as he himself said to Pilate: "For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth." For the Father is indeed a witness, of whom

<margin>John 8, John 15</margin> Jesus Christ himself says: "And the Father who sent me bears witness of me." And the Holy Spirit is also a witness, of whom he said to the same disciples: "When the Paraclete <note>original: paracletus; a title for the Holy Spirit meaning Advocate or Comforter</note> comes, whom I will send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness of me." But this <note>Jesus</note> is the only person who endured death for the testimony of the truth, which is why this same Son is worthily and uniquely called "the witness."

<margin>Martyrs testify less perfectly than Christ.</margin> And indeed many witnesses of the truth suffered death because of the word of their testimony, and for this reason the Holy Church has been accustomed to call them by the Greek name "martyrs." But there is no small distance between them and Him, for which reason he is also splendidly called, with an additional title, the **faithful witness**. For what this witness testified to, he saw and heard before he came into this world; he saw and heard it first, I say, and afterward he was born into this world, and for this he came into the world: to bear witness to the truth, just as he himself said before the aforementioned governor <note>referring to Pontius Pilate</note>.

<margin>John 3</margin> Hence also John the Baptist says: "He who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies." All others have come from the earth and were born before they knew anything; they afterward received from elsewhere, from another judge, what they might say in testifying—and even this they did not do perfectly, but only in part, as one of them, the Apostle Paul, says:

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part." Therefore, he alone is that **faithful witness**—that is, one of such a kind that, before he came here to testify, he had seen and heard the matter. He is so certain that he knew and prophesied not just in part, but the whole perfectly. Add to this that having died for that same testimony of the truth, he conquered death itself and rose from the dead, which other witnesses before him did not do. For this is what is said next:

## The Firstborn of the Dead.

That is, the first of those rising from the dead. For the resurrection <gloss>indeed</gloss>

# On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse

For us there will be a regeneration, because while being born now generates us for corruption, then, by rising again, we will be regenerated for incorruption. Hence the Lord says of the regeneration:
<margin>Matthew 19</margin>
"When the Son of Man shall sit on the seat of his majesty." He said "in the regeneration" instead of saying "in the universal resurrection." In that regeneration of the dead, this witness is without doubt the **firstborn**, because he rose before all of them, namely, never to die again. Truly, no one before him
<margin>Romans 6</margin>
rose in such a way as to never die again. But he also granted this to other witnesses—of whom the first was Abel the Just—and he brought it about that they too may rise and die no more. It is a very beautiful and splendid expression to call the first one rising the **firstborn of the dead**. Indeed, delighted by this splendor, we say that in such a "birth," the blessed souls of the apostles stood as mothers, since they grieved with maternal affection for the dying Lord Jesus Christ until he should rise. For this reason, he used a similar comparison to them or for their sake:
<margin>John 16</margin>
"A woman, when she is giving birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has brought forth the child, she no longer remembers the anguish for joy, because a human being is born into the world." At last, this witness, having been thus regenerated to immortality and incorruption,

### Who loved us, and washed us from our sins in his blood.

<margin>A beautiful order of speech</margin> What was greatest in the work of the "faithful witness," he had delayed for a little while by first saying: "Who is the faithful witness," and immediately adding, "the firstborn of the dead." But now, with a grateful discourse, he repeats it more beautifully and splendidly by saying: *Who loved us, and washed us from our sins in his blood.* Let us linger for a little while in this sweetest honeycomb of thanksgiving, and let us suck the word that is sweet to our throats, <margin>Psalms 19 and 118 <note>Rupert refers to the Vulgate numbering; modern Psalms 19:10 and 119:103</note></margin> more than honey and the honeycomb to our mouth. *Who loved us,* he says. For this reason, Paul the Apostle says to the Ephesians: <margin>Ephesians 1</margin> "As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and spotless in his sight in love. Who predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the purpose..."

<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 1</header>

<margin>Why does Christ come with clouds?</margin> He will come with clouds. Is it so that He might be hidden or concealed by the clouds? Certainly not. For then He who previously came in secret will come openly; and as it is written here, every eye shall see Him. Why then will He come with clouds?

<margin>Isaiah 26</margin> Let us consult another scripture. The prophet Isaiah, having first spoken about the wicked man with a question, saying: "And he shall not see the glory of the Lord," immediately added through a kind of concession: "Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see," and straightaway added: "Let them see and be ashamed, the jealous of the people, and let fire devour your enemies." <note>original: "Et non videbit gloriam domini... Videant & confundantur zelantes populi." Rupert is harmonizing the idea that the wicked will see Christ's coming but remain excluded from the vision of His divine glory.</note> As if he had uselessly conceded "let your hand be exalted and let them not see," he corrected himself, saying, "let them see and be ashamed." Therefore, in a certain way they will not see, and in another way the wicked also will see Him coming. So that the wicked might not see the glory of the Lord, He will come with clouds; but so that the wicked who see might be put to shame, every eye shall see Him. The clouds, indeed, with which He will come, will hide His glory so that the wicked may not see it; but they will not hide the power of His majesty from every eye. For what kind of clouds will those be then? Not at all like the ones we often see now, dropping rain and cooling the earth, but stormy clouds, breathing fire, hurling lightning.

<margin>Psalm 49</margin> For "fire shall burn in His sight, and a mighty storm round about Him." <note>original: "ignis in conspectu eius ardebit, & in conspectu eius tempestas valida." From Psalm 50:3 (Psalm 49 in the Vulgate).</note>

<margin>2 Thessalonians 1</margin> Striving to express the vehemence of such clouds—of burning clouds—Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, says: "If indeed it is righteous in the sight of God to repay with tribulation those who trouble you, and to give you who are troubled rest with us, in the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of His power, in a flame of fire, giving vengeance to those who did not know God," etc. <note>original: "in flamma ignis, dantis vindictam his qui non nouerunt deum." From 2 Thessalonians 1:6-8.</note> Every eye shall see this; the wicked shall see so that they may be put to shame, but they shall not see the glory of the Lord, for His hand shall be exalted so that they do not see it. Those clouds drawn over them will hide from the wicked the radiance of His body—or rather His "glorious body"—to which,

<margin>Philippians 3</margin> as the Apostle says, our lowly body shall be reformed and conformed <note>original: "humilitatis corpus reformatum configurabit." From Philippians 3:21, describing the transformation of the faithful at the resurrection.</note>—but they will not hide the Son of Man Himself. Every eye shall see Him, and the wicked who see shall be put to shame; however, His glory...

# On the Apocalypse, Chapter 1

...they will see. <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on how different groups will witness the Second Coming.</note> Those who are to be with the Lord forever, as the <margin>1 Thessalonians 4</margin> apostle says, will be snatched up to meet the Lord in the clouds. **And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him.**

<margin>John, the imitator of Zechariah</margin> The apostle and evangelist—who drew wisdom from the very chest of the Lord <note>A reference to the Beloved Disciple leaning against Jesus at the Last Supper (John 13:23-25).</note> and was a Hebrew among Hebrews whom the Savior loved most dearly—said this by drawing on the testimony <margin>Zechariah 12</margin> of an older prophet. And again another scripture says: 'They shall look on him whom they have pierced.'**" <margin>Zechariah 12</margin> However, what he omitted there—namely the following part, "and they shall mourn for him with a mourning as if for an only-begotten son"—he has added here in this way: **"And all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him."** What he says here as "all the tribes of the earth" is nonetheless found in the same prophet, where it is written immediately: "And the land shall mourn, family by family apart. The families of the house of David apart, and their women (or wives) apart. <margin><insert>note</insert></margin> The families of the house of Nathan apart, and their women apart. # Commentary of Rupert, Book 1
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 1</header>

...concluding also with "amen," so that everyone who hears may wake up to believe. What follows is:

> I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.

<margin>
Against the heretics who deny the divinity of Christ.
</margin>
Everything he has said so far regarding the person of the Son was not enough, nor was it sufficient for salvation for one believing or confessing. For what in those previous titles would offend Cerinthus, Ebion, or Arius, <note>Rupert names three famous early heretics: Cerinthus and Ebion, who viewed Jesus as merely human, and Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being inferior to the Father.</note> or any other heretical enemy of Christ’s divinity? Would they be offended by him being called a "faithful witness," or "the firstborn of the dead"—that is, that the Lord Jesus was the first to rise from the dead—or that he is "the prince of the kings of the earth," and that "he loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood," and that "he is coming with the clouds" to judge the living and the dead? Even a heretic of that sort would concede and confess such things. But that he is the same God, coequal to God the Father, remaining without beginning with the Father or in the Father—this they would not confess. Therefore, not content with having spoken those things rightly, he adds this which is the highest point, upon which the Christian faith stands as its supreme step. He feels as loftily concerning the divinity of Christ as he does of the Father, as is worthy, and speaks in his person—and evidently with a louder thunder—so that the talkative frogs <note>original: "ranæ loquaces." A common medieval metaphor for heretics, referencing the "unclean spirits like frogs" in Revelation 16:13.</note> who contradict him might be crushed.

<margin>
Alpha and Omega
</margin>
*I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.* By saying these things, or rather introducing him speaking, he makes the Son equal to the Father, of whom he had said the same above: "who is, and who was, and who is to come." What he meant and what he wishes to be understood by "Alpha and Omega," he immediately explains by saying "the beginning and the end." For these are two letters of the Greeks—the language in which he wrote this book to the churches—I say, these are the first and the last letters of that language: $\alpha$ [Alpha] and $\omega$ [Omega]. So that there may be no doubt as to what kind of beginning or end he is, or of what thing: being reminded by Alpha, which (as has been said) is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, let us look back to the start of Holy Scripture, where 
<margin>
Genesis 1
</margin>
it is written: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the ear-* <meta>Catchword: ter- [earth]</meta>

# On Revelation Chapter 1
<header>*On Revelation Chapter 1*</header>

<margin>Matthew, last chapter</margin>
...scripture: and through Omega (ω), which is the last letter, we are likewise warned to look toward the end of that same scripture in the Gospel volume: where it is written: *And behold, I am with you all days even to the consummation of the age* <note>original: "Math. vlt." refers to Matthew 28:20.</note>, so that we may truly believe and confess that he is the Alpha (α) and the beginning, in whom all things were made, and the end or consummation, by which all things are restored and perfected. Furthermore, it should also be
<margin>The mystery of the number in Alpha and Omega</margin>
known that Alpha signifies "One," while Omega signifies "eight hundred" among the Greeks. For all letters among the Greeks compose words and form numbers: and just as each letter is later in the alphabetical order, so do they denote larger numbers by their characters. As has been said, the letter Alpha signifies One, and Omega signifies eight hundred. And in this, surely, the beauty of the mystery is great and delightful: namely, that he who in the beginning was the one only-begotten or unique Son, will at the end of the ages have "sons of God" with him—not indeed begotten, but adopted—numbering as if eight hundred, that is, innumerable. These he will reward by distributing them through various mansions according to the eight beatitudes, and in rewarding them, he distributes them. Where else besides this place does the Lord God say this? Not only in his Gospel, where he says to the Jews: *I am the beginning, who also speaks to you* <note>Rupert quotes the Vulgate version of John 8:25.</note>: but also in Isaiah
<margin>John 8, Isaiah 43</margin>
the person of the Savior himself speaks: *Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none. I am the Lord, and there is no savior besides me.* <note>Isaiah 43:10-11.</note> Furthermore, when (as was said before) he comes with the clouds, when every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him—those who spoke evil against him, asking when he would die and when his name would perish <note>A reference to Psalm 41:5.</note>: those who, by piercing or transfixing him, wished to bring it about that he should not exist at all, so that his memory would be completely removed from the earth: then the Lord God will opportunely say here—then, I say, he will cry out and shout and prevail over those enemies of his, and he will say this to them: *I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end.* It is as
<margin>Psalm 40, Matthew 13, Luke 4</margin>
if he were saying: "No, I am not the 'son of the carpenter' as you reproached me, nor did I begin to be from that carpenter Joseph; nor have I perished or ceased to be, as you wished me to perish, but I am..."

### On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse

...and Thyatira, and Sardis, and Philadelphia, and Laodicea.

<margin>Why John placed the title of his name three times in Chapter 1.</margin>
Behold, now for the third time the diligent and careful author has placed the title of his name at the beginning of this work. First, when he said: *He made it known by sending through his angel to his servant John.* <note>original: "significauit mittens per angelum suum seruo suo Ioanni" from Revelation 1:1</note> Second, when he said: *John to the seven churches which are in Asia.* <note>original: "Ioannes septem ecclesijs que sunt in Asia" from Revelation 1:4</note> And now for the third time, saying: *I, John, your brother.* <note>original: "Ego Ioannes frater vester" from Revelation 1:9</note> For what reason does he, being about to speak or narrate, triple the placement of his name in this way? Was it by chance, or because he was eager to spread his name that he repeats and reiterates it?

Certainly not; rather, looking to our benefit, he fortifies and defends the very difficult revelations he is beginning to write down, lest they be despised. He does this so that the book would not be criticized for its difficulty and judged to be lacking in worthy meaning—as was to happen—or lest it be denied to belong to the one to whom it truly belongs: namely, John the apostle and evangelist, the beloved of Jesus Christ. For this rejection actually happened long after that time. 

Some, interpreting future promises with a "Jewish understanding" <note>Rupert uses the term "Jewish understanding" here to refer to "Chiliasm" or Millenarianism—the belief in a literal, physical 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth, which many medieval theologians viewed as an overly literal or "carnal" interpretation of scripture.</note>, and teaching that these promises were to be manifested physically—claiming that the saints would reign with Christ for a thousand years in physical delights on this earth—tried to assert proof for this dogma of theirs by taking evidence from this Revelation. On the other hand, others thought this book should be completely rejected from the <term>canon of scriptures</term> <note>The official list of books recognized as divinely inspired and authoritative for the Church.</note> and cast aside (as church history testifies), arguing against its individual chapters. They said that the title of the book was not true, but that John’s name had merely been placed upon someone else’s writing. Hence, they claimed it was not by John, and that this book could be seen as a "revelation" covered by a thick veil of ignorance. Among these was Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, a man of great learning and grace in the word of God.

<margin>See *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 5, chapter 8; Book 7, chapter 22; also Book 2, chapters 19 and 31.</margin>
<margin>The words of Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians.</margin>
<note>While the margin mentions Dionysius of Corinth, the text discusses Dionysius of Alexandria. Rupert is likely drawing from Eusebius’s *Church History*, which quotes both.</note>
"I," he says, "dare by no means to despise or reject the writing of this book. Rather, I judge that the things written in it exceed and stand above the measure of human learning; and there is in it a certain hidden, recondite <note>original: "recons," likely an abbreviation for *reconditus*, meaning deep or concealed.</note>, and admirable sense for all, which I also admi..."

### xxxiiii Commentary of Rupert, Book 1.

...I revere and worship, even if I do not understand: and I feel thus, that certain divine mysteries are covered in human words, not so much discerning by my own judgment, as believing by faith. <margin>Heretics hostile to this book.</margin>
By these and similar objections and responses, this book of heavenly revelations was discussed and handled; and unless the Holy Spirit, who revealed all these things, had prepared men of reasonable reverence to defend them, pigs would have trampled such great and precious pearls, and heretics would have defiled them. <note>This is an allusion to Matthew 7:6; Rupert views critics of the Apocalypse as "pigs" (porci) who cannot appreciate spiritual value.</note> What would have happened if the authority of such a great and significant name had not stood at the beginning of the discourse? <margin>Deuteronomy 17; John 8.</margin>
<margin>The humility of John.</margin>
And note how much this authority of the name itself shines through the grace of holy humility: *your brother* (he says) *and partner in the tribulation, and the kingdom, and the patience of Jesus.* <note>original: "frater vester & particeps in tribulatione..." from Revelation 1:9</note> For he could have said: "I, John, teacher and apostle, your preacher and your evangelist, that disciple whom Jesus loved, whose partners and whose brothers you have merited to be." <margin>Matthew 18</margin>

What then is the moderation or modesty of a little child? *For as long a time,* says the Apostle, *as the heir is a child...* <note>The text cuts off here at the start of a quote from Galatians 4:1.</note>

<header>On Chapter 1 of Revelation</header>

[John] preached [the Word] born from the Father's heart before all ages; and because of the testimony of Jesus Christ, by which he bore witness that He was the Word made flesh. Now, "Patmos" is interpreted as "a boiling strait" <note>original: "fretum" — Rupert uses a common medieval etymology, linking the name of the island to the Greek "pathos" or the Latin "fretum," implying a place of turbulent water or suffering.</note>: for the sea boils there more intensely because it is narrow. To him exiled there, to whom the earth was denied, heaven was opened. It is therefore an example for all the saints, that the more they are afflicted in the "strait" of this present world, the more abundantly celestial secrets are revealed to them. Having already designated his person, as well as the place and cause of his exile, he took care to indicate the time: "I was," you say, "in the spirit on the Lord's day."

For the quality of things is usually shown according to the quality of the times. <margin>Genesis 18 & 19. Genesis 3. 1 Kings 3.</margin> This is why Abraham, in the heat of his faith, saw angels at noon; and Lot, during the destruction of Sodom, in the evening; Adam in the afternoon; Solomon also, who was not to keep his wisdom, received it in the night. Thus, in this place, "the Lord’s day" is clearly understood as the faith which was already manifest in the whole world when he saw these things. <margin>How John was in the spirit.</margin> But in what way or in what spirit do we think he was? For if he was only in his own spirit, the vision would be unworthy, and much would be detracted from the seer: so that neither he could be rightly called a prophet, nor his words a prophecy, nor his visions revelations—since he would not understand them if he saw them only in his own spirit. <margin>Genesis 41.</margin> For example: Pharaoh, because he saw seven ears of grain and seven oxen—not indeed with his body, but in his spirit (for he was sleeping with the eyes of his body closed)—because he saw but did not understand, he was not a prophet. Joseph, however, because he saw not in his own spirit but in the spirit of God—that is, he understood—he was a prophet. For Pharaoh's spirit was merely shaped so that he might see; but Joseph’s mind was illuminated by the spirit of God so that he might understand. The Apostle briefly distinguishes these modes of vision when, having first said: "If I pray in a tongue, and my spirit does not pray, my mind is without fruit," <margin>1 Corinthians 14.</margin> he immediately adds: "What then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind." What he says about prayer or singing psalms should be understood in the same way regarding vision. For once images are perceived through vision...

<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 1</header>

<margin>Matthew 4.</margin>
...images: for unless understanding, which is proper to the mind, is added, no revelation, knowledge, prophecy, or doctrine occurs. But was there such blindness in John's vision that signs of things were formed in his spirit, but the understanding of those same things did not shine in his mind? Far be it from that disciple whom Jesus loved! Otherwise, how could this book be called the *Apocalypse*—which means *Revelation* <note>original: "Apocalypsis id est reuelatio"</note>? Why would it deserve to be called a prophecy, when he himself says, *Blessed is he who reads and he who hears the words of the prophecy of this book*? Therefore, when he says, *I was in the spirit*, let us understand the *Holy* Spirit. Just as in that other place, *Jesus was led into the desert by the spirit* (Matthew 4), we rightly understand it to mean the Holy Spirit.

<margin>John also was caught up to the third heaven.</margin>
<margin>Galatians 1.</margin>
Nor do we hesitate to say that what he means by *I was in the spirit* is the same as if he had said, *I was caught up even to the third heaven* <note>Rupert refers to the mystical experience described by St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 12, interpreting it as the highest form of spiritual insight.</note>. For just because the Apostle Paul alone wrote this about himself, we should not think that no other saint besides him was caught up there. It is much like what he says elsewhere: *the gospel which was preached by me is not according to man; for I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through the revelation of Jesus Christ* (Galatians 1). We should not perceive this to mean that no other saint learned the truth of Christ through God's revelation, or that everyone except Paul received it from men. It should by no means be thought that by saying these things, Paul was setting himself above the blessed John or the other apostles—or even the prophets—who surely all learned not from or through man, but through the revelation of God or of Jesus Christ. For all of them, this experience was to be caught up to the "third heaven," which is to say, to see celestial things through the <term>intellectual eye</term> <note>In medieval theology, "intellectual" sight refers to the mind's direct perception of spiritual truth, higher than physical sight or mental imagination.</note>.

<margin>Three modes of visions.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 41.</margin>
<margin>2 Corinthians 12.</margin>
For there are three heavens, and three modes of visions. There is **corporal vision**, by which we perceive bodies or physical things with the power of the mind using the eyes of the body. There is **spiritual vision**, by which we see certain images while sleeping or even while thinking, but do not yet understand them; this is how Pharaoh saw the seven ears of grain and the seven oxen, as we have already said (Genesis 41). And there is **intellectual vision**, by which the mind is illuminated by the Holy Spirit so that it understands, just as Joseph understood what was signified by those same images. Are not the words contained in this book...

He distinguishes this from "corporal" (physical) and "spiritual" (imagistic) visions, noting that true revelation requires mental understanding.</summary>

To this I say: It was certainly necessary because the Gospel faith was being endangered among the Corinthians and the Galatians. It was as if pseudo-apostles were preaching in the place of the Apostle Paul, trying to lead the faithful into circumcision and Jewish rituals. They disparaged the Apostle Paul, as if in such a great matter he was not to be heard, claiming he did not know the truth of the Gospel and was not one of the "great apostles." Therefore, he asserted such things as were granted to him about himself—not to place himself above the others, but to show he was equal to the apostles—namely, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain.

xl
<header>xl Commentary of Rupert, Book 1</header>

<margin>The history regarding the occasion for writing the Gospel</margin>
...by bishops and delegations from many churches, to speak more profoundly <note>original: "altius facere sermonem," literally "to make a higher discourse"</note> concerning the divinity of Christ, which is co-eternal with the Father. This was because in the writings of the three other Evangelists—namely Matthew, Mark, and Luke—there seemed to be sufficient testimony concerning his humanity and the things he did as a man. Why was this necessary? It was because while John was in exile, heretics—namely **Marcion**, **Cerinthus**, and **Ebion**, and other "antichrists"—had broken into the Church like wolves into a sheepfold left without a shepherd. These men denied that Christ existed before Mary; they had stained the simplicity of the Gospel faith with perverse doctrine. Therefore, John "heard behind him a great voice like a trumpet" <note>A reference to Revelation 1:10.</note> because he was to be greatly urged by nearly all the bishops of Asia. It was as if he were rising for war to encounter the faithless heretics; having seized the sword of the Word of God, he was to defend the borders of the ecclesiastical faith. By this "great voice," we understand the vehement insistence of everyone by which he was to be compelled. At the same time, because the truth of the faith does not love corners <note>original: "veritas fidei non angulos amat," a common medieval proverb meaning that truth seeks the light and is not meant to be a secret or "occult" knowledge.</note> and does not desire to speak in secret, but openly to the whole world, it was fitting to signify this not by just any voice, but by a "great voice like a trumpet." "What you see," he said, "write." This is the voice of all the bishops of Asia.

<margin>John 13</margin>
<margin>The Gospel of John against Cerinthus, Ebion, Marcion, etc.</margin>
> O John, beloved of Jesus Christ, you who reclined upon his chest and drank the flowing streams of Gospel truth from that sacred fountain of the Lord's breast: because Marcion, Cerinthus, and Ebion, and other antichrists, broke into the Church during your absence and exile and stained the simplicity of the Gospel faith with perverse doctrine—denying that Christ existed before Mary—and since the other Evangelists (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) have established sufficient testimony in their writings regarding his humanity: you, write with your Gospel pen what you see, what you know, and what you hold concerning the antiquity of his divinity. By the revealed light of truth, dispel all the darkness of the heretics. And send it to the seven churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Send to the seven churches...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on why the Apostle John wrote his Gospel and the Apocalypse. xli
# On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse

[...to the seven churche]s, that is, hand it over to the universal Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, ordered and confirmed by the sevenfold Holy Spirit. For indeed, in Asia Minor there are seven metropolitan cities, of which Ephesus is the head. Nevertheless, because he speaks to the seven churches of Asia, he surely speaks to the whole Church: which, although it is one, is encompassed by the number seven, by which "totality" <note>original: "universitas"</note> is often accustomed to be designated. Specifically, he directs his prophecy to those seven churches of Asia over which divine grace placed him as a preacher; but nonetheless, he desires to hand these things over to the universal Church, which he knows were revealed to him for the common progress of all, since he says without exception: *Blessed is he who reads and hears the words of this prophecy.* It follows.

*And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me.*

As the bishops of Asia were asking John, as was said above, to speak more profoundly <note>original: "altius facere sermonem," meaning to provide a more "high" or theological discourse compared to the earlier Gospels</note> concerning the divinity of Christ co-eternal with the Father, what does he do? Truly, he turned toward prayer and fasting <note>original: "orationem ieiuniumque"</note>: responding that he would not do otherwise unless, after a fast was proclaimed, everyone prayed together to the Lord so that he himself might be able to write things worthy of Him. This he did—or rather, since he was seeing these visions, this is what he was about to do. Rightly, therefore, he says, *“and I turned,”* to see the voice that was speaking with me. For he who was asked to ascend, in a certain way, into heaven and to demonstrate to men the divinity hidden there, took refuge in prayer and fasting. Being anxious and suspicious of his own fragility, he is rightly said to "turn" or to "have turned," so that he might see the voice which speaks with him. That is, so that he might obtain by the gift of heavenly grace what he is asked to utter; and so that he himself might first deserve to see or know what he is to show or write down for others.

<margin>A *podere* is a garm[ent]</margin>
*And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to the feet <term>podere: a long priestly garment, from the Greek "podērēs," meaning reaching the feet</term>, and girded about the chest with a golden sash.*

### **But his head and his hair were white like white wool, and like snow.**

<margin>His head and hair are white with divinity.</margin>

This was said of the Son of Man, the Son of God. He [John] saw such a one in the spirit, who, having also been struck in the body <note>This likely refers to John's physical sufferings or exile on Patmos.</note> or physically driven, was to write of such a one for the reason already stated. # On Apocalypse Chapter I. [Page] xlv

...[born of] Mary. But he, providing for himself—or rather, looking out for his Church, whose faith was in peril—already showed to this John his head, white with antiquity. This head was begotten without time, born of the Father before the ages, existing not only before Mary or before Abraham, but even before the Day Star <note>original: *Luciferum*. In this context, it refers to the "light-bearer" or the morning star, symbolizing the first light of creation rather than the fallen angel.</note>.

<margin>The hairs are the divine words.</margin>
What, then, are the hairs, so white with antiquity like white wool and like snow? They are hair because they proceed from the head and are many: for the words of God are many, which proceed from or through the one Word <note>The "Word" (Logos) refers to Christ himself, the eternal reason of God, as described in the Gospel of John.</note> who was in the beginning. For God the Word, in his own substance, is one Word and one Head; however, the many words which God spoke to holy men or prophets are like the many hairs of a single head. Why is this hair compared to wool? Just as a garment is made by weaving wool that has been spun, so from these hairs—that is, the manifold words of God poured into the tongue and voice of the prophets—Holy Scripture was woven together through writing. And why not just any wool, but as he says, "white" wool—or as it is written in Daniel, "pure wool"?

<margin>Psalm 11. Psalm 18.</margin>
Clearly because those words are holy and pure; they are right and beyond reproach. Hence that saying: *The words of the Lord are pure words.* <note>original: *Eloquia domini eloquia casta*. From Psalm 12:6 in modern numbering.</note> Also: *The law of the Lord is spotless* <margin>Psalm 18.</margin> or irreproachable, *converting souls.* Converting souls, I say, and washing them from all sins. For this reason he added, "and like snow." For snow sometimes signifies cleansing. 

<margin>Psalm 50. Isaiah 1.</margin>
Thus the prophet says in the Psalm: *You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.* <margin>Psalm 50.</margin> Also in the prophet: *Even if your sins be like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow.* <margin>Isaiah 1.</margin> Finally, it should be known that whoever rises before this white head and shows reverence to his white hair—that is, whoever worthily receives his words—by the very fact that he receives and meditates on his words, he himself also grows white <note>Meaning he becomes spiritually pure and wise.</note> and deserves to be called an "elder." 

<margin>Wisdom 4.</margin>
As Wisdom shows when it says: *Venerable old age is not that which is long-lived, nor is it measured by the number of years.* Rather, a man's gray hair is his understanding, and the age of old age is an unstained life. It follows.

<margin>John 1.</margin>

<margin>Deuteronomy 4. 1 Thessalonians 5. Matthew 5.</margin>

<margin>One light is illuminating, the other is illuminated.</margin>
and here he is seen in the midst of the golden lampstands. **On Chapter 1 of the Apocalypse**

<margin>Luke, final chapter.</margin>
...as if in a burning furnace. ## And his voice was like the voice of many waters.

<margin>Luke 24. The voice of many waters, i.e., of many prophets.</margin>
By the name of "waters," the divine scriptures are usually understood, a point which is surely more than proven by the scriptures themselves. It is established, however, that whatever that Son of Man—who has such a white head and feet like fine brass—spoke during his passions or his temptations, or speaks even now, harmonizes with the holy scriptures and agrees with their voices and meanings. Indeed, his life and death, his resurrection and ascension also, proceeded in such a way so that the scriptures might be fulfilled. Therefore, "his voice was like the voice of many waters"—that is, his teaching or his entire work is the truth and the fulfillment of the scriptures, which are many: namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. *For it is necessary,* he says, *that all things be fulfilled which were written in the Law, and the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me.* <note>Luke 24:44</note> Alternatively: "His voice was like the voice of many waters," meaning like the voice of many peoples, according to what the Psalmist says in Christ's own person: *I will confess to you among the peoples, and I will sing a psalm to you among the nations.* <note>Psalm 57:9</note> Finally, many peoples today harmonize with his voice through the words of the scriptures which are brought forth in his person; these peoples, as is well known, are usually signified by the name of "waters."

### And his face was like the sun shining in its strength.

<margin>Isaiah 30, 1 John 3.</margin>
His "face"—his presence—will shine like the sun, because he truly is the sun; and he will shine "in his strength," that is, in his majesty and divinity. Then that prophecy of Isaiah will be fulfilled: *And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of their blow.* <note>Isaiah 30:26</note> Who is this who will then shine like the sun without the variations of waxing and waning <note>original: "crementi & decrementi," referring to the phases of the moon</note> which now vary in this world, if not the Church, which will then be like her Sun, her God? *We know,* says that same John, *that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.* <note>1 John 3:2</note> And how great will that light of the sun itself be? *Like the light of seven days,* he says. This is to say: as much brightness as God the Word possessed when all things were made in six days and all things were completed through him on the seventh day—of that much brightness will he then be in his flesh in the presence of God the Father.

### On Revelation Chapter 1

Following the authority of those who came before us, we stated above that an angel appeared to this John in the form of Christ, because of what was said at the very beginning: *and he signified it, sending by his angel to his servant John.* <note>original: "et fignificauit mittens per angelum fuum feruo fuo Ioanni" — Revelation 1:1.</note> <margin>A lengthy inquiry regarding John’s angel</margin> But it can now be asked why the one who appeared declared himself to be Christ with such a great and manifest description: **I am, he said, the first and the last, and the living one, etc.** Add to this the fact that when John fell at his feet as if dead, he was not forbidden from falling, nor was he corrected for having fallen before his feet. I am your fellow servant, and of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book; worship God.** <note>Revelation 22:8–9. The one who was showing the visions was clearly an angel; however, the one who was shown is called the "Son of Man." <term>Son of Man</term> <note>A title Jesus frequently used for himself, signifying both his humanity and his role as the divine judge mentioned in the Book of Daniel.</note> Accordingly, regarding the one whose voice he heard in this place—like a trumpet saying: *Write what you see*—we must concede that this was the angel showing these things, of whom it was said: **And he signified it, sending by his angel.** But regarding the one whom he saw, it is permitted to understand that it was the one he professed himself to be: namely, the "first and the last," which is to say, Christ the Son of God.

# On Revelation, Chapter 1, Verse 11

<margin>
A lengthy inquiry regarding John’s angel

Following the authority of those who came before us, we stated above that an <term>angel</term> <note>In this context, Rupert explores the "Angel of the Lord," a figure in scripture that often speaks as God himself.</note> appeared to this John in the form of Christ, because of what was said at the very beginning: *and he signified it, sending by his angel to his servant John.* <note>Revelation 1:1.</note> But the question can now be asked: why did the one who appeared profess himself to be Christ with such a great and manifest description? The one who was showing things was clearly an angel; however, the one who was shown is called the **Son of Man.** 

Accordingly, it must be granted that the one whose voice he heard in this place—like a trumpet saying: *What you see, write*—was the angel who was showing these things, of whom it was also said: *And he signified it, sending by his angel.* But the one whom he actually saw, we may understand to be the one he professed himself to be: namely, the **first and the last,** which is to say, Christ the Son of God.

### And I have the keys of death and of hell.

That is, the power of forgiving sins. For by forgiving sins, I close off death to those who believe in me, and I block hell. Alternatively, "of death and of hell" refers to a double death: namely of the soul and of the body. For by the name of "death," that which is commonly witnessed—the dissolution of the body—is rightly signified; while by "hell," the death of the soul, which is eternal, is signified. He himself has the keys—that is, the power—over both deaths, <margin>1 Samuel 2.</margin> just as the prophetess Hannah says in her Song: *The Lord kills and brings to life; he leads down to the grave and brings back.* <note>1 Samuel 2:6. In the Latin Vulgate, "grave" is *inferos* (the underworld/hell).</note>

### Write therefore the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which must be done hereafter.

This expression or word in the imperative mood, by which he says "write," is a bestowing of a gift and grace, as if he were saying: "Receive the ability and the authority to write." Hence this blessed John is truly blessed and to be honored; he who grew and was increased among the twelve apostles in the same way that <margin>The prerogative of John above the gifts of the other apostles.</margin> the blessed Joseph—"the increasing son" <note>Rupert plays on the etymology of Joseph's name, which means "to add" or "increase" (Genesis 49:22).</note>—grew among the twelve patriarchs. For just as Joseph received double portions, his father saying: *I will give to you one portion beyond your brothers...* <note>Genesis 48:22.</note>
