[...your brothers], <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion of the "portion" given to John.</note> meaning Shechem or Sichem, which in the Gospel is called Sychar <note>Sychar is the town in Samaria mentioned in John 4:5; Rupert is linking this to the "extra portion" Jacob gave to Joseph in Genesis 48:22.</note>. Just so, this beloved disciple, set apart from his other brother apostles, received one excellent portion by the gift of his loving Lord Jesus. This was so that he, who was already an apostle, might also become an evangelist and write such a divine Gospel, and furthermore, that he might hand down such a great and marvelous revelation to the Scriptures. "Write, therefore," He says, "the things you have seen"—namely, those things you saw while following me with the other apostles—or even "the things you have now seen" alone, so that your Gospel might be of the quality signified by my appearance or habit <note>original: "schema vel habitus," referring to the glorious appearance of Christ in the vision.</note> which you have just seen. Write also "those things which are now" to be corrected or praised in the seven churches of Asia, and "those things which must happen hereafter," namely the various labors and trials of the Church.

**The mystery** <term>mystery: original *sacramentum*, here meaning a sacred secret or symbolic truth rather than a ritual</term> **of the seven stars, which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches.**

Since He made a threefold distinction of things to be written, saying: "the things you have seen," "the things which are," and "the things which must happen hereafter," He now reveals only the middle one—that is, "the things which are." He opens the door of understanding, as it were, to one about to enter, so that the man [John] might not lack the authority to touch the consciences of those who then lived or presided over the churches. For the Son of Man could indeed have explained the rest in the same way, saying: "The mystery of the Son of Man thus clothed, thus girded, having such a head and such eyes, is this or that." But the matter did not demand it so much, nor did the necessity of the task urge it so strongly.

<margin>The authority of prelates.</margin>
For he who only teaches what the Catholic faith holds, or what it ought to hold, does not need such great protection of divine authority or will. However, that authority is necessary for those who rebuke and strike at morals—who treat or dispute regarding the hidden consciences of men or their most private lives, and write down the accounts to be read. For in the former case [teaching faith], with the testimonies of the Scriptures supporting him, even a person who is lazy in governing his own life will willingly consent to the faith. In the latter case [rebuking morals], where witnesses of the hidden conscience are lacking, even a vigorous fighter for the faith is indignant at being rebuked concerning the state of his own life, when...

He preferred to call the leaders <term>leaders: original *praesules*, referring to bishops or those in authority</term> of the churches both "angels" and "stars," even though some may be blameworthy in their own lives; and he honored all the churches with the beautiful names or significant images of "golden lampstands," even though in some of them many things are obscure. **A** soul to whom it has been granted to draw out the desired sweetness hidden within the scriptures rejoices in the Song of Songs when she says: *The king has brought me into his chambers.* And again: *The king has brought me into the wine cellar.* <note>Rupert is quoting Song of Solomon 1:4 and 2:4, interpreting the "wine cellar" as a metaphor for deep, mystical understanding of the Bible.</note> However, our own faith is like a young girl; see her standing outside, looking in as if through the tiny cracks of a closed storehouse. John's Gospel against Cerinthus and other antichrists.

**AND** to the angel of the church of Ephesus write: These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks.

Here now the seven spirits of God begin to speak, who are in the presence of the throne of God. For he who speaks is indeed the Son of Man himself, who walks in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks, who was dead and lives, who has a <term>rhomphaea</term> <note>A large, double-edged sword (from the Greek *rhomphaia*), here symbolizing the power of the Word of God to judge and discern.</note> sharp on both sides, who has eyes like a flame of fire, who has the seven spirits of God, who has the key of David, who is the beginning of the creation of God. But consider carefully, because throughout the individual chapters of his seven speeches he cries out thus: *He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.* Therefore, the seven spirits of God are speaking, while here the one Son of Man, or Son of God, is the speaker. I say they speak from that dwelling place of his, in which they dwell in all fullness bodily <note>Rupert is referencing Colossians 2:9, suggesting that the "fullness of the Godhead" dwells in Christ, including the sevenfold Spirit.</note> in the presence of the throne of God—that is, as an example for the church of God. For clearly this Son of Man is set forth for the church of God to imitate, having in himself the seven spirits of God.

Here, the spirit of **fear** speaks to the churches in the first place; in the second, the spirit of **piety**; in the third, the spirit of **knowledge**; in the fourth, the spirit of **fortitude**; in the fifth, the spirit of **counsel**; in the sixth, the spirit of **understanding**; and in the seventh, the spirit of **wisdom**. <note>Rupert is listing the "Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit" found in Isaiah 11:2–3. He correlates each gift to one of the seven churches in Revelation, suggesting a progression of spiritual growth.</note> For as the Church imitates Christ, she begins from fear and, by ascending, arrives at wisdom.

### On Revelation Chapter 2.

<margin>Proverbs 1</margin>
<margin>Isaiah 11</margin>
<margin>note</margin>
It is written: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* <note>original: "Initium sapientiae timor domini"</note> Furthermore, where the Son of God descends to instruct that church, the first is the spirit of wisdom, and the last is the spirit of fear, just as the prophet says: *And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.* <note>Rupert is citing the "Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit" from Isaiah 11:2-3, which was a cornerstone of medieval theology.</note> Therefore, with that same spirit leading the way, let him who has an ear for hearing hear what each of these spirits says to the churches, according to the character of its own dignity; and first, let us hear what the **spirit of the fear of the Lord** says. To the angel, he says, of the church of Ephesus, write.

<margin>The spirit of the fear of the Lord speaks to the Angel of Ephesus</margin>
That he who says these things to the churches is the "spirit of fear" is made more clearly manifest from what he says: *Be mindful, therefore, from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do your former works. Otherwise, I will come to you and move your lampstand out of its place, unless you do penance.* The state of those to whom it is appropriate to say these things is hinted at by the name "Ephesus," or rather the interpretation of the name. For **Ephesus** is interpreted as "a great fall," or "my will in her." <note>Medieval scholars often used etymologies (sometimes creative ones) to find deeper spiritual meanings in names. Here, Ephesus is linked to the Greek *ephesis* (desire/will) and the idea of a "fall" from initial grace.</note> Indeed, it is a great fall to have left one's first charity and to have fallen away from it. But the "will of God" is that he who has so fallen or slipped should do penance. The angel—that is, the priest <gloss>that is, the priest</gloss>—of the church of Ephesus was of this kind then, and many today are priests, or those living under priests in the church, all of whom the spirit of fear rebukes in this one angel, partly by terrifying them and partly by reviving them with praise. He begins, however, like this:

> These things says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand.

These stars are the angels of the seven churches, as was said before. From this saying, a healthy fear constrains such "stars," because they see that although these stars are in heaven, they must be held so that they do not fall to the earth. For many stars have fallen from heaven, and in them were made the princes of darkness. <note>A reference to the fall of Lucifer and the rebel angels.</note> Therefore, by saying, "he who holds the seven stars in his right hand," he simultaneously hints in a terrible way that he who thinks he stands should take care lest he fall. For he does not stand by his own power, but is contained by the right hand of the Lord. This must be feared most greatly for this reason: because he himself who holds these same stars keeps watch with vigilance, lest perhaps because of that very brightness, the "foot of pride" should come upon someone.

Clearly, these are indeed good works: to labor within the rule of the Catholic faith, and to have patience in this labor, even by disputing against perverse dogmas, whose evil fabricators are so many and so talkative that you cannot endure them—such as Marcion and Cerinthus <note>Marcion and Cerinthus were prominent early Christian heretics; Marcion rejected the Old Testament, while Cerinthus was an early Gnostic opponent of the Apostle John.</note> were at that time, and many other heretics. <margin>Judgment must not be rushed against bishops and clerics.</margin>
As with many testimonies of Holy Scripture, so too does this passage [teach] us that we ought not to rush to judgment upon the "angels" of the church—that is, the bishops—and upon any of the ecclesiastical ranks. For he did not say, "Because you have left your first charity, I am coming to you now and will move your lampstand from its place." Rather, he gave a great interval to his voice, never putting a bridle on a running sentence [of judgment], by saying first: "Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works." Only then does he add: "Otherwise"—that is, if you add contempt to the fact that I already have this against you, that you have left your first charity—"I will come to you," etc. This order of God's judgment is [shown] throughout the Scriptures, but for the sake of example, only two men are presented: namely, Saul and David.

The example of Saul, who did not repent correctly.
1 Samuel 15.

Saul was a "son of one year" <note>original: "Filius vnius erat Saul"; a literal rendering of the Vulgate’s 1 Samuel 13:1, traditionally interpreted to mean he was as innocent or humble as a one-year-old child when he began his reign.</note> when he began to reign, and for two years he reigned over Israel. Which is to say: he was humble like a boy of [one] year, and was small in his own eyes when he was made king, and for two years he reigned over [Israel] with that same humility. Whence, the Lord speaking through him, Samuel said: "Was it not when you were small in your own eyes that you were made head of the tribes of Israel?"

Were you lifted up in pride? He <note>King Saul</note> fell from this humility when, against the law, he offered a burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum"; a sacrificial animal completely consumed by fire.</note>, since he was not a priest from the lineage of Aaron, but a man from the tribe of Benjamin. Likewise, because he had fallen from humility, he spared Agag, the king of the Amalekites, and the best of the flocks of sheep, contrary to the command of the Lord. And again, the Scripture says: He offered a burnt offering to the Lord from the first of the spoils which he had brought from Amalek. Rebuked for having abandoned his first humility, he did not remember from where he had fallen, nor did he perform penance; indeed, by offering the burnt offering again, he increased his sin and repeated his presumption. He did say, "I have sinned," as if he remembered from where he had fallen, but he did not say or feel it humbly. For he added: *But now, honor me before the elders of my people, and before Israel, and return with me.* <note>1 Samuel 15:30</note>. Therefore, he wished to trade his confession by saying "I have sinned," seeking not God's honor or glory, but his own. Justly, therefore, his throne <note>original: "solium"</note> had to be moved from its place, because he did not truly repent.

But David himself was a "little one" <note>original: "parvulus"; meaning small or of low status.</note>, of whom his father
<margin>The example of David rightly repenting. 1 Kings 16; 2 Kings 6 <note>In the modern Bible, these are 1 Samuel 16 and 2 Samuel 6.</note></margin>
Jesse said to Samuel: *There remains yet a little one, and he keeps the sheep.* And even when he was already reigning, he was nonetheless humble. For of his humility it is written: *And when the ark of the Lord entered the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul, looking through a window, saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart.* But he said: *As the Lord lives, I will be made even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes.* <note>2 Samuel 6:16–22</note>. From this humility he then 
<margin>2 Kings 12 <note>Modern: 2 Samuel 12.</note></margin>
fell, by sinning with the wife of Uriah, whom he took. Wherefore the Lord said to him through the prophet: *Why then have you despised the word of the Lord, to do evil in my sight?* And immediately after: *For which reason the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me.* But he was at once mindful of where he had fallen, and that he had left his first charity <note>The "first charity" refers back to the text of Revelation 2:4-5 discussed on the previous page.</note>, and he said: *I have sinned against the Lord.* Likewise in the
<margin>Psalm 50 <note>Modern: Psalm 51, the Miserere.</note></margin>
Psalm: *For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you.* Therefore, the Lord did not come to this man as He had come to Saul, to move his throne or his lampstand <note>Rupert equates the royal throne of the Old Testament kings with the "lampstand" of the bishops in Revelation, both signifying divinely appointed authority.</note>...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz contrasts King Saul’s prideful, performative repentance with King David’s genuine humility. He argues that while both fell from grace, David’s sincere admission of guilt preserved his "lampstand" (authority), whereas Saul’s focus on his own social status led to his downfall.</summary>

He condemns them in this passage.

And the arrangement of the speech should be noted, for how artfully it is done! Before he released the harshness of the rebuke, he 
<margin>The manner of rebuking sinners.</margin>
praised the things that were praiseworthy. "I know your works," he said, "and your labor, and your patience," and so forth. And after he rebuked and held out threats, he again praised what was praiseworthy: "Because," he says, "you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate." In this way, he coated the bitterness of the rebuke with the sweetness of praise, so that he might not offend or terrify the listener too much. He spoke in this same way with the Samaritan woman; before he said, "For you have had 
<margin>John 4</margin>
five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband," he first said in praise: "You have spoken well, 'I have no husband'." <note>John 4:17-18</note>. And

--- Page 110 ---
<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation, specifically his analysis of the Letter to the Church at Ephesus. After discussing the rebuke of the Nicolaitans on the previous page, Rupert now examines the pedagogical method used by Christ—praising before correcting—and the significance of the "sevenfold" Church.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book II</header>

After he <note>Referring to Christ in the Gospel of John 4:18</note> expressed to her that she had had so many husbands, he praised her again, saying: *In this, you have spoken the truth.* This is a great and worthy model of instruction from the Spirit of God: to indeed rebuke those things which require correction, but in the midst of rebuking, to offer praise both before and after for whatever was well said or done by the same person who is being rebuked in other matters. This is done so that, as far as possible, the person may remain well-disposed and not flee, confused or terrified, as a sinner's soul often cannot bear to listen. Likewise, it should be noted that nothing has more power over an intelligent mind than what follows any rebuke or invective.

<margin><unclear>The utterance of the Spirit</unclear></margin>
> **He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.** <gloss><unclear>one who has a heartfelt heart, not merely a physical one, for this is how we understand it</unclear></gloss>

<margin>Matthew 13.</margin>
For this kind of expression is like a most powerful shout, reaching all the way to the inner ear of the heart. Hence the Evangelist says: *Jesus, saying these things, cried out: **He who has ears to hear, let him hear.*** <note>Rupert links the phrasing in Revelation to Jesus' frequent exhortation in the Gospels.</note> By such a proclamation, he powerfully refutes the negligent soul, showing a person to be exceedingly deaf—even if they possess open physical ears—if they do not hear the force of such a great warning within, or if they do not feel the necessity of such a great judgment in their inner being. Clearly, he does not say what the Spirit says to the church of Ephesus, but what the Spirit says to the **churches**. 
<margin>What is said to one, is said to all churches</margin>
It must be understood that what he writes to each individual, he says to all the churches. Indeed, in all churches there are those who may hear worthily: those to whom things of fear ought to be said, those for whom things of piety are meant, and those for whom things of **knowledge**, **fortitude**, **counsel**, **understanding**, and **wisdom** are intended. <note>Rupert is listing the "Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit" found in Isaiah 11:2-3.</note> For this reason, seven churches are written to, and it is called the "sevenfold church," because whoever is in the church stands in one of these levels of grace. 
<margin>Refrain verses.</margin>
Therefore, this verse is pronounced to each individual church as a kind of refrain <term>refrain: Rupert uses the term "intercalary," referring to lines repeated at intervals in a poem or song</term> regarding the individual Spirits of God: *he who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.* To this is added another verse, which varies in each of these utterances of the Spirit according to the quality of the well-deserved rewards.

<summary>Rupert explains that Christ corrects through a balance of praise and rebuke to keep the soul receptive, and argues that the "seven churches" represent the entire Church categorized by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.</summary>

## To the one who conquers <gloss>to the one who is to conquer</gloss> I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.

<margin>Genesis 3.</margin>
<margin>Christ is the tree of life. John 6.</margin>
In this stage—that is, in the spirit of fear <note>Rupert identifies the stages of the seven churches with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit from Isaiah 11:2; here, Ephesus corresponds to the "Spirit of the Fear of the Lord."</note>—to "conquer" means to yield to the one who rebukes, to perform penance, and to do one's first works. Furthermore, because the first humans did not yield to the God who rebuked them—but rather increased their sin by defending it with a proud defense—the tree of life, which God had planted in the middle of paradise, was closed off to them. For the Lord God said: *Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, therefore, lest perhaps he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever,* <note>original: "ne forte mittat manum suam, & sumat etiã de ligno vitæ..."</note> the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight <note>The Latin "paradisus voluptatis" is the Vulgate's term for the Garden of Eden.</note>, and placed before paradise the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way to the tree of life. What was therefore closed to the first man who did not perform penance is beautifully promised again to this one who does perform penance: that he may eat from the tree of life which is, he says, *in the paradise of my God*, and that he may live forever once he has eaten from it. He said "of my God" according to the nature of our flesh which he assumed. For according to the nature of his own divinity, it could have been said: "which is in the paradise of my Father." He defined both in the Gospel, saying to his brothers, his apostles: *I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.* But surely, in order for us to rise and live forever, must we eat from that physical tree? Certainly not; rather, *whoever eats*, he says, *my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.* For Christ is the tree of life, by whose vision in the heavenly paradise, and by whose body in the present Church, souls are refreshed. That physical tree of life would not have brought back to life a man already dead by the death of the soul—that is, by sin—but it would have made the flesh live forever, which would have been a most unhappy state. Indeed, if a man dead in soul were to live forever in body, he would never be restored in eternity, and he would be eternally miserable, just as the demons are. This...

The spirit of piety is needed in tribulations.
Smyrna <note>original Greek: σμυρνα</note>

After the spirit of fear, moving upward, is the spirit of piety: and that spirit undoubtedly speaks here, suggesting how to endure persecution—a cause or intention with which the name of the church certainly agrees. For Smyrna is translated as "myrrh," which signifies the mortification of the flesh <note>The Latin *mortificatio* refers to "dying to the world" or the subduing of physical desires, often through suffering or discipline.</note>. Most truly, those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice have the greatest need for the spirit of piety, so that they may be pious in their sufferings and gentle in insults or reproaches, not returning evil for evil, or curse for curse, but on the contrary, giving a blessing. Indeed, in the meantime, they are refreshed by their own tears, sighing for eternal life: in the hope of which they suffer, and for the delay of which they weep, just as each of them speaks in the psalm:

<margin>Psalm 41.</margin>
> My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily: where is your God? <note>original: "Fuerunt mihi lachrymę meæ panes..." from Psalm 42:3 in modern numbering.</note>

And from what greater principle ought the spirit of piety to begin its words, intending to comfort those in tribulation? For it says: "These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives." And it places before the eyes of the one in tribulation the First and the Last, who was dead and lives, so that he may not wonder at the heat of the trial which happens for his testing, as if something new were occurring. It is as if this spirit says to the very one it wishes to comfort: "You, cast down from whatever temporal height, because of jus-" <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "justice" (iustitiam).</note>

He emphasizes that Christ, who died and rose, serves as the ultimate comfort for those suffering for their faith.</summary>

<margin>Job 1.</margin>

The devil hopes that, tossed about amidst the storms of such injuries, you might fall and, if possible, be swallowed up after losing your faith. # On Chapter 2 of the Apocalypse

<margin>Whom the daughters of Midian represent.</margin>
Those who are weak and overflowing with vices, possessing no manly strength for the constancy of life, become notable in the church under the Christian name once they have received honors, even though they are obscure in their character. This is the counsel or suggestion of **Balaam**—that is, of all those who, following his way, love the "rewards of iniquity." <note>A reference to 2 Peter 2:15. Rupert is comparing contemporary priests who take bribes to the biblical Balaam who was hired to curse Israel.</note> For they do not promote the "sons" of the church for their virtues, but rather the "daughters"—that is, weak and vicious souls—to ecclesiastical honors in exchange for gifts <note>Rupert uses "daughters" allegorically to refer to men who lack moral discipline and "sons" to refer to those with spiritual strength.</note>. Do those who are thus promoted not hold the **doctrine of the Nicolaitans**? 

<margin>The doctrine of the Nicolaitans.</margin>
For **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian writer. He defended the deacon Nicolaus against charges of heresy, though Rupert here repeats the common medieval tradition that the Nicolaitans practiced sexual permissiveness.</note> reports that when **Nicolaus** was rebuked for his jealousy regarding his most beautiful wife, he replied that anyone who wished might take her as a wife; and he taught the unfaithful that the apostles permitted a promiscuous and communal sharing of women.

Is this not close to that doctrine, by which these men, being unable to have a legitimate marriage—as it is forbidden by ecclesiastical laws—nevertheless remain incontinent? Indeed, they rush into something even worse: they imitate marriages whenever they wish, and because they have no "lawful bed" <note>Meaning a marriage recognized by the Church.</note> as they wander about in this way, do they really believe they have broken no bond of marriage? Moreover, they commit fornication with these women and are initiated into the rites of **Baal-Peor** <note>original: "Beelphegor," a pagan deity whose worship involved sexual rituals (Numbers 25). Rupert uses this to describe clerics living in sin.</note>—namely, all those who, following the example of such men, become bolder in committing incest or adultery.

<margin>
Fornicating clerics are similar to the Nicolaitans. 1 Chronicles 15; Ezekiel 44; Numbers 22.
</margin>
<margin>
The murmuring of the people is like the speaking of the donkey.
</margin>
And while it was a miracle then that the Lord opened the mouth of the mute beast of burden, and the animal, speaking with a human voice, rebuked the foolishness of the prophet who gave such counsel; yet even now something very similar occurs when the common crowd convicts and rebukes the rulers of the church with their shouts, because such a pestilence—such a great stain on holy orders—has occurred because of the rulers' own greed.

# On Apocalypse Chapter 2.
### 84

<margin>
Progress in works from fear to charity. 1 John 4.
</margin>

In his usual manner, he first praises what is worthy of praise, and later mentions what is blameworthy with fatherly correction. "I know," he says, "your works," and this I know and approve, because you have progressed from good things to better. For this is what he says when repeating: **and your latter works are more than the former.** For example: his latter works are more numerous or better than the former when he, who began a good work out of fear, reaches charity <note>In medieval theology, *charitas* (charity) is the highest form of love—a selfless, divine love for God and neighbor.</note>, which, when perfect, casts out fear. For he seems to imply this when, having first said, "I know your works," he immediately added, **and faith and charity.** For the beginning of good works is the fear of God which is conceived through faith; but the perfection is charity, which excludes servile fear. And however great the works of fear may be—which are earlier in time or order—without doubt the works of charity are latter in time, yet greater in dignity and merit. Therefore, in his own person, this "angel" of Thyatira <note>The "angel" refers to the bishop or leader of the local church.</note> is honored with great testimony from the supreme Judge because, according to the very name of Thyatira—which is translated as "an offering" <note>original: "hostiam." Medieval commentators often used etymologies to explain spiritual truths; here, Thyatira is linked to the Greek *thyein*, to sacrifice.</note>—he presented himself to God as a living sacrifice through faith and charity.

**But I have** (he says) **against you, that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols.**

<margin>
Jezebel serves as a type of heretics.
</margin>

<margin>
Jezebel was the first to shed blood.
</margin>

It is as if he says: In your own work you are indeed faithful and praiseworthy; but in this you are blameworthy: that, <note>The original Latin uses the abbreviation "quod" here.</note> being content with your own salvation, you do not refute with a worthy attack the heretical treachery which destroys others. For the name Jezebel, which signifies "a flow of blood," <note>original: "fluxum sanguinis." This is a traditional medieval etymological interpretation of the Hebrew name Jezebel.</note> suits heretics. And specifically, it is proven that there was a woman in the aforementioned church teaching the stated crimes, who was a figure for the whole "Jezebel" <note>Meaning the spirit of heresy or false teaching.</note> throughout the world. For the one Jezebel, wife of Ahab king of Israel, prefigured all heretical treachery in both name and deed: because both her name is interpreted (as already said) as a flow of blood, and she herself was the first to persecute and kill the prophets of the Lord. For before her, no one is read to have killed prophets.

<summary>Rupert explains that the leader of Thyatira is praised for growing from fear-based faith into perfect charity, but is rebuked for tolerating a "Jezebel" figure who represents the blood-stained path of heresy.</summary>

lxxxix
### On Revelation Chapter 2

<margin>The punishment of Jezebel awaits all heretics.</margin>
...the son of Ahaziah <note>original: "Ochoziæ." This refers to the rescue of Joash by his aunt Jehosheba from the massacre of the royal family (2 Kings 11:2).</note> was stolen by the sister of that same Ahaziah from the midst of the king’s sons when they were being killed. It is clear, therefore, that the universal punishment decreed for this woman—or rather, for all heretical teaching—is decreed following the example of that historical Jezebel, so that the punishment might be just and similar for her who made herself similar in guilt. It would be too long to dwell on each individual part according to the prescribed similarity: how every soul that is a teacher of heretical doctrine is cast into a bed for her husband—or rather, her adulterer, the devil—and in what kind of tribulation those who commit adultery with her (that is, those who delight in imitating her) shall find themselves; how her children are "killed with death," that is, killed in such a way that they are always trapped in death, tormented in both body and soul. Let us proceed with the rest.

> **"And all the churches shall know," he says, "that I am he who searches the hearts and kidneys <term>renes</term> <note>original: "renes" — In biblical physiology, the kidneys (often translated as "reins") were considered the seat of emotions and secret desires, while the heart was the seat of the will and intellect.</note>, and I will give to each of you according to your works."**

<margin>Men perform penance in different ways.</margin>
Lest we stray too far seeking why he says here, "Because I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts," let us hold in memory the condition he placed among these threats, saying: "unless they do penance for their works." For because there are some who do penance to obtain God’s eternal grace, others who do it to maintain earthly happiness, and others who are entirely unrepentant, it was necessary for the Judge—who declares he will return to each according to his works—to show how he can know the quality or merit of any penitent or impenitent person's work. And "all the churches shall know this," he says, namely in the future when it is repaid to each according to his works. For now, few know and discern how fitting rewards or punishments are repaid to individuals in the things they sometimes suffer in the present by God's judgment.

<margin>God’s differing retribution: Ahab (3 Kings 22) and David.</margin>
For example, the often-mentioned Ahab indeed performed penance, but his entire penance was not in his heart, but around his "kidneys." <note>Rupert suggests Ahab's repentance was motivated by physical fear rather than a spiritual change of heart.</note> For by repenting he did not care or fear lest he be an outsider to the kingdom of God, but only this: lest he be deprived of his own earthly kingdom. In contrast, David, who killed Uriah, per[formed penance]...

<summary>Rupert explains that God judges the internal motivations of repentance, distinguishing between those who fear losing earthly status (like King Ahab) and those who truly seek God's grace (like David).</summary>

Moreover, the "depth of Satan" which he now strikes down is that pride of his by which he strove to be like the Most High, by demanding that sacrifices be made to him in idols—since it is owed to the Most High alone that sacrifice be offered to Him.

<summary>Rupert of Deutz distinguishes between sincere and false repentance using the historical examples of David, Ahab, and Joram, explaining that God searches the "kidneys" (the seat of hidden desires). He then identifies the "depth of Satan" as the prideful desire to receive the worship and sacrifices due only to God.</summary>

**To him who overcomes and keeps my works until the end, I will give him power over the nations, and he shall rule them with a rod of iron, and they shall be shattered like a potter's vessel.**

<margin>The conqueror of human passions.</margin>
At this level, "to overcome" is to conquer all the passions that make a person weak: to drive out and put to flight joy, fear, hope, and sorrow from the soul. That is, not to rejoice in the world, not to fear the world, not to hope for worldly things, and not to grieve for personal matters. ## CHAPTER III.

<margin>The Spirit of Counsel</margin>
**And write to the angel of the church of Sardis: These things says He who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars. I know your works, that you have a name that you are alive, and you are dead.**

<margin>Where hidden sins are discussed.</margin>
The spirit of counsel—which follows upward after the spirit of strength <note>original: "spiritum fortitudinis"; Rupert is referencing the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit from Isaiah 11:2</note>—speaks here in the person of the Son of God according to its own order. And to whom is it more fitting for this spirit to speak than to him who has a name that he is alive and yet is dead? For in secret cases we are accustomed to use counsel. Now, the work of him who has a name that he lives and yet is dead is secret and hidden. For anyone whose sin is public or known does not have a "name" here that he is alive; indeed, if he previously held a reputation for life or holiness, once his "dead works" became clear, he has already lost that reputation or name, and it is spread abroad that he is dead. 

Therefore, to this man who, although he was dead, has a name that he lived—that is, one whose sin or work was not so public that it created a scandal in the church by a bad example, but who while doing evil inwardly, maintained a good reputation outwardly where it was necessary for him to preach by virtue of his office—the Son of God rightly ought to use the spirit of counsel. That is, he does not proclaim the nature or name of that death-bearing work by a public description, following the gospel rule which he himself prescribed:
<margin>Matthew 18</margin>
"If," he says, "your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone," etc.

<margin>What this hidden sin was.</margin>
It is nonetheless allowed to be conjectured that the "death" of this dead man of whom he speaks was a sin of the flesh. For he says later: "But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments; they shall walk with me in white." And in truth, it sometimes happens that an "angel"—that is, a priest or a bishop—who is a man of good reputation, secretly commits a sin of the flesh; and by doing this, he is dead while under the name of one living. Now let us follow the order. "Write," he says, "to the angel of the church of Sardis."

The name of Sardis, being that of a precious stone <note>original: "Sardis lapidis... preciosi"; the sardius or carnelian stone was often associated with the blood of martyrs or divine beauty in medieval lapidaries</note>, certainly suits that angel; however, the reality that is understood by the name of "stones" among the ornaments of the church does not suit him, for the reason already stated. **"These things says He who has the seven spirits of God."** In the other letters, He begins in such a way that the opening reflects the nature of the case He is about to address; thus the listener is made attentive, teachable, or well-disposed by the first words he hears. For his case is obscure, and it is proper that it be covered with counsel. **"I know,"** He says, **"your works, that you have a name that you live, and you are dead."** It is as if He were to say: "Men, who see only the outward face, think that you are alive; but I, who see into the heart and am the Knower of secrets, know that you are dead." For He rebukes him privately, between Himself and the man alone. No one besides Himself and the man's own conscience knows what He is saying or in what manner the man is "dead," unless perhaps anyone reading this should happen to guess or suspect. But in law, suspicion has no place in an accusation; nor should anyone's status be put at risk because of another person's suspicion. Therefore, He does not wish to dwell any longer on the record of this man's deadly work, but immediately gives the counsel by which he might be saved.

<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book II</header>

...requires great concern. "Strengthen," He says, "the rest, which were about to die." <note>Revelation 3:2</note> Therefore, some things still live, and are not yet dead, even in one who is dead in such a way. For the office lives; that which he celebrates by baptizing and consecrating the sacrament lives <note>original: "Viuit enim officium." Rupert argues here for the "ex opere operato" principle—that the holy office and the sacraments (like Baptism or the Eucharist) remain valid and "alive" even if the priest performing them is in a state of mortal sin, though this state is precarious.</note>. For then, by the severity of the law <note>original: "legali seueritate"; referring to canon law or ecclesiastical discipline</note>, he will be deposed from office and will be like a pagan and a tax collector <note>A reference to Matthew 18:17, regarding the final stage of church discipline.</note>.

Therefore they were about to die, and therefore your other works must be strengthened, because I do not find them full before my God. For the works of a holy ministry are "full" in that place where they have a saving effect: where they are not performed for judgment, but are profitable for the forgiveness of sins. Certainly, they are not performed with this fullness for him or by him who is dead through evil-doing.

**Therefore keep in mind how you have received and heard, and keep it, and repent.**

<margin>What kind of people bishops and priests ought to be.</margin>
"How," He says, "you received and heard." You received by example; you heard by command. Not given to wine, not a striker but modest: Not quarrelsome, not greedy: one who rules his own house well." <note>original: "Oportet episcopum esse..." Rupert is quoting the qualifications for a bishop from 1 Timothy 3:2-4.</note>
<margin>1 Timothy 3. Leviticus 21.</margin>
He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. But you also received this in the Law <note>The Old Testament Law, specifically the priestly requirements in Leviticus.</note>: "Everyone from the offspring of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall not approach to offer sacrifices to God. If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small or large or crooked nose, if a broken foot or hand, if hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if having a white spot in his eye, if a chronic scab, if a skin disease on his body, or if he is ruptured <note>original: "herniosus"; refers to physical defects that disqualified men from the Aaronic priesthood in the Old Testament.</note>." Likewise: "Every man of your offspring who approaches the holy things while in a state of uncleanness shall perish before the Lord."

<summary>Rupert explains that while a sinful priest’s official acts (like sacraments) remain valid for a time, they lack spiritual "fullness" and will be stripped away by God if the priest does not repent. I will not come to you as I do to those men who watch and wait; their Lord comes when He returns from the wedding, giving thanks to them and blessing them because they were awake for His arrival. I will not come to you as a joyful and festive bridegroom, but like a thief, who breaks into the house while the master of the house is unaware, and kills the master of the house whom he finds sleeping. For it follows that death, overtaking one who does not watch, seizes him like a thief.
<margin>1 Thessalonians 5</margin>

**But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments.**

In your own person you are indeed blameworthy, but this works in your favor: that you did not also destroy others by your example. For (as I said above) although you are dead, you have a name that you are alive. "Names," He says, "a few"; that is, you have a few named people with you who are known to me by name and are written in the book of life according to their merits. Because they have not defiled their garments—that is, they have kept their bodies incorrupt <note>Rupert interprets "garments" as a metaphor for the physical body, a common theme in medieval ascetic theology where physical purity reflects spiritual state.</note>.

**They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy.**

"With me," He says—namely, with the Son of the Virgin. "With me," whose virginal flesh dedicated an example of continence; I, who am the virginal flower, the lily of virginity, and the crown of virgins. They shall walk with me in white—that is, in immaculate bodies, with which they shall rise again, shining like new lambs. And wherever I go, they shall follow me, the Lamb of God, because they are worthy of my company.

### viii Commentary of Rupert, Book 2.

[I will] confess his name before my Father, and before His angels. <note>Rupert is completing the quotation of Revelation 3:5 from the previous page.</note>

To overcome at this stage is to conquer the impulses of the flesh by the fire of the Holy Spirit, and by His power to keep the garment of the body unstained. Whoever overcomes in this way, He says, shall be clothed in white garments, just as I said: "so that he may walk with me in white." And I will not blot out his name from the book of life. He seems to have said less here than the dignity of the merit deserves: namely, by that mode of speech which is called in Greek <term>tapeinosis</term> <note>original: ταπείνωσις; a rhetorical device where an understatement is used to suggest a much greater meaning.</note>, that is, the humbling of a great thing. For this can truly be said of one who, after fornications and adulteries, has turned back and performed penance. But what He had stated as "less" here, He fulfilled more magnificently by adding: **And I will confess his name before my Father, and before His angels.** Therefore, in that first part through a negative—when He says, "I will not blot out the name of him who overcomes"—He simultaneously strikes the one who does not overcome; for it follows that He *will* blot out that person's name. Here, however, through an affirmation—"and I will confess his name"—He designates more abundantly the glory and honor stored up for the one who overcomes. 

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
For this is just as magnificent as what the Apostle [Paul] said concerning the fathers [the Patriarchs], after he had commemorated at length the faith, obedience, and expectation of those wanderers: "for which cause," he says, "God is not ashamed to be called their God." <note>Rupert draws a parallel between Jesus "confessing a name" and God "not being ashamed" of the faithful in Hebrews 11:16.</note> Finally, here also when He says, "I will confess his name," it is to be understood in the same sense as if He had said: I will not be ashamed to confess his name—that such a man is my disciple. Since he walks in white garments, I will not be ashamed before my Father and His angels that he is my companion in my walking.

<margin>Sirach 32</margin>
**He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.**
To hear what this Spirit says is to do all things with counsel. "Do all things with counsel," says the Scripture, "and after the deed you will not repent." <note>original: Eccle. xxxij; Rupert cites the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 32:24 from the Vulgate bible.</note> For He did not speak of just any kind of counsel, but of that counsel which Holy Scripture describes to us when naming the Holy Spirit the "Spirit of Counsel," whom we understand to be speaking here. For Pharaoh had a foolish counsel, as it is written...

The time of temptation is not far off, from which you must be saved; indeed, it is like an hour that passes quickly. For behold, I come quickly, I come breaking your chains, so that, released and a stranger to the body <note>original: "peregrinus a corpore," a reference to being away from the earthly body to be present with the Lord, as in 2 Corinthians 5:8</note>, you may be present with God and fully enjoy that thing which you have deserved to understand here for your consolation. Thus far, the sweetness of grace has flowed from the lips of the Holy and True One; he has blessed the beloved messenger of love, magnifying the joy and exultation which he has stored up for him. It remains for him to warn that same man of the need for vigilance and concern: lest he think he has already attained his goal, or trust too much in himself before the end of his course and become careless. Therefore, he says:

->**Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown.**<-

<margin>How someone may lose their crown.</margin>
It is as if he says: stand firm with a steady foot in humility, lest you fall by a slipping foot, and by falling lose the crown prepared for you, and another succeeding in your place should receive it. And indeed, it cannot happen that any of those whom God foreknew and predestined to the crown should lose their reward. Nevertheless, it both can happen—and has happened—that someone whom God called to the crown by a visible calling <note>term: "visible calling" <gloss>vocatione visibili</gloss>. This refers to an outward appointment to a religious office or a public invitation to the faith, which Rupert distinguishes from God's hidden, eternal plan of predestination.</note>, or a calling that could be heard by men, might lose it. For example, the Lord called Judas to the apostolic crown, yet he did not predestine him to the crown, because he foreknew he would be unworthy of it. Thus, another received his crown—that is, the honor of the apostolate—just as it is written: 
<margin>Psalm 108. Acts 1.</margin>
"Let his days be few, and let another take his office." <note>original: "episcopatum eius accipiat alter." Rupert quotes the Latin Vulgate of Psalm 108 (Psalm 109 in English bibles), which Peter applies to Judas in Acts 1:20.</note> Therefore, as long as anyone is still struggling in this life, let them not be overly confident about the crown, because even if God (who foreknows all things) knows that your head will be worthy of the crown at the end, you yourself do not know it.

### On Chapter 3 of the Apocalypse

<meta>catchword: father and</meta>

To conquer at this stage means to have the inextinguishable lamp of brotherly love leading the way, and to always have an open door: never to be shut out, nor to be caught in the snares <note>original: "cassibus irretiri"</note> of heretics, but to bring forth whatever one finds through that door for the edification of others, and to never cease from this pursuit of love because of any adversities or the spiteful detractions of the envious. To the one who conquers in this way, he says, **I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.** This is a worthy and fitting reward for such a victor: that he who, possessing this grace, wrote or taught things by which the faith of the Church might be strengthened, should himself be a pillar in the temple of God. **And he shall go out no more,** he says. It is as if he were to say: As long as he is at the door which I have set open before him, let him be careful lest he slip. But when, through his reward, he has been established inside like a pillar, there will be no reason for him to fear, because he shall go out no more, nor shall his foot stumble

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 2

...is my mother, whoever does the will of my father who is in heaven. <note>Rupert is completing the quote from Matthew 12:50: "For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother."</note>
<margin>
Colossians 3.
How David spiritually becomes the father of Christ.
</margin>
For in the inner man, where the generation of Christ is specifically reckoned, there is neither male nor female. Finally, the Gospel generation <note>original: "generatio," referring here to lineage or family descent</note> of Christ is entirely spiritual, and according to the spirit, David is also the father of Christ: namely, because believing in his heart and bringing forth with his mouth the Word of God which is Christ, he published it in his writings—the first of the prophets and the most illustrious of the patriarchs. Otherwise, unless he had been a father through faith in Christ, he would have been his predecessor according to the flesh in vain. Hence Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah <note>Three kings of Judah who, though physical ancestors of Jesus, are omitted from the genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew, likely due to their wickedness or the judgment on the house of Ahab.</note>, who persecuted and killed the prophets—the heralds of that same Christ and that same Word of God—were not reckoned in that generation. Therefore, when it is said of the one who conquers in this way—so that, having understanding, he helps and cooperates so that the word of God may grow and advance: **And I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem,** it is the same as if he were to say: he shall be called and shall be my father and my mother, and he shall inherit this eternal name. He said "of the new Jerusalem" because of the new life: because he has stripped off the old man and put on the new.
<margin>Ephesians 4.</margin>
He also praiseworthily asserts that it "descended from heaven": because clearly his conduct is in heaven. On account of brotherly love <note>The name of the city "Philadelphia" literally translates to "brotherly love."</note>, for which this angel of Philadelphia is praised, he "descends," that is, he condescends to the little ones. For example: Paul was caught up to the third heaven
<margin>2 Corinthians 12.</margin>
and there he heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to speak; but for the sake of the weak he "descended" when he said: *Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and the wife to her husband.*
<margin>1 Corinthians 7.</margin>
There are countless "descents" of this kind, but this one is sufficient for an example, pertaining to the matter or the cause of this angel: whose praise or merit is the work of love. Finally, he adds: **and my new name.** The name of the person who says these things is the "Son of God." He himself writes this name, without doubt, upon the one who conquers: for all who are beloved are called, and are, the sons of God. Furthermore, when he says **I will write,** it means "I will make it appear." For we are indeed the sons of God now (says the Apostle John himself, who writes these things at the command of the Son of God) but it has not yet appeared what we shall be.
<margin>1 John 3.</margin>

<summary>Rupert explains that the "new name" and the "New Jerusalem" represent a spiritual lineage and a life of brotherly love. He argues that being a member of Christ's family comes from doing God's will and "descending" in humility to help others, rather than through physical descent.</summary>

# On Revelation, Chapter 3

We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. <note>Rupert is quoting 1 John 3:2 to explain the transformative power of the "beatific vision," the direct sight of God.</note> Therefore, to write in such a way that the name of each of the children of God can be read is to make them manifest, so that the merits of each individual may be known and seen by all. And this name—namely, "son of God"—shall be written upon all the elect, although wherever or in whom there is now a greater degree of brotherly love, a greater splendor of this name ought to appear in that person. Moreover, that name of God, which is "Father," or that name of his city, the "New Jerusalem," <note>original: "nouæ Hierusalem"</note> which is "Mother," <note>In medieval theology, the New Jerusalem or the Church was frequently identified as the "Mother" of the faithful.</note> must be written upon those who, having progressed as if into the full maturity of faith, have been strong enough and eager to spread the word of God through love.

<margin>
Luke 10.
Matthew 13.
</margin>
He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. In this place, to "hear" is to be stirred to the study of the word of God, to approach his feet so that one may drink from his teaching, to sit with Mary at the feet of the Lord, <note>A reference to Mary of Bethany (Luke 10:39), who sat at Jesus' feet to listen, representing the "contemplative life."</note> and to apply the submissive soul to hearing the words of his mouth, and to give all one's own so that one may purchase the one precious pearl of his grace. This is done so that, perceiving the truth with the eye of the intellect and being well instructed, he may be made fit to instruct others also, possessing as an eternal inheritance the inscription of so great a name, which he who is holy and true promises.

And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God's creation: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot.

<margin>
The Spirit of Wisdom
</margin>
Here now, in the last—that is, the seventh—place, he who we saw above speaks in the faithful and true witness; that is, he is the seventh spirit, the Spirit of Wisdom, <note>original: "spiritus sapientiae"</note> calling his worker to a true Sabbath-rest <term>sabbatismus: from the Greek 'sabbatismos,' meaning a spiritual rest or state of holy peace</term>, so that he might rest in humility. Thus, he should not be weary even with a single word or superfluous thought by magnifying himself or attributing his works to himself. For what does he have from himself except all things that are evil? And from whom, if not from God, does he have all the good things he possesses? He exhorts this angel to look thoroughly into this.

# Rupert's Commentary, Book 2

...saying, "and you do not know that you are wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17); and then adding: "and anoint your eyes with eye-salve so that you may see" (Revelation 3:18). For indeed, God had worked several good things in him or through him, which is why he could say, 

<margin>Laodicea.</margin> 
"Because I am rich, and have become wealthy, and have need of nothing." The name Laodicea is fitting for such a person. For it is interpreted as "a tribe beloved by the Lord," <note>original: "tribus amabilis domino." Rupert uses a medieval etymology common in his era to link the name to the church's initial good standing.</note> evidently because of the good works God had performed through him. It is also interpreted as "those who were in vomit." <note>Rupert here connects the name to the threat in Revelation 3:16, where the lukewarm are told they will be "spit out" or vomited.</note> This interpretation also fits him because he boasted in the riches of those same good works, so that it was rightly said to him: "I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth."

And so, let us also hear what this seventh spirit says, and by hearing let us progress toward the rest of humility and wisdom. For he says: "These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God" (Revelation 3:14). 

<margin>Amen.</margin> 
"Amen"—that is, the truthful one, or Truth itself. He explains this very thing in the words that follow. For there follows: "The faithful and true witness." To what purpose did such a description of the speaker and the words that follow pertain? Namely, so that whoever is conscious of having done good works—like this "angel" of Laodicea <note>In the letters to the seven churches, the "angel" is traditionally understood as the bishop or leader of that specific Christian community.</note>—should know and reflect that it is not necessary for him to testify about himself before the proper time, claiming he is rich and wealthy. Indeed, such testimony does not belong to him, but to him who has been established as both witness and judge of all, and who is to be revealed in his own time. 

Let such a person know that all testimony and judgment of good deeds must be left to Him; let him testify only concerning his own evil deeds against himself, and accuse himself. Therefore he says: "These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness." "Amen," that is, Truth, because he cannot be deceived or be ignorant of anything. 

<margin>Faithful and true witness.</margin> 
"Faithful witness," because he does not know how to lie, so as to call good evil or evil good. "True," because he will render to each according to his works. In the same way, why was it relevant for him to add, "who is the beginning of the creation of God"? 

<margin>The beginning of the creation of God. Ephesians 2.</margin> 
For what is the "creation of God" in this context? Surely it is the "new man," or the generation and re-creation of man, when you walk in the newness of life by doing good works. For this is why the Apostle says: "For it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast; for we are his..." <note>Rupert is quoting Ephesians 2:8–10, arguing that any "good works" a person does are actually God's own creation within them, leaving no room for the pride seen in Laodicea.</note>

<summary>Rupert explains the spiritual condition of the Laodicean church, interpreting their "wealth" as a dangerous pride in their own good deeds. He argues that Christ, as the "Amen" and "Faithful Witness," is the only true judge of a person's merits.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter 3

...workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them. <note>original: "factura, creati in Christo Iesu in operibus bonis..." Such are your works as I know them; such is how I judge them. You are not "cold," in the sense of being numb toward good work, nor are you "hot," in the sense of offering thanksgiving to God as you ought to have done. Nevertheless, [it should have been] not like that Pharisee who, justifying himself, looked down upon the tax collector, <note>A reference to the Parable of the Pharisee and the Publican in Luke 18:9–14.</note> but like the Psalmist, who, humbly praising the Lord working within him, says: "Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to Your name give glory." <note>original: "non nobis, domine non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam." This is Psalm 115:1 in modern Bibles, numbered as 113 in the Vulgate used by Rupert.</note> "I wish you were cold or hot." This might be appropriately said, for example, to a proud virgin. "I wish you were cold or hot," that is...

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on the Book of Revelation, Chapter 3. Having previously addressed the pride and spiritual blindness of the "lukewarm" bishop of Laodicea, Rupert now interprets Christ's remedy: the application of the "eye-salve" of humility and the transformative power of divine discipline.</meta>

<page-num>cxi</page-num>
<header>On Revelation, Chapter 3</header>

### And anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.

<margin>Eye-salve is humility. Luke 10.</margin>
The eye-salve <term>collyrium: a medicinal ointment used in antiquity for treating eye infections</term> by which the defects of the eyes are cleansed, signifies the sweetness of humility. This humility assists the "little ones," so that those mysteries which are hidden from the wise and the prudent may be revealed to them. <note>original: "sapientibus & prudentibus abscondita sunt"; a reference to Christ’s prayer in Matthew 11:25 and Luke 10:21.</note> Therefore, "anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see"—that is, purify your heart with true humility, so that you may see your own poverty and recognize the true riches of God’s goodness.

### Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten.

It is as if he says: The things I speak to you in rebuke and correction, receive them as the grace and goodwill of a lover. For it is not the habit of Wisdom to allow the child she loves to be youthfully puffed up and vanish into vanity; rather, she both loves and chastens. She strikes the unrestrained child, and the same one she once nursed as an infant, she now beats and strikes with a rod when he becomes too talkative and reckless. Thus, while I chasten you—while I prick you as if with nails driven deep—I truly love you all the more.

### Be zealous, therefore, and repent.

"Be zealous" <note>original: "Aemulare"</note>—that is, by loving him who loves and chastens you, imitate him with a good fervor of the soul. You who were lukewarm, grow hot through this zeal; and because you have been ungrateful to your lover until now by not returning his love, repent. Until now, he has struck down the "haughty eyebrow" <note>original: "superciliū"; a Latin idiom for pride or arrogance.</note> of the one who seems wealthy and rich, who vainly imagines himself to abound in good works. Now, he asks quite amiably of this man, or of any such wealthy person, that he share the glory of his works with God, or with the Son of God, who grants all things. This is so that he may glory in God, or cause God to be glorified in him, and so that he may glorify the Holy One in all his works.
<margin>1 Corinthians 1.</margin>

### Behold, he says, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him and dine with him.

The meaning is this: that which I have said to you so far in rebuke is like someone standing at a rich man's door and knocking, so that, being admitted as a guest, he may dine with him on the treasures stored within. If he is admitted, the "feast of charity" <note>original: "conuiuiū charitatis"</note> is celebrated, because charity cannot exist between fewer than two people. Thus...

<summary>Rupert explains that Christ’s rebukes are acts of love intended to foster humility, which he likens to a medicinal eye-salve that allows the soul to see its own poverty. He concludes by interpreting Christ’s "knocking at the door" as an invitation to a communal feast of love between the believer and God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 3:20-21. Rupert is finishing his explanation of the "knocking at the door" and beginning his interpretation of the "throne" promised to the victor, linking Christ's victory to his humility.</meta>

<page-num>cxii</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book II</header>

For what do you say—that you are rich? You boast in a good conscience; but look, I stand and knock at the door of your heart. Admit me, and have me as a participant or companion of your glory, so that you do not boast alone, but with me. Indeed, boast not in yourself, but in me, through whom you have been made rich. If in this way you or anyone else hearing my voice opens the door to me, and carries out all good things by referring them to the glory of God, I will enter in to him, and in his heart, as if in the house of a friend, I will have confidence. And now indeed I will dine—that is, I will take delight with him in the good things of his conscience—and he himself in the future shall enjoy my good things with me.

**To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on His throne.**

<margin>One must be humbled in all things</margin>
At this level, to "overcome" means to drive far away all the levity of boasting and vain glory through the maturity of wisdom. It means that even when a person appears great to others, they remain small in their own eyes, according to what that same Wisdom says:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 3</margin>
The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God. <note>original: "Quanto magnus es, humilia te in omnibus & coram deo inuenies gratiam." Quoted from Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 3:18.</note> For humility, whose company Wisdom has never lacked, is accustomed to fly toward heaven.

<margin>To sit on my throne</margin>
Therefore he says: "To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne"—not so that he might be made equal to divinity <term>divinitati: the state of being God</term>, but so that he might be joined to eternity. "Just as I also overcame," he says. How did he who speaks these things—Christ—overcome, except through the inestimable greatness of his humility and charity?

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
For since he was in the form of God, he did not wish to boast in that form alone, but (pay close attention) he wished for humans—who had become inglorious through the sin of the first man—to become fellow participants in his glory. Therefore, "he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant"; therefore "he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even death on a cross." <note>original: "semetipsum exinaniuit... factus obediens vsque ad mortem"; a reference to the famous "Christ Hymn" in Philippians 2:6-8.</note> This is the supreme victory of humility and wisdom, which destroyed the pride and foolishness of the first man. "I have overcome," he says, and because of this, I have sat with my Father on his throne. For because of this, God exalted him and gave hi... <note>original catchword: "donauit il" refers to "donavit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen" (gave him the name that is above every name).</note>

<summary>Rupert explains that true spiritual victory comes through humility rather than self-glory, illustrating this through Christ's own "victory" of self-emptying and the cross. He argues that by humbling oneself, a believer shares in the eternal "throne" of Christ's glory.</summary>

<margin>The argument for the following books.</margin>
In most things, the distinct character of each spirit reveals itself through symbolic deeds <note>original: "facta imaginaria." In medieval theology, this refers to truth conveyed through mental images or prophetic visions.</note>. To show this with a brief indication: after the most orderly throne of God is placed in heaven—in whose arrangement the **spirit of wisdom** is rightly proclaimed—the Lamb opens the book signed with seven seals, loosening its fasteners. This is clearly the praiseworthy work of the **spirit of understanding**, which is second in order. Then, the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>A traditional title for Christ, derived from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6.</note> is seen standing by the altar of the temple, and through the mystic songs of the seven trumpets, the mystery of God is completed; we do not doubt that this pertains to the **spirit of counsel**. In the fourth place, a great red dragon having seven heads attacks the woman. With Michael and his angels fighting, the dragon is cast down to the earth with his angels; there, without a doubt, the **spirit of fortitude** (which is fourth) is commended. In the fifth place is the **spirit of knowledge** in the seven <term>phials|A shallow, broad-mouthed bowl or vessel used in ancient rituals; often translated as "vials" in older bibles</term> of the angels. In the sixth place, the praise of **piety** is shown in the blood of the martyrs of Jesus, with which the woman is shown to be drunk <note>Rupert interprets the "drunkenness" of the woman not as her own sin, but as the occasion that reveals the piety and devotion of the martyrs who shed their blood.</note>. In the seventh place, however, in the coming hour of the judgment of God—when all the dead are returned from the earth, the sea, and the underworld—everything undoubtedly looks toward the **spirit of the fear of the Lord**. Then comes the end, where Jerusalem is shown adorned: the wife of the Lamb, the city of God.

<margin>The first voice like the sound of a trumpet</margin>
This first voice is his—the same as the one heard earlier, which said: "Write what you see." Therefore, he did not simply say, "and the voice which I heard," but "the *first* voice which I heard." However, in words and in sense, it was not the same as the first one: for then it was said, "write what you see," but now he is told, "come up here." Both then and now the voice was like a trumpet, because clearly he intends to speak nothing in secret, but to speak openly to the world whatever he says or shows. It is as if he were saying, "I immediately understood through a spiritual sense those things which were being shown to me through images," so that we might not doubt that what the voice said pertains to the intellect: *and I will show you what must take place soon after these things.* For it is not as some heretics have claimed—that prophetic visions of this kind occurred in such a way that the prophets themselves did not understand what realities or meanings their visions contained. Consequently, there was no need for him to say here, "and I will show you what you have seen, and what things are, and what must take place after these," in the same way he had said earlier: *Write, therefore, what you have seen, and what things are, and what must take place after these.* For those things which he had seen, and those which then existed, he already knew; because he had seen the past while walking with the Lord until His end, and he was then seeing the present state of the Church. However, he did not yet know the future. Therefore, the voice rightly instructs him only concerning future things: *I will show you,* it says, *what must take place soon after these things.* Nevertheless, those things he had seen, even those that had passed, he saw as many and deeply mystical images—not so much for his own instruction as for ours.

### On Revelation, Chapter 15

<margin>The prophets and teachers of the Law are compared to narrow cups.</margin>
...there would be) no languages nor speeches where their voices were not heard <note>original: "non essent loquelae neque sermones, quorum non audirentur voces eorum"; a reference to Psalm 19:3, implying that the Gospel is now spoken in every tongue</note>; that is, so that all kinds of languages might be born in their mouths. Thus he says: **And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvelous.** Indeed, after that sign where he had seen the Lamb standing upon Mount Sion with the 144,000 singing a new song, this sign is truly great and marvelous: namely, that while the Son of Man is harvesting the vintage of the earth, those seven angels have the seven last plagues, and in them the wrath of God is fulfilled.

<margin>The seven angels with the vials represent all the preachers of the Gospel.</margin>
For who are these seven angels, if not the universal preachers of the Gospel, the messengers of truth? Because the Holy Spirit—who gave them the <term>vials</term> <note>original: "phialas"; also translated as "bowls"</note> already mentioned and those to be mentioned later—is sevenfold <note>referring to the seven gifts of the Spirit</note>, they are rightly encompassed by the number seven, and through them all preachers are understood together. Furthermore, he calls these the "last plagues" in respect to the "first plagues," which we mentioned earlier when the seven angels sounded the trumpets. We must later explain in order how those were the first and these are the last. However, it should be briefly tasted here that those plagues are called "first" because they struck the bodies; but these are "last" because they reach even to the souls. From this, we should also note what he says: "because in them the wrath of God is fulfilled." For wrath begins with the killing of bodies, and after it has killed, it is fulfilled by sending souls into <term>Gehenna</term> <note>a place of spiritual punishment or hell</note>. It follows:

-> **And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire, and those who had overcome the beast and his image standing upon the sea of glass mingled, having the harps of God, and they sang the song of Moses the servant [of God]...** <-

<summary>Rupert explains that the "vials" of Revelation represent the wide-reaching preaching of the Gospel, contrasting it with the "narrow" reach of the Old Testament Law. He also defines the "last plagues" as those which affect the soul rather than just the body.</summary>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 9

...[the servant] of God <note>original: "ui dei"; the text is continuing the phrase "Moysi famuli dei," meaning "of Moses the servant of God"</note>, and the song of the lamb, saying: 
> **Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of ages. Who shall not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name? For you alone are holy, because all nations shall come and worship in your sight, because your judgments are made manifest.**

<margin>Vessels of mercy preserved from the wrath of God.</margin>
<margin>Romans 1.</margin>
These people have been reserved as <term>vessels of mercy</term> <note>original: "vasis misericordiae"; a concept from Romans 9:23 describing those chosen for salvation</note>. By singing of their salvation and playing the harp to celebrate the grace of their Savior, they have happily escaped from the land and the sea, from the rivers and the springs of waters, from the heat of the sun or fire, from the seat or the dark kingdom of the beast, from the great river Euphrates, and from the air (or the powers of this air)—into all of which the aforementioned bowls of God’s wrath are later described as being poured out. For these are they who, when the wrath of God was revealed from heaven through the Gospel against all the impiety and injustice of men <note>Romans 1:18</note>, believed and performed penance, and were baptized for the remission of sins. Therefore, they are separated in the order of the narrative from those "children of wrath" who refused to believe; first the salvation of the former is told, and then the destruction of the latter. Thus he says:

<margin>The sea of glass is baptism.</margin>
**And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire.** This sea is the sacrament of the baptism of Christ; it is that water which visibly flowed with blood from his pierced side as he hung on the cross <note>referring to the "blood and water" from the side of Jesus in John 19:34</note>. It wipes away and cleanses all sins, but not without the invisible power or presence of the Holy Spirit. Rightly, therefore, when he had said, "and I saw as it were a sea," he added, **mingled with fire**, because certainly in baptism (as has already been stated), the visible water would achieve nothing without the invisible power of the Spirit. And beautifully, although he could have said, "And I saw water," he preferred to say, "**And I saw as it were a sea**," because indeed...

<margin>Exodus 14. The holy fathers under the Law [through a figure].</margin>
...**OF CHRIST** by which sins are swallowed up, bears no small or unknown similarity to the Red Sea <note>original: "rubro mari"</note>, in which Pharaoh perished with his chariots and horsemen. But the Catholic faith knows that those earlier harpists or singers...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the "sea of glass mingled with fire" as a symbol for Christian baptism, which cleanses sin through the combined power of water and the Holy Spirit. He draws a typology between the salvation of the faithful in Revelation and the Israelites crossing the Red Sea in Exodus.</summary>
