<margin>
Those who were instructed <note>original: "cathezizati"</note> were baptized through the passion of Christ. 
1 Corinthians 10.
</margin>
Those who were seen above standing with the lamb upon Mount Zion, together with these younger ones, stood upon this sea. This means they were saved or brought to perfection not without the water of baptism, the blood of Christ’s passion, and the fire of the Holy Spirit. For those <term>shadowy sacraments</term> <note>original: "sacramenta umbratica"; symbolic rituals that were only a "shadow" of the reality to come</note>—for example, the fact that they were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, that they ate manna, and that they drank water from the rock—did not, I say, bring them to perfection. Rather, they were as if <term>catechized</term> <note>original: "cathezizati"; historically, this refers to those receiving basic instruction in the faith before full initiation</note> through all those things, and were finally regenerated by the passion of the coming Savior. This happened for them all at once when (as has already been said) his side was opened and, with water and blood flowing out, the sacrament of baptism was established. For we are baptized individually for this reason: because we were not yet incorporated into the church which was regenerated then; indeed, we did not yet exist at all. Therefore, as he now says:

### And I saw those who had conquered the beast and its image standing over the sea of glass.

<margin>
Why that sea is called "glassy."
</margin>
We rightly understand this to refer to all the saints of both the Old and the New Testaments. For surely both those who believed he *would* come, and these who believe that **CHRIST HAS COME**, conquer the beast and its image—that is, the devil and every wicked man who imitates him—through that same faith while they believe and are baptized. Ultimately, all crimes and all sins, both original and actual, which that beast and its image forced upon them through persuasion or example, are drowned in this sea. But they themselves stand *over* the sea; that is, they are survivors so that they may cross over to the true Promised Land. The "letter of the law" once hid that land while promising it, but now the "spirit of the gospel" reveals it. For this reason, it is beautifully called a **sea of glass**: because just as what is contained in glass shines through, so in this sacrament of the Gospel nothing is now hidden. Instead, what was first performed as a <term>figure</term> <note>original: "figura"; a prophetic symbol or "type" that points to a later reality</note> is now performed in reality, and everything is made manifest. But you also rightly understand why it is called a "glassy sea" so that you may know that...

<summary>Rupert explains that the saints of the Old Testament were not saved by their own rituals (like manna or the Red Sea crossing) but were "catechized" by them until Christ's passion provided true baptism. The "glassy sea" symbolizes the Gospel, which—unlike the obscure law—is transparent and reveals the full truth of salvation.</summary>

In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, by the Lord's command, that lamb was sacrificed as a type of the same Christ, the Son of God, so that he might take away our sins by being sacrificed.

> Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, O King of the ages.

There are, then, two greatest things which they <term>harp</term> <note>original: "citarizant." For when they say, "great and wonderful are your works," it is a praise of his strength; when they add, "just and true are your ways," it is a confession of his justice.

Clearly, these two things in the soul of the one confessing are not of equal merit. For someone deserves well who, seeing the wonderful works of the strongest of spirits, fears, praises, and confesses. But he does best who strives to defend God's justice in those same works—where he understands it—against the slanderer. And where his understanding fails, being of lesser perception, he nonetheless worships with love and says what the Apostle teaches each of us to say: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and [unsearchable his ways!]* <note>Romans 11:33</note>

<summary>Rupert explains that the song sung by the victors in Revelation is both the "Song of Moses" and the "Song of the Lamb" because the Red Sea crossing was a historical precursor to the spiritual reality of Christian baptism. # Who will not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name?

<margin>
No one can resist God. John 9; Psalm 75 <note>original: "Ioan. ix. psal. lxxv." Rupert cites Job 9 rather than John 9, and Psalm 76 in modern numbering.</note>
</margin>
When they say, *Who will not fear*, it is to be understood: "and have peace?" For thus another Scripture says: *Who has resisted him, and had peace?* <note>Job 9:4</note>. Likewise, it is written elsewhere: *You are terrible, and who shall resist you?* <note>Psalm 76:7</note>; it is understood, of course: "No one." And immediately a very weighty reason is given why no one can resist: *From that time [comes] your wrath.* The meaning is this: From the moment a sinner sins—not by slipping through weakness or erring through ignorance, but by resisting you through pride—from that time your wrath comes, so that, evidently, you no longer ignore the sin or call back the one who has turned away, but strike and strongly break him. Therefore, *Who will not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name?* is the same as if he said: "Since your works are so great and wonderful, Lord, and your ways so just and true, where will the proud and ungrateful appear?"

<margin>
Isaiah 2.
</margin>
For he who does not fear now as one who is subject, will fear—or rather, will be thrown into confusion as one who is crushed—according to what is said through Isaiah in a prophetic invective against him: *Enter into the rock, hide in a pit in the ground from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he shall rise up to strike the earth.* <note>Isaiah 2:10</note>.

> After these things I looked, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels, having the seven plagues, went out of the temple, clothed in clean, white stone, <note>original: "vestiti lapide mundo." This reflects a variant in some Latin Vulgate manuscripts of Revelation 15:6 which read "stone" rather than the "linen" found in most modern translations.</note> and girded about the breasts with golden girdles. And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls <note>original: "phialas." While often translated as "vials," these were shallow, broad offering bowls.</note> full of the wrath of the living God forever and ever.

<margin>
Order of the narrative.
</margin>
"After these things," he says, "I saw"—it is understood to be that which I had already begun to narrate above. For I had said: *And I saw another great and wonderful sign in heaven, seven angels having the seven last plagues, for in them the wrath of God is completed.* But when he had begun to say this, he immediately paused it and made a beautiful digression, so that he might first write what he had seen at the same time: namely, the sea of glass, and those who, by standing upon it, escaped those plagues by the grace of Christ; and then [he returns to] the order of those same plagues.

First salvation is offered to believers, then damnation is set before unbelievers. "Therefore," he says, "after these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony was opened in heaven." The "temple of the tabernacle of testimony" was the Church of the former time <note>The era of the Old Testament.</note>, whose entire ritual or figurative order was initiated from the tabernacle of testimony which Moses made in the wilderness. This temple—that is, this Church—was enclosed within only one nation, Judea, where alone God was known <note>original: "in qua sola notus erat deus"; a reference to Psalm 76:1.</note>. It was enclosed by the narrowness of that place, and enclosed by the mystical and figurative reasons for its ceremonies that were not yet understood. But when the Lord Jesus gave up his spirit, and by his death established the aforementioned sacrament of baptism, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom; and rising himself from the dead, *he opened the minds of his disciples so they might understand the scriptures.* <note>Luke 24:45</note>. Thus, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony was opened. Where? "In heaven," he says. "Heaven," or the "heavens," are all the holy ones in whom God dwells, and especially the apostles. For of them it is written: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1</note>. Therefore, it was opened "in heaven"—that is, in the hearts of the apostles—to whom, as was said above, he opened their minds so they might understand the scriptures. And so, with the temple thus opened:

Matthew 10.

"Having," he says, "the seven plagues." That is, they were commanded to preach wrath, indignation, and tribulation upon every soul of man who does evil—the Jew first, and then the Greek—and conversely, glory, honor, and peace to every soul of man who does good—the Jew first, and then the Greek <note>Rupert is paraphrasing Romans 2:8–10 to explain the "plagues" as the consequences of the Gospel message.</note>; evidently, such as those men were...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 9

->**And the first went, and poured out his vial onto the earth; and there was made a cruel and most grievous wound upon the men who have the mark of the beast, and those who worshipped its image.**<-

Here we must now recall the order of the first plagues, namely those which occurred earlier at the voices of the seven angels sounding their trumpets <note>original: "septem angelorum tubis canentium." Rupert is linking the "Trumpets" of Revelation 8–11 with the "Vials" or "Bowls" of Revelation 16.</note>. For it is in respect to those that these are called the "last" plagues.

<margin>The seven first plagues through the seven trumpets.</margin>
At the voice of the first angel, a third part of the earth was burned; at the voice of the second, a third part of the sea became blood; and at the voice of the third, a third part of the rivers was turned into **wormwood** <note>original: "absynthium." In Revelation 8:11, this star makes the water bitter and deadly.</note>; and at the voice of the fourth, a third part of the sun, moon, and stars was darkened; at the voice of the fifth angel, warlike locusts came out from the pit of the abyss <note>The "bottomless pit" or "abyssi."</note> onto the earth; and at the voice of the sixth, the four angels who were bound at the great river **Euphrates** were loosed; and at the voice of the seventh, victorious voices were made in heaven.

<margin>The seven last plagues through the seven bowls.</margin>
These latest plagues are poured out in the same order through those same parts of the world. For the first is poured onto the earth, the second into the sea, the third into the rivers and upon the springs of waters, the fourth onto the sun, the fifth onto the seat of the beast, the sixth into the great river Euphrates, and the seventh is poured into the air. In place of the "pit of the abyss," he wrote the "seat of the beast" in this sequence; the rest he expressed with the same names. Now there...

<note>original: "Nunc er..." The text cuts off here with a catchword "er," likely for "ergo" (therefore), intended for the next page.</note>

Therefore, these last plagues must be compared to those first ones, each to each, and we must see—as the truth deigns to reveal itself—by what reasoning these are called or truly are the "last" following the others.

->**"And there was made," it says, "a cruel and most grievous wound upon the men who have the mark of the beast, and those who worshipped its image."**<-

<margin>The Gentiles given over to a depraved mind through contempt. Romans 1 <note>The original margin cites Romans 8, but the text quotes Romans 1:28.</note></margin>
The "mark of the beast"—that is, the devil—is pride. Anyone who sins knowingly and out of contempt is rightly judged to have this mark, just as the Apostle says concerning certain people: "Because when they had known God, they did not glorify him as God, or give thanks." Indeed, as the same author says: "They did not see fit to acknowledge God." And so, in what follows—**"and upon those who worshipped its image"**—it is easy to understand the crime of idolatry, because the Apostle says of them in that same passage: "And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of beasts, and of four-footed animals, and of serpents." <margin>A cruel and most grievous wound.</margin> Upon these people, indeed, was made a "cruel and most grievous wound." "Therefore," he says, "God delivered them over to shameful passions, to do those things which are not fitting." For their women changed the natural use into that use which is against nature. Likewise, the males, having left the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males with males working filthiness, and receiving in themselves the reward that was due for their error <note>original: "mercedem quam oportuit erroris sui." Rupert is quoting the Vulgate of Romans 1:27, interpreting the "grievous wound" of Revelation as the spiritual and physical corruption of those who reject God.</note>. What could be worse or more cruel than this wound? This is why, when he had said "a cruel wound," he added "and most grievous." For this is not only a sin, but also the most grievous punishment of sin. Therefore, the first angel poured out his vial onto the earth—that is, upon those who committed the sin of the Sodomites, whose sin was "fullness of bread and idleness" <note>This refers to Ezekiel 16:49, which defines the sin of Sodom.</note>. The earth received them—the earth which (as Scripture <margin>Genesis 13</margin> reports) was previously irrigated like the **paradise of the Lord** <note>original: "paradisus domini." In Genesis 13:10, the plain of the Jordan is compared to the Garden of Eden before the destruction of Sodom.</note>. These people, I say, he rebuked and convicted of being so grievously ulcerated for this reason: because they did not see fit to acknowledge God; and he openly pronounced that for this sin—or rather, by this...

<summary>Rupert interprets the "grievous wound" of the first vial as the moral corruption and "shameful passions" described by St. Paul in Romans, linking the plague to the pride and idolatry of those who reject God.</summary>

the punishment of sin ought by right to be transferred to the punishment of eternal <note>original: "aeterni," completing the OCR fragment "a ni"</note> fire. <margin>
The difference between the first trumpet and the first vial.
</margin>
Namely, because the Scripture in which that trumpet sounded—where we read that the "cry of the Sodomites" ascended to God—brought forth almost no sentence of damnation or judgment regarding the final day in its teaching. Instead, it narrated only what was done presently and visibly; specifically, that they were punished with bodily death through a rain of fire and sulfur. Here, on the contrary, where the preachers of the Gospel reveal the wrath of God from heaven, no visible or present corporal vengeance descends from heaven upon similar sinners. Instead,

<margin>
Romans 1.

Because there, by reason of the historical time, the future punishment of sinners was kept silent, here it is openly pronounced; and conversely, the corporal or present punishment that was enacted there is indeed commemorated here as an example, but it is not actually inflicted. Therefore, rightly that plague is called one of the first,

<margin>
Another difference.
</margin>
and this one is called one of the last. It should be noted first, because in the earlier account [the Trumpets], it is narrated that only a third part of the earth or the trees was burned up—by which trees, through figurative speech, men are signified. Here, however, it is not a "third part" of men, but rather men in general are narrated to have been struck by a cruel and most grievous wound. Finally, both the Sodomites and the Egyptians, as well as the Canaanites—nations which endured various judgments in those ancient times—were all part of the "third part" of men:

<margin>
Genesis 9.
</margin>

But on the last day of the great judgment, will only that one part of the human race which issued from Ham be judged according to its works? Nay, without distinction of persons or nations, there shall be "wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of man that worketh evil" <note>Quoting Romans 2:8-9</note>.

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains that while Old Testament punishments (like those of Sodom) were physical and limited to specific lineages like Ham's, the New Testament judgments (the Vials) are spiritual, eternal, and universal to all who do evil.</summary>

The Apostle says, to the Jew first and also to the Greek <note>original: "Iudæi primum & Græci"</note>, neither of whom descend from Ham, but one from the descendants of Shem, and the other from the descendants of Japheth <note>According to the "Table of Nations" in Genesis, Shem was the ancestor of the Semitic peoples (Jews) and Japheth of the Europeans (Greeks), while Ham was the ancestor of the peoples of Africa and Canaan.</note>. The "sea" refers to all those who, puffed up by the power of this world, imitate the swelling pride of Pharaoh and Egypt. For Pharaoh and his Egyptian servants swelled like the sea and raised their waves against the Lord. For just as a swollen sea is churned within itself by reciprocal waves—being driven now by the tide coming in and now by the tide going out <note>original: "accessibus nunc recessibus," literally the coming and going of the tides.</note>, until at last, exhausted within itself, it is bridled and calmed—so Pharaoh or Egypt fluctuated while contending against God. Now he would say, "I have sinned," and then again he would harden his heart. This was like the ebbing and flowing of the sea, until finally they perished in the very element suited to their character: namely, they died in the middle of the sea.

So it is for all who similarly fluctuate within themselves while contending against the Lord. For example, the Psalmist says of such people: "When he slew them, then they sought him, and they returned and came to him early in the morning. <margin>Psalm 77.</margin>
<note>This is Psalm 78:34-37 in modern Bibles.</note>. All those, I say, who persevere in this kind of infidelity are rightly understood under the name of "the sea." Upon them the vial of God's wrath is poured out in such a way that it becomes a "last plague" <term>plaga nouissima</term> <note>Rupert distinguishes "first" plagues (temporal/physical punishments) from "last" plagues (eternal/spiritual condemnation).</note> in the manner mentioned above.

<margin>The plague of the second trumpet upon the Egyptians. Exodus 13.</margin>
they were struck ten times with the lesser plagues of present evils, and finally, as we read and sing, they were drowned in the Red Sea. Their pride, burning with the fire of envy, is signified there, where at the sounding of the second angel, and like...

<margin>The second plague of the vial.</margin>
"At the second plague," he says, "a great mountain, burning with fire, was cast into the sea." <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 8:8, the second trumpet, to draw a parallel with the second vial he is currently explaining.</note> The preaching of the Gospel brings no such thing upon the impious who are like them, but it terribly condemns them to the future judgment. And so, just as the sinking of the burning mountain followed the song of the angel <note>Rupert often refers to the sounding of the trumpets as "songs" or "canticles" of the angels.</note> in the first instance, so this pouring out of the vial into the sea is called the second among the latest plagues.

"And it became," he says, "blood like that of a dead man." <note>Revelation 16:3</note> That is, the damnation of such impious people will be like the damnation of the devil, who has truly been dead for a long time—that is, he is opposed to the life of God. For they shall be joined with him when the Judge says: *Depart into the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels.* <note>Matthew 25:41</note> "And every living soul," he says, "died in the sea." This is because, clearly, it is not just a third part of the human race (of which the Egyptians were a part—for they themselves were born from one of the descendants of Ham, as has already been said), but every soul without distinction will be judged, whoever is in a sea of this kind, whether it be the soul of a Jew or a Greek. And rightly so: a soul that dies in this way is said to die "living" because whoever knowingly, and envying the good, works evil, is said to "live in sin"—just like Pharaoh, who persecuted the children of Israel not through ignorance, but through envy.

Upon such rivers and springs of water, when the third angel sounded his trumpet, a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven <note>Revelation 8:10</note>, that is, the wrath of God which destroyed the seven nations at the entry of the children of Israel under the leadership of Joshua. ...the sons of Israel, and they were already being tormented. Why then did Amalek come—who was descended from Edom, the brother of Jacob—and fight with Israel? Why did Edom himself come out armed to meet his brother?

<margin>The plague of the third [vial].</margin>
**And it became, he says, blood.**

Then [at the sounding of the trumpet] it did not happen this way; instead, a third part of the waters turned into wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they were made bitter. For many of the Canaanites—who belonged to that "third part" of humanity we have often mentioned <note>Rupert historically identifies the descendants of Ham (Canaanites/Egyptians) as the "third part" of the world's population in his symbolic scheme.</note>—survived at that time, and the children of Israel lived among them and <margin>Psalm 105</margin> <note>Psalm 106 in modern Bibles.</note> *learned their works, and served their idols, and it became a stumbling block to them.* This was surely the "turning of the waters into wormwood" for them; the waters became so bitter to those who drank that they incurred the wrath of their God because of it.

Furthermore, here where the third of the final plagues is poured out—that is, the third vial—it is not so. <margin>Water [becomes] blood.</margin> It is not a third part of the waters that becomes wormwood, but it universally becomes blood. For it is not only the descendants of Ham (who, as has often been said, was one of the three sons of Noah), but the whole universe of persecuting nations is condemned to eternal judgment through this third vial of God's wrath, so that there no longer remain any from among them who might be able to persecute or solicit His saints further. It follows.

<summary>Rupert explains the third vial of wrath, contrasting its total judgment (turning all water to blood) with the partial judgment of the third trumpet (wormwood). He uses the historical enmity of Amalek and Edom to show that the enemies of God's people are judged for their malice, not out of necessity.</summary>

> And I heard the angel of the waters saying: You are just, you who are, and who were holy, who have judged these things; because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you have also given them blood to drink, as they deserve. <note>original: "Et audiui angelū aquarū dicentē: Iustus es qui es, & qui eras sanctus..." This is Revelation 16:5-6.</note>

<margin>The angel of the waters, that is, of the faithful.</margin>
Who is this angel of the waters? Or rather, what kind of waters are these? Certainly, they are the faithful ones, of whom it is written in Isaiah: *His waters are faithful.* <margin>Isaiah 34</margin> <note>The text cites Chapter 34, but this passage is actually Isaiah 33:15-16. Rupert uses the word "faithful" (fideles) where the common Latin Bible uses "sure" (certae) to link the verse to the "faithful" believers.</note> *He who walks in justice and speaks the truth, who rejects greed born of oppression, and shakes his hands free from every bribe; who plugs his ear lest he hear of blood, and closes his eyes lest he see evil: he shall dwell on high, the heights of rocks shall be his stronghold, bread is given to him, and his waters are faithful.* Furthermore, these faithful waters are "living waters" which flow from the belly of the believer, just as the giver of those waters says: <margin>John 7</margin> *He who believes in me, as the scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.* <note>original: "flumina de vētre eius fluēt aquæ viuę."</note>

Therefore, this "angel of the waters" is the one to whom those waters belong, to whom they were given, and from whose belly they flow. Specifically, he represents every <term>scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven</term> <margin>Matthew 13. Malachi 2.</margin> <note>Rupert is referencing Matthew 13:52, where a "scribe" means a teacher of the faith.</note> and every faithful interpreter of the saints—or even the original authors of the scriptures. Because such a person’s "lips guard knowledge," he deserves in this passage to be called notably the "angel of the waters." This is not because he is only one man according to his person, but because according to faith, there is a single understanding among all. For indeed, among all who truly dwell within the "waters" of the holy scriptures, there is one spirit and one faith; and if you consult them rightly, they all speak in harmony and agree on this: that God is a just judge. Therefore, the angel of the waters says:

> You are just, you who are, and who were holy, who have judged these things; because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you have also given them blood to drink, as they deserve.

This description of the eternal God has already been used frequently in this scripture: *Who was, and who is, and who is to come.* However, this third part—"and who is to come"—is not mentioned here. This is because this confession of God's justice belongs to that final time, after which He is no longer "to come" <note>Rupert argues that because the judgment is currently happening in the vision, the "future" aspect of God's arrival is fulfilled.</note>. Therefore: *You who are, and who were*—that is, you who now remain forever, and who were before all ages.

<summary>Rupert identifies the "Angel of the Waters" not as a literal celestial being, but as the collective voice of faithful teachers and biblical interpreters who recognize the justice of God's final judgment.</summary>

<meta>catchword: concerning the bowl</meta>

...of those killed for the word of God and for the testimony which they held, and they cried out with a loud voice saying: "How long, O holy and true Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" <note>original: "Vsquequo domine sanctus & verus..." Quoting Revelation 6:9-10.</note> But as for the phrase, "I heard the altar saying," and the meaning being, "I heard those who were under the altar saying," this is not an unusual way of speaking among Grammarians. It is a figure of speech <note>original: *pertropum*, from the Greek *tropos*</note> called <gloss>metonymy</gloss> <gloss>metonymia</gloss>, which signifies the thing contained by naming the thing that contains it. Therefore, "I heard the altar saying," means I heard those under the altar whom I had heard before—not now crying out and demanding judgment or vengeance for their blood, but now that the vengeance they required has been carried out, they are praising the justice of the one who judges and avenges, saying: "Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments." True indeed in word, just in action.

Psalm 89:36 (88:37 in the Vulgate).</note>—namely, the Church, concerning which or in which Christ is the <term>Sun of Justice</term> <note>Latin: *sol iustitiae*. ...of the bowl of God's wrath, so that they might go into eternal fire.
Therefore, he poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to him to afflict men with heat and with fire.
This power was granted to this angel, namely to afflict carnal men—among whom, for example, there is jealousy and strife, which proves they are merely human—with a double evil: heat and fire. That is, with the power of judging in the present and in the future.
<margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin>
For concerning those who are outside, the Apostle [Paul] says: "What is it to us to judge?" <note>original: "quid ad nos iudicare?" referring to 1 Corinthians 5:12</note> and it should be understood as "in the present." For the prelates <term>prelates: high-ranking Church officials such as bishops or abbots</term> already judge those who are within the Church. For example, the same Apostle says: "I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged... to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord." <note>1 Corinthians 5:3-5</note> To judge in such a way is certainly to afflict men with "heat."
<margin>Heat: excommunication by the prelates.</margin>
For they burn with a certain heat of shame when they are separated from the assembly of the Church, so that it is not permitted even to say "hail" <note>a greeting or blessing</note> to them, nor to take food with such a person.
<margin>2 John 1</margin>

<header>On the 16th Chapter of the Apocalypse</header>

...of the beast, and his kingdom became dark. And they gnawed their tongues for pain, and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and wounds, and they did not repent of their works. <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 16:10–11.</note>

When the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, the smoking pit of the abyss was opened to them; but here, where the fifth angel poured out his bowl, the seat of the beast grows dark. In the other instances, both in the sounding of the trumpets and the pouring of the bowls, the objects or parts of the world are mentioned by the same names: the earth, the sea, the rivers and springs, the sun, and the river Euphrates. Here, however, the naming varies, since the "seat of the beast" is written instead of the "pit of the abyss."

<margin>
The seat of the beast is a lie.
</margin>

<margin>
The fifth bowl is against heretics.
</margin>

What, I ask, is the seat of the beast, if not that upon which the beast rests? And what is that if not a lie <note>original: "mendacium"</note>? Indeed, just as the authority of God is nothing but the truth, so the support of the devil is nothing but a lie. Therefore, just as a lie is understood there in the pit of the abyss, so it is rightly understood here in the seat of the beast. Certainly, from the moment when the devil’s lie manifested itself through the tongues of heretics, the venerable order of the holy fathers rose up against it, convicted their treachery <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> with ready testimonies from the Scriptures, and furthermore condemned it with an eternal curse <term>anathema: a formal ecclesiastical curse that excommunicates a person or denounces a doctrine</term>. From that time, this angel poured out his bowl upon the seat of the beast. But what did the heretics do in response? Did they rest and obey the victorious truth? Not at all; on the contrary, they grew more insane, expanded their impiety further, and caused the whole world to suffer in their madness. It follows, then:

**And his kingdom became dark, and they gnawed their tongues for pain.**

For they themselves are, or were, the kingdom of the beast, since they are the ones in whom that seat of the beast—that is, falsehood—found a prepared place. Therefore, when the bowl was poured out, the kingdom of the beast became dark: because once the judicial sentences were passed upon the treachery of the heretics, they, smoking with fury and envy, were blinded even further. But how did these people gnaw their tongues?

Truly, they think against themselves and speak against themselves, fighting against one another through the contradictions of their various sects. For this "pain" is not to be understood in any other way than in that place where it is written: *Behold, he is in labor with injustice; he has conceived pain and brought forth iniquity.* <note>Quoting Psalm 7:14.</note> Likewise: *His mouth is full of cursing, and bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are labor and pain.* <note>Quoting Psalm 10:7 (Psalm 9:28 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> Because of this kind of pain, they have gnawed their tongues; that is, because of the envy that leads them to create sects contrary to one another, they have infested themselves with their own tongues. <margin>The blasphemy of Arius out of hatred.</margin>
A remarkable thing. "And they blasphemed God," it says. Why? "Because of their pains and their wounds"—that is, because of their private envies and hatreds, which are indeed wounds not of the body, but of the heart. This is astonishing, yet it is true. For example, as the records of the Church testify, it was because of his hatred for his bishop, Alexander, that the priest Arius <term>Arius: A 4th-century priest whose denial of Christ’s full divinity led to the Council of Nicaea and the first major split in Christianity.</term> broke out into blasphemy against God. To stir up a scandal against Alexander—because he hated and envied him—Arius began to teach dogmas about the Son of God that were contrary to the truth. Therefore, it is spoken truly and universally of all heretics: they blasphemed God because of their pains and wounds. Finally, it says:

->*And they did not repent of their works.*<-

<margin>Heretics sin against the Holy Spirit.</margin>
How could those who spoke words against the Holy Spirit perform penance <note>original: "pœnitentiam," meaning repentance or the act of penance.</note>? Indeed, as the authority of the earlier Church Fathers hands down to us, a person speaks a word against the Holy Spirit when they contradict the Holy Scriptures not out of ignorance, but out of envy—for these Scriptures are undoubtedly the voices of...

<margin>The plague of the sixth trumpet upon bodies.</margin>
When the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, four angels were released who had been bound at the great river Euphrates, and the plague was one that seized the people of God through the four principal kingdoms of the world, under which the children of Israel or Judah were afflicted by the judgment of God. <note>Rupert is comparing the "Trumpets" of Revelation 9 with the "Bowls" of Revelation 16. <margin>The plague of the sixth bowl upon souls.</margin>
But truly, this bowl of the wrath of God is poured into the river—into that river, not so that such angels might be released, but so that its waters might be dried up, and the way prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. Therefore, the bowl of God's wrath is poured into the water of the river, and for that reason, we must understand this "water" to be something to which the wrath of God is deservedly owed. Otherwise, since the sea, the rivers, and the springs of water have already been condemned to blood by the previous bowls, why is it that the river Euphrates deserves its own specific bowl? ...which we have not yet touched upon in the previous bowls, because here it is rightly understood that through the waters of that river, and then through the three unclean spirits crawling out in the manner of frogs, [certain things] are signified. Truly this evil is three-pronged, and its parts are the magic of the sorcerers, the fabrications of the philosophers, and the fables of the poets. Their profound malice and turbid talkativeness are fittingly signified by the waters 
<margin>Euphrates.</margin>
of the Euphrates. Because, as is evident, the Euphrates is the river of Babylon, and flowing through it, it is divided into many heads; by its very name in the Scriptures, it is accustomed to signify the entire generation of the impious—the city contrary to the generation of the righteous, the city of the devil contrary to the city of God. Babylon is interpreted as "confusion." <note>Rupert relies on the traditional medieval etymological link between Babylon and the Hebrew 'Babel' (confusion), representing the chaotic city of man.</note> Therefore, after the bowls were poured out onto the sea and the rivers and springs of water, this one too was poured into the Euphrates: because the tyrants or impious kings, along with the nations subject to them, acquire condemnation for themselves. That same wrath is also owed to those who drove them to madness and increased their errors with empty talk—or rather, with writings that are contentious, deceitful, and full of fables.
<margin>
The Prophets
did not cross 
the Euphrates
as the Apostles
did.
</margin>
Before the wrath of God from heaven was revealed upon the waters through the Gospel of Christ, the holy kings could not cross them—that is, those who were the leaders and authors of the Scriptures of truth. Some of these were indeed kings in their earthly status, who are rightly said to have "come from the rising of the sun," because they did not come or act of their own accord; rather, they received what they spoke from the illumination of the Divinity. Those kings were not able to cross those waters; they could not, with their [simple] Hebrew tongue, contend with the eloquent Greeks, the learned Latin grammarians, the rhetoricians, the logicians <term>dialecticians: practitioners of formal logic</term>, and the many poets—epic, comic, and satiric.

<summary>Rupert interprets the Euphrates as a symbol of worldly "confusion" and pagan intellectualism (philosophy, poetry, and magic). <margin>The unclean spirits preside over magicians, poets, and philosophers.</margin>
By "unclean spirits," he means the "sects" <note>original: "sectas" — here referring to schools of thought or disciplines.</note> of a sort of wisdom and knowledge: the magical, the poetic, and the philosophical. Poets, under honorable names, ask those same unclean spirits to breathe into them, calling them "gods" with sacrilegious presumption when they are actually demons. Furthermore, he who breathed his spirit into the philosophers was also undoubtedly unclean. 
<margin>Romans 1.</margin>
Does the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note> not say of them: *because claiming to be wise, they became fools, and vanished into their own thoughts*? And see how far into uncleanness they vanished—they who, serving the creature rather than the Creator, were for that reason already delivered up into shameful passions or into the desires of their hearts for uncleanness. Therefore they are rightly called "unclean spirits." Furthermore, by the name of the "dragon," the devil is meant; while by the name of the "beast," the beast-like kingdom of the devil is rightly understood to be designated in this place. For in the Book of Daniel, four principal kingdoms of the world are signified by four beasts—namely, the Babylonian, the Persian (or Median), the Macedonian, and the Roman. From the mouth of the dragon the first spirit <note>The spirit of Magic.</note> proceeded, because human curiosity learned the magic art from the storytelling of the devil. From the mouth of the beast the next spirit <note>The spirit of Poetry.</note> went out, because the ignobility of the human mind, by flattering the beast-like kingdom of this world, elevated earthly kings (who were but men) into gods through poetic fictions, and translated them into heaven and the spheres of the stars with fabulous nonsense...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the "three unclean spirits like frogs" as the disciplines of magic, poetry, and philosophy, which he views as demonic corruptions of human thought. He links the "dragon" to the origin of magic and the "beast" to the poetic deification of secular rulers.</summary>

This is understood, however, with a distinction: we should weigh more of the wrath of the living God in this seventh bowl than in that seventh trumpet. For these are the "last plagues," while those were the first. They are distinguished by the fact that those [the trumpets] are divisions and distinctions of visible evils, while these [the bowls] are of invisible ones. Therefore, in that seventh trumpet, we understand the visible conflagration of this whole world; in this seventh bowl, we rightly understand that fullness of damnation by which the demons are to be punished—those who now wander through this air, having been cast down from heaven. For this is what it says:

> **And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air.**

<margin>The pouring of the seventh bowl upon the demons.</margin>
That is, upon the aerial throngs or powers. The seventh bowl is rightly poured upon them because, clearly, whatever evils are punished in the preceding six bowls redound upon those who were the instigators of those very evils. Hence, they are the principalities and powers, and the rulers of this world, of darkness...

But those men who are of this sort—impious, and rebels against justice and truth—the more they are rebuked, the worse they become; indeed, they sometimes even resist the word, and they contradict and curse. It follows, therefore:

<margin>
Blasphemies of the impious against the word of God. 
Acts 18.
</margin>
> **And men blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it had become exceedingly great.** 

Which is to say: the impious turned themselves to blasphemies because of the insurmountable constancy of the preaching. Because they could not be defended by reason, they raged with curses, for there was such a great spirit of wisdom and strength in those preachers that they could in no way be overcome. Such first were the Jews, of whom Luke speaks in the Acts of the Apostles:

Ultimately, in this place, the waters are the peoples or nations. Because this whore sits upon many waters—that is, because there are many peoples or nations over whom lust dominates—therefore, when he had said, "I will show you the condemnation of the whore," he added "the great." But certainly such greatness of hers is deceptive, because it does not stand. Nor was it in vain that it pleased the Spirit to signify the nations or peoples here through "waters." For nations flow through the generation of the flesh, and they flow away from their very beginning...

<margin>The Whore, desire</margin>

Therefore, that very multitude of waters—that is, of peoples or nations—is the beast. This is truly the case, because the woman who sits upon such a multitude of waters is the "whore," which is <term>cupiditas: a technical term in medieval theology for disordered desire or greed for worldly things</term>, which drives her to live in a beastly manner. <margin>Kings in seven parts of the kingdoms.</margin>
The one and the same Alexander <note>original: "Alexandrum"; referring to Alexander the Great</note>, after his death, was divided into the four winds of heaven, and one kingdom began to have four kings, and in this way the ten horns are made—that is, ten kings. Truly, the **names of blasphemy** were names of usurped divinity: because, clearly, by flattering their kings while governing the kingdoms of the world, they wished them to be held as gods, and they especially exalted the deceased to heaven with false praises. "Upon such a beast I saw," he said, "a woman sitting," that is, **desire** <note>original: "cupiditatem"</note> and the corruption of all vices reigning.

> **And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet color, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication, and upon her forehead was a name written: Mystery, Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth. <margin>Two causes of damnation against this whore.</margin>
About to see the damnation of the woman or the whore according to the response of the speaking angel: 
> **Come; I will show unto thee the judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters,**

he first testifies that he has seen the causes of that same damnation. The first of these is that she took up a public profession of the fornications and abominations of the earth. For it is said: 
> **And on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications and abominations.**

Clearly, he accuses her of public profession; namely, that the **City of the Devil** <note>A common medieval trope, derived from St. Augustine, contrasting the 'City of God' with the 'City of Man/Devil'</note> does not only sin or commit "fornication," but even glories in those very sins and fornications of hers. The second cause of her damnation is that she shed the blood of the saints who did not consent to her. For this is what he says when reporting his vision: "And I saw," he said, "the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus." Therefore, let us look more diligently at these two causes of her damnation prescribed here.

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 17. On the previous page, Rupert established that the woman represents "cupiditas" (disordered desire or greed) and began discussing her visual appearance as described in the biblical text. He continues here by interpreting her clothing and ornaments as symbols of royal pride and the violent history of earthly empires.</meta>

### And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet.

<margin>The greed of kings.</margin>
Purple is the garment of royalty, and it signifies all the courtly power or pride of the kingdoms and kings of this world. Furthermore, who does not know that murderous cruelty has almost always accompanied royal power? Books are full—indeed, the theaters of the world are already satiated—with the tragedies of kings who, out of a greed for ruling, not only took up arms against foreigners, but even drove the cruel sword into their own kinsmen, brothers, or even parents, because they would not endure partners or rivals in their kingdom. Therefore, scarlet <note>original: "coccinum"; often associated with blood or fire</note> is rightly joined with purple by saying: *And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet*, because indeed the fiery cruelty of murders has always accompanied the purple of kingdoms. It is beautifully stated that she was "clothed" in purple, for by this saying he reminds the watchful listener how much vanity exists in the royal dress of the proud. For on the outside they can be colored with beautiful appearances—of which royal purple seems the finest—but inside, or beneath that same purple, their mortal bodies are no less wretched and decaying than those of peasants, not only because of the ulcers of overflowing lust, but also through various types of accidental diseases.

### And gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls.

<margin>False and borrowed beauty in gold and gems.</margin>
All these are the riches of the woman; all these are the fruits of human greed <note>original: "cupiditatis"</note>, which is false and deceptive. For human presumption seeks a beauty outside itself and affects a borrowed brilliance as if it were its own; since it is unable to change its own nature—for she herself is but mud—she surrounds herself with shimmering gold, precious stones, and pearls. Thus, even while sometimes foul with sores or pale with leprosy, she may shine most proudly from above with such trappings that do not truly belong to her. Moreover, in this regard, she is always a great burden to the rational intentions of the elect <note>the "electi" or those chosen by God</note>, and she wearies their minds with manifold temptation. It follows:

### Having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the Whore of Babylon’s purple and scarlet clothing as symbols of royal pride and the bloodstained history of earthly power. He contrasts the external splendor of gold and jewels with the internal corruption and mortality common to all people.</summary>
<keywords>Revelation 17, Whore of Babylon, purple and scarlet, royal pride, greed, vanity, Rupert of Deutz, biblical commentary, mortality, corruption</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s exposition of Revelation 17, moving from the description of the woman’s clothing to the "golden cup" she holds. In the previous section, Rupert associated her scarlet and purple garments with the bloodstained pride of earthly kingdoms. ...of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication.
<margin>Her drink: error and oblivion</margin>
For what purpose is she said to have a cup in her hand, if not to serve and offer her drink to all who pass by? And what is her drink, except error and oblivion, by which the human senses—soaked in the allurements of vices—withdraw from God? Therefore, the woman is said to have in her hand a cup full of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication, by which surely the entire fruit or effect of greed <note>original: "cupiditas"; Rupert uses this term to mean a disordered, grasping desire for power or material things</note> is to subvert the rational man and to utterly overwhelm his senses. Thus, he commits fornication in mind and body away from the living and true God, handed over in his soul to idolatry and subjected in his body to every impurity and all shameful passions. And one must note the persistence of her wicked intention: to better entice and more quickly deceive, she is said to have in her hand not a wooden or bronze cup, but a golden one. Surely this woman seized such a cup when, to more easily seduce the greedy and ambitious eyes of men, the kings of the world established idols that were not only stone or wood, but even golden; to worship these was indeed the height of abominations and the beginning of all impurity and fornication.
<margin>1 Kings 12: The golden calves of Jeroboam.</margin>
For example: when Jeroboam made golden calves—not wooden or stone ones—placing one in Bethel and the other in Dan <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel; he set up these idols to prevent his people from traveling to the Temple in Jerusalem</note>, then surely the woman had a golden cup in her hand, full of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication. This was because the greed for ruling, which sat so heavily upon that man, deceived the eyes of the common people through the beauty of the gold, so that they drank the fornication of the one saying: *These are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of Egypt*, so that they might commit fornication away from their God, and withdraw from the house of David and from the temple of the Lord which was in Jerusalem. This was especially effective because among such gods they were permitted to eat and commit fornication, to pollute and be polluted, and to afflict their own bodies with every abomination and impurity. The Gentiles practiced such outrages not even in secret, but—what is worse—they frequented them boastfully, publicly, and everywhere. From which also...

<summary>Rupert interprets the Woman's golden cup as a symbol of "error and oblivion," using the biblical story of Jeroboam’s golden calves to illustrate how the "gold" of worldly power and beauty seduces people into idolatry and moral decay.</summary>

Gymnasiums of the youths

...concerning a certain sacrilegious man of the Jewish nation, it is written in the book of Maccabees that he dared to establish a gymnasium and a center for youth training <note>original: "ephebiā"; referring to the Greek system of physical and social education for young men</note> in Jerusalem according to the custom of the Gentiles, and to place the best of the youths in brothels. <margin>Proverbs 2</margin>
For this is the same as saying: the citizens of the devil's city do not even hide the works of their own filthiness; rather, they "rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the most wicked things." <note>Quoting Proverbs 2:14</note> Finally, what does it mean to have a name written on the forehead, which is "Babylon," if not to bear witness to works of confusion by public profession? <note>Rupert follows the common medieval etymology where "Babylon" means "confusion."</note>

<margin>Jeremiah 3</margin>
Hence, God says to the prostituted Judea through the prophet by way of reproach: "You have been made with the forehead of a harlot woman, and you refused to blush." <note>Quoting Jeremiah 3:3</note> Therefore, this woman is rightly said to have a name written on her forehead—*Babylon the Great, the mother of the fornications and the abominations of the earth*—because she herself is the body or the entire assembly of the impious, who invented fornications and abominations and walk boldly <note>original: "frontosi"; literally "forehead-y," meaning brazen or shameless</note> in these inventions of theirs. Of them it is likewise written: "They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and they did not hide it."

<margin>
Isaiah 3
</margin>
But since this is so, and she has such a thing written on her forehead, and she prides herself in the worst matters—saying that she is Babylon the Great and magnifying her fornications—how is that which is given as written in the open also called a "mystery"? For the text says: *And on her forehead was written a mystery.* This is said either ironically, or because nature itself intends every act of fornication in which this prostitute glories to be a "mystery"—that is, a secret. Even though the prostitute's boldness proclaims it, natural shame still struggles to keep it hidden.

<margin>
How a public crime is here called a "mystery"
</margin>
This (as has already been said above) is the first cause shown for her damnation. There follows another cause being declared:

> **And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.**

<summary>Rupert interprets the title on the woman's forehead as a sign of shamelessness, where sin is publicly displayed rather than hidden. He explains the "mystery" of her name as an ironic contrast between the public nature of her crimes and the natural instinct to hide such shameful acts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 17, specifically moving from the harlot's outward appearance and title to her actions—the shedding of blood. Rupert is identifying the "harlot" not as a single individual, but as a collective body of the unfaithful throughout history, beginning with those who persecuted the prophets in the Old Testament.</meta>

<page-num>456</page-num>

He had already seen the attire of this harlot, which was of such a kind that, if it were the only thing [against her], it could have sufficed for her condemnation. But she, not content to be such as the previous description indicates, added this other evil: that she shed the blood of the saints, because she saw that they did not consent to the impurities of her fornications. Rightly, therefore, he interjected the repeated word of the vision, saying: *And I saw* <note>original: "Et vidi"</note>, because he did not see another woman or harlot, but another iniquity of the same one. Furthermore, it should be noted 

<margin>The blood of the saints and martyrs.</margin>
that he made a distinction between the "saints" and "martyrs of Jesus" by saying: *of the blood of the saints, and of the blood of the martyrs of Jesus*. This wonder belongs to an imperfect heart. For a perfect heart does not much admire or highly value the purple and scarlet, the gold, precious stones, and pearls of the harlot. Thus, this John also testifies that he "wondered with great admiration" in the person of those who, having weak hearts, looked upon the brilliance of the great harlot while they themselves were being troubled; for truly, in his own right, he would never deign to wonder at such things. Furthermore, for any of God's elect who wonder (or have wondered) at that harlot through weakness, the consolation of the Holy Spirit has not been—and cannot be—lacking. ### Page 464 Rupert’s Commentary. Book 10.

> and he is of the seven, and goes into destruction. <note>original: "et de septem est, et in interitum vadet." Revelation 17:11</note>

In this passage, the beast must be understood as one specific head of the beast, which is clearly the **Antichrist**. This beast, he says, is both the eighth and is of the seven. This is the same as saying that the Antichrist is one and the same head of the beast, being both the eighth and the seventh. This, of course, could not stand or be understood unless it were established that in one and the same Antichrist there are two aspects existing together. For that <term>son of perdition</term> <note>A biblical title for the Antichrist, implying one destined for waste and ruin.</note> is simultaneously both man and devil. Therefore, if you only attend to what is seen outwardly in the Antichrist, he is "of the seven," because he is of the same kind or nature as the other kings or impious men. If, however, you look at what lies hidden within, he is the eighth head, because he is the devil, who—before he entered the dwelling of that lost man—raised himself up against God in heaven and even now remains invisibly proud. Nevertheless, he says, "he goes into destruction," because it is as easy for God to send both man and devil together into destruction as it is to send a simple or lone man, so that it may be truly said of both that "he was and is not," while God always is. It follows:

> And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but they will receive power as kings for one hour after the beast. <note>Revelation 17:12</note>

<margin>
The Antichrist as a man is the seventh beast; as the devil, he is the eighth.
</margin>
This has already been discussed above: there are indeed seven very well-known kingdoms in the series of the Holy Scriptures which exercised enmity against the saints of the Most High. However, there are ten kings of those same kingdoms because one of them—the **kingdom of the Macedonians**—was divided among the four successors of **Alexander the Great** through the "four winds of heaven" after his death. Each of these successors placed crowns upon themselves, and in this way, ten kings were created. For this reason, he said earlier "and there are seven kings," but now says "there are ten kings." This is because three of those successors of Alexander are recorded as having done nothing against the people of God; only that fourth one, who held **Syria** <note>Reference to the Seleucid Empire, specifically Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a famous persecutor of the Jews.</note>, was an enemy. Therefore, they are ten in number, but in terms of [their actions...]

# On Revelation, Chapter 17

465

G

...in action pertaining to the present cause—that is, for the persecution of martyrs—there are only seven. However, since he said a little while ago, "five have fallen, and one is," <note>original: "quinque ceciderunt, & unus est"</note> why does he now say, "who have not yet received a kingdom"? <note>original: "qui regnum nondum acceperunt"</note> Clearly, he says this with a wonderful irony, as if to say: they indeed seemed to reign, and they usurped the rank and the name of "kingdom" for themselves, but in truth they never reigned. For their kingdom is not truly a kingdom; the kingdom belongs to the Lord alone. 

This refers to what he said earlier in his rebuke: "Why do you wonder?" <note>original: "Quare miraris?"</note> For truly, kings of this sort are not to be wondered at, but are to be judged as miserable; they committed so many homicides in order to reign, yet they have fallen and are dead, and they "have not yet received a kingdom." But what then? "They will receive power," he says, "as if they were kings, for one hour after the beast." <note>original: "post bestiam." Note: Standard biblical versions usually say "with the beast" (cum bestia), but Rupert's text reads "after" or "following."</note> They do not receive a true kingdom, but they will receive a certain power "as kings," and this for "one hour after the beast," as if he were saying: You should not think that their voices or their power ought to be called a "kingdom" anymore. For the word "kingdom" implies a long duration of power. But they have received, or will receive, power not for a long duration, but for "one hour." 

Now, he said "they will receive" in the future tense because when the Antichrist comes, he will restore the strengths or the kingdoms of those same kings who have already fallen for the purpose of persecuting the saints. Furthermore, he briefly hints at what kind of power they will receive when he says, "after the beast." For it is the same as if he were saying: "for the shedding of the blood of the saints," because the power of the beast is not truly for reigning, but for raging—for the shedding of blood. Therefore, it was beautifully and truly said, "that they have not yet received a kingdom." It follows:

> These have one purpose, and they will hand over their strength and power to the beast. These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because he is the Lord of lords and King of kings, and those who are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful.

"These," he says, "have one purpose": it is understood that when the Antichrist comes and remains for a short time, all <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the next page.</note>

po<gloss>t</gloss>eſtas <note>The small 't' was added as an interlinear correction in the original manuscript to complete the word "potestas" (power).</note>

<summary>Rupert argues that the "ten kings" mentioned in Revelation do not possess true sovereignty, which belongs only to God, but rather a fleeting, "one-hour" power used for persecution. He interprets their future "kingdom" as a restoration of ancient persecutory powers by the Antichrist to wage war against the Lamb.</summary>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book [X]

466

...for they will conspire to the consensus of that **son of perdition** <note>original: "filij perditionis." A title for the Antichrist drawn from 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>. What of those kings who existed before the coming of that same Antichrist? Did they not already share one plan with the one who is to come? Did they not have the same intention? Did they not have the same will? For by whatever plan, intention, and will he will persecute the saints when he comes, with that same will the King of Egypt and the others—about whom we have already spoken—afflicted the people of God in each of their own times. Their goal was that no one would remain mindful of the one true God; and in them and through them, the devil worked to make void the faith of the promise—specifically the promise of the "seed," which is Christ, whom God promised to our fathers. <margin>The ancient plan of the serpent.</margin> This was the ancient plan of that serpent from the moment he first deceived man: namely, that no human should be saved. With this same plan, he armed all those we have often mentioned: the Egyptians, the carnal Israelites, the Babylonians, the Persians or Medes, the Macedonians, the kings named Antiochus, the Roman Caesars, and finally, he will raise up the head of this same plan in that often-mentioned **man of sin**, the Antichrist. Truly, therefore, they share one plan.

**And they will hand over their strength, he says, and their power to the beast.** <note>original: "Et virtutẽ... & ptãtem suã bestiæ tradẽt." Revelation 17:13.</note> 
This is as if he were to say: "What they intended, they were not or will not be able to fulfill, but the devil whom they serve will make his own man, the Antichrist, the heir of their strength and power." It is as if the devil hopes that what he could not accomplish through the others, he might at least be able to achieve through this "illustrious" <term>egregium</term> <note>Rupert uses this term ironically to describe the Antichrist as a "distinguished" or "preeminent" vessel of evil.</note> successor. But what follows?

**These will fight with the lamb, he says, and the lamb will overcome them.** <note>original: "Hi cũ agno pugnabũt... & agnus vícet illos." Revelation 17:14.</note>
All of them were conquered long ago, each in their own time, and yet they will all be conquered together once more in the person of the Antichrist. And it is a beautiful thing that, although he could have said, "these will fight with Christ, and Christ will overcome them," he preferred to say: "These will fight with the lamb, and the lamb will overcome them." For truly, that first enemy—the Egyptian king—was conquered through the sacrifice of the lamb <margin>Exodus 12.</margin> so that he might release the children of Israel; and when he pursued them, he was overwhelmed <note>original: "rumensus" likely a variant or error for "submersus" (drowned/submerged).</note> in the sea. Therefore, although he speaks of the future, saying, "These will fight with the lamb, and the lamb will overcome them," nevertheless also...

He explains the symbolic significance of Christ being called "the Lamb" in this conflict, linking the final victory to the original defeat of Pharaoh during the Exodus.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter 17

467

It must be understood regarding the time before this John, that they fought with the Lamb, and the Lamb conquered them. For John here bears the likeness <note>original: "typum gerit." In medieval theology, a 'type' is a historical person or event that foreshadows a spiritual reality.</note> of all those who, from of old since the people of God began to be afflicted under the aforementioned kingdoms, earned divine consolation. This is wonderful, indeed praiseworthy and true, because before this Lamb had come into this world, these [kings] fought with the Lamb, and he himself conquered them. Whence quite elegantly in the prophet it is commanded that his name be called: <margin>Isaiah 8</margin> "Strip the spoils quickly, plunder fast" <note>original: "velociter spolia detrahe, cito prędare." This refers to the prophetic name 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz' in Isaiah 8:1–4, symbolizing the rapid defeat of Israel's enemies.</note> or, "Hasten to take the spoils, hurry to plunder." Why? Because, he says, before the child knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians. This is the same as if he were to say: This child who is the Savior, before he comes into this world by birth, knowing or having experienced his mother, the Virgin, and Joseph, his adoptive father, he himself will deliver Israel from the hand of its enemies. <margin>Christ conquered those kings before he was born.</margin> A wonderful acceleration, a marvelous haste, that a child not yet born should himself deliver the people who hold or expect the promise of his birth. This, however, is so true that he who does not believe it is not a believer. For it is necessary to believe that before this child was born of his mother, he was God Almighty with the Father. Whence, when it had been said: "And the Lamb will conquer them," it immediately followed:

->**For he is the Lord of lords and King of kings.**<-

Did he not, before he was born, conquer the Babylonians as well, and the Persians or Medes, and the Macedonians, who fought against him—that is, against his own people who held faith in his coming—and held them captive? For what else was being demonstrated to King Nebuchadnezzar or to the prophet Daniel when the stone cut without hands <margin>Daniel 2</margin> struck the great statue, and the gold, silver, bronze, and iron were crushed together? <note>Referring to the vision in Daniel 2:31-45, where a stone (Christ) destroys a statue representing successive worldly empires.</note> What, I say, did it mean except that Christ, who is (as is said here) the Lamb, was hastening to conquer with wonderful haste (as has been said) before he was born, and did not allow his chosen ones, held captive under those kingdoms, to be tempted beyond what they were able to bear?

<summary>Rupert argues that Christ, the eternal "Lamb," defeated historical pagan empires like Babylon and Persia even before his physical birth. He links this to the prophetic "stone" in Daniel and the rapid victory promised in Isaiah, emphasizing Christ's eternal divinity.</summary>

### Rupert’s Commentary, Book 10

470

A strange assertion, a strange and violent loathing of the ungodly! How can the kings, who are represented by the horns, be said to hate their own harlot <note>The "harlot" here is a metaphor for the enticing but corrupting glory and greed of the material world.</note> with whom they themselves commit fornication? For they are the very same kings, and no others, of whom it was said above: *Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits upon many waters*, to which was added: *with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication.* Therefore, the very ones who fornicate with her are said to hate her, and to make her desolate and naked, and to eat her flesh, and to burn her with fire. This is strange, yet it is true. For who does not know how much the kings of the world have always been restless with hatred? And against whom have they been hostile in their restlessness, if not against that very greed or worldly glory with which they surely committed fornication by preferring it to their Creator? The instruments of their fornication were the beauties of cities and the wealthy multitudes of the nations over whom they ruled, and all other such things in the world that provoke the "lust of the eyes." Yet they never permitted these things to flourish in peace; they desolated everything with wars, slaughtered crowds of men with the sword, and burned cities and fortresses with fire. Nor did they do these things in a hostile manner only against each other—kings against kings, or kingdoms against kingdoms—but individual kings very often brought these evils upon their own people and their own cities.

<margin>Nero’s hatred toward the Roman realm.</margin>
For to say nothing of the others, who ever existed as a more cruel or wicked enemy to the Roman city, its people, and its Senate than its own emperor, Nero? He made the city desolate; he, by killing the people and the Senate, in a certain sense "ate her flesh." He also burned the city with physical fire, solely so that he might delight in the beauty of the flame, watching in that likeness how Troy had once burned; and sitting in the highest tower of Maecenas, dancing at such a spectacle, he sang the *Iliad* aloud.

<margin>Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 2, Poem 6.</margin>
Someone, remembering and mourning such great cruelty, sang thus:

> We know how much ruin he wrought,
> With the city in flames and the senators slain,
> That cruel man who, having murdered his brother,
> Was drenched in his mother’s spilled blood.
> Alas, a heavy fate! etc. <note>original: "Novimus quantas dederit ruinas... Heu gravem sortem." Rupert quotes Boethius to illustrate the self-destructive nature of tyrants who destroy the very "harlot" (the world/state) they desire to possess.</note>

It is true, therefore, that the kings of the earth, who abandoned God to commit fornication with the beauty of worldly creation, hated their harlot; and what kind of violent hatreds they threatened...

<summary>Rupert explains the paradox of Revelation 17:16, where the kings of the earth destroy the Harlot they once loved. He uses the Emperor Nero as a historical example of a ruler destroying his own kingdom and people out of perverse desire and cruelty.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter 17

<margin>Isaiah 57. The wretched condition of temporal kingdoms.</margin>
...they offered the price of their fornication, and they have returned it to him. <note>original: "strabāt pręciū suę fornicationis, illi reddiderūt." Rupert is likely referring to the cyclic nature of worldly greed.</note> "There is no peace for the wicked," says the Lord. <note>A reference to Isaiah 48:22 or 57:21.</note> O, therefore, how wretched is the condition of Babylon, the earthly city, which commits fornication away from God with her lovers! For she does not even merely fornicate with lovers, but with enemies; and if there is any love among them, it is mixed with such bitterness of gall that they hostilly tear apart the very one with whom they fornicate. The cause or inciter of these evils is the devil. Therefore, the Scripture did not only say, "and the ten horns which you saw, these shall hate the harlot," but it says, "and the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these shall hate their harlot," etc. He immediately adds:
**For God has put it into their hearts to do what is pleasing to him, to give their kingdom to the beast until the words of God are fulfilled.**

"To do," he says, "what is pleasing to him." To whom? This seems to refer to God, because it was phrased this way: "God gave it into their hearts." And so it is understood that they do what is pleasing to *him*—meaning to God. However, because he had previously stated, "And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these shall hate the harlot," and then, after saying "to do what is pleasing to him," he added "to give their kingdom to the beast," it is more correctly referred to the same beast. That is, so that they may do what is pleasing to *it*—meaning the beast—and then give their kingdom to the beast. This means they expend the strength of their whole kingdom upon the devil by doing his will, which is always opposed to God's good purpose.

<margin>Doing evil does not please God. Psalm 5. Isaiah 45.</margin>
For what do they do but evil? Now, evil does not please God; indeed, He himself hates those who work evil, as Scripture bears witness, saying: "You have hated all who work iniquity." <note>Psalm 5:5.</note> Likewise: "For you are not a God who wills iniquity." <note>Psalm 5:4.</note> But on the other hand, the Scripture says: "Making peace, and creating evil." <note>Isaiah 45:7.</note> Between these statements, according to the logic of truth and according to the truthful authority of the orthodox <term>Fathers</term> <note>The early Christian theologians and bishops who established church doctrine.</note>, it must be said and held that that "evil"—

<margin>In what way God creates evil.</margin>
which is affliction or war, the opposite of the "peace" of which it was said "making peace"—God sometimes creates for the sake of correction. But "evil" in the sense of iniquity or sin, He neither creates, nor is it pleasing to Him. And it is indeed of His will that war or some other such affliction, when...

<summary>Rupert explains that while the wicked kings serve the Beast (the Devil) out of their own malice, God paradoxically uses their actions to fulfill His divine judgment. He clarifies the theological distinction between the "evil" of sin (which God hates) and the "evil" of suffering or punishment (which God may ordain for correction).</summary>

### Rupert of Deutz: Commentary on Revelation, Book 10

472

...should come upon those who, because of their preceding sins, deserve to suffer, they cannot escape; however, it was never, nor is it now, pleasing to Him that men should do evil or that they should become evil. 

The question is therefore asked: If the evil they do, or the very fact that they are evil, is not pleasing to God, how is it stated here previously: "For God has put it into their hearts"? <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 17:17: "For God has put it into their hearts to accomplish his purpose."</note> While this is being asked, one must simultaneously or consequently ask about what the Psalmist says:
<margin>Psalm 103</margin>
> He turned their heart so that they hated his people, and dealt deceitfully with his servants. <note>original: "conuertit cor eorum vt odirent populum eius, & dolum facerent in seruos eius." This is Psalm 105:25 in modern numbering (104 in the Vulgate).</note>

However, that must be understood in such a way that no suspicion ever finds a place in the heart of man as if God were ever the author of hatred or deceit; to even suspect such a thing is the height of madness and impiety. For God neither hardened Pharaoh, nor did He turn the heart of the Egyptians toward hatred by desiring their hardness or hatred, but only by doing good things for the children of Israel, multiplying them in that land just as He had promised to Abraham, saying:
<margin>Genesis 22</margin>
> I will bless you, and I will multiply your seed. <note>original: "Benedicā tibi, & multiplicabo semen tuum."</note>

<margin>How God hardened Pharaoh’s heart.</margin>
But Pharaoh and the Egyptians were as proud as they were envious; and according to the custom of the envious, the more or greater divine benefits they saw bestowed upon those whom they envied, the more they raged against them with greater hatred. 
<margin>Exodus 7</margin>
Foreseeing this, God said to Moses:
> I will harden Pharaoh's heart. <note>original: "Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis."</note>

This is the same as if He were to say: "I indeed will perform signs and wonders for the children of Israel before Pharaoh and his servants; but because they are envious, this will serve for nothing else for them except that they will be hardened with greater hatred against them." Father Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential theologian whose works Rupert frequently cites to support his interpretations.</note> explains the aforementioned verse in this sense. Therefore, what is said here—"For God has put it into their hearts"—must be understood in this way: we should by no means suspect that God put anything into the hearts of any of those kings so that they would do something evil, or that they themselves would become evil. Rather, God performed the good things He willed for each kingdom in its own time, but the kings of the world were as proud as they were envious, and they were envious of each other's prosperity. 

For example: God made the affairs of Babylon prosperous, so that they might be stronger than the other nations. And lest there be any doubt that this [was given] to them by God...

<summary>Rupert explains that God does not "create" evil in human hearts; rather, the wicked (like Pharaoh) react to God's blessings with envy and pride, which "hardens" them. He applies this logic to Revelation, arguing that God's "putting it into the hearts" of kings refers to His providential governance that the wicked misuse.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter 17

<margin>Jeremiah 27</margin>

This means that the success granted to one nation by the gift of God incited the envious hearts of others toward hatred. In this way, they were stirred up against one another through envy, so that they might spend all the power of their kingdoms in a competitive service to diabolical malice. For how long?
