Eventually, both Israel and Judah would be led away as captives to the Assyrians and Chaldeans <note>The Chaldeans are the Neo-Babylonians.</note>; God foretold this more than once through the prophets. The books of the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel are full of—

### 477 On Revelation Chapter 18

...before a great crowd of Jews, at the very moment of his passion—the suffering through which it was brought about that the city of the devil should fall. > And she has become the habitation of demons, and the

<margin>Through Christ’s passion, Babylon fell.</margin>
How has she both "fallen" and yet remained so enclosed and fortified that the birds cannot fly away? To this, it must be briefly said that it was this angel crying out—that is, Christ suffering—whose passion stood out as his "great cry." Regarding this, the Apostle says: *Who in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with a strong cry and many tears to God, who was able to save him from death, was heard for his reverence* <note>original: "qui in diebus carnis suæ preces supplicationesque ad deum, qui illum saluum facere possit a morte, cum clamore valido ac multis lachrymis offerens, exauditus est pro sua reuerentia," quoting Hebrews 5:7</note>. In such a manner, at his cry, the city of the devil fell, so that all the **elect** <note>Those chosen by God for salvation</note>—and they alone—might escape and leap over its ruins, the chains of their sins (both original and actual) having been broken because of the justice of their faith. Therefore, it is rightly said both that *Babylon has fallen*, and nevertheless that she *has become the habitation of demons, and the prison of every unclean spirit, and the prison of every unclean and hateful bird*. 

<margin>The double punishment of demons.</margin>
For clearly, it is in the elect alone that the entire structure of sin and the whole power of death and hell collapses; whereas in the **reprobrate** <note>Those who reject God's grace and are lost</note>, both the damnation of sin and the penal prison of hell remain. As for what he said, *the habitation of demons...*

# 478 Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...spirits, he repeated this by saying, "and the prison of every unclean spirit." For indeed, demons are unclean spirits. And for what reason did he repeat this? Evidently because the damned angels—who are demons or malignant spirits—will suffer punishment for a twofold reason. One reason is because they grew proud against the Creator in heaven. The other is because they polluted the human race with every filth of vice, having first deceived it through the serpent’s initial transgression. On account of the first reason they are called **demons**—that is, "knowing ones" <note>Rupert relies on a common medieval etymology, derived from the Greek *daimon*, which scholars of the time linked to the word for "knowing" or "wise," suggesting they possessed knowledge but lacked charity</note>—because they raised themselves up against the knowledge of God. On account of the second reason they are called **unclean spirits**, because they are most filthy; for, as has already been said, they have afflicted the human race through their suggestions with many kinds of passions of uncleanness and shame. Furthermore, "unclean and hateful birds" are rightly understood as all the proud, both demons and humans. For flight signifies the rush toward profit, and the levity and vanity of the proud. Nor are they compared to just any birds, but to unclean ones. For example, owls or hoopoes <note>original: "noctuas siue upupis"</note>, which delight in sitting upon human dung, and for that reason are rightly held to be unclean and hateful. 

Babylon has become a prison for such birds; and as was said through Isaiah, <margin>Isaiah 8</margin> they will not be able to fly away from their distress <note>original: "non poterit auolare de angustia"</note>. The cause or reasoning which follows is again manifest and was partly explained above:

> Because all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of
> her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed
> fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth 
> have become rich through the abundance of her luxuries.

Three things are stated here: that all nations drank of the wrath of her fornication; that the kings of the earth committed fornication with her; and that the merchants of the earth were made rich by her luxuries. In summary, the whole reproach of fornication is imputed to the kings, <margin>The chief blame lies with the kings.</margin> and they are more frequently noted in this reading as guilty of the crime of this same fornication. And deservedly so: because they not only accepted what that harlot taught, but they even reinforced it by the decree of their empire and by the strength of the sword. Furthermore, the nations who were subject to the kings—whether because of the kings' command or of their own accord—worshiped monsters instead of God; rightly, he says, they drank of the wrath of the same fornication...

<summary>Rupert explains that demons are punished for both their pride against God and their corruption of humanity, comparing the proud to "unclean birds" trapped in Babylon. He emphasizes that the kings of the earth bear the greatest guilt for state-sanctioned idolatry and vice.</summary>

...drank. <note>The transcription begins mid-sentence with "runt," the ending of "biberunt" (they have drunk), referring to the nations drinking the wine of Babylon's wrath.</note> Yet he does not say they drank of her fornication, but of the **wrath of her fornication**. <margin>Romans 1</margin>

# On Revelation, Chapter 18

...her sins. For he says, **"her sins have reached even to heaven"** <note>original: *peruenerunt peccata eius vsque ad coelum*</note>. That is, because by her fornication and by intoxicating herself with the blood of the saints, she went so far as to kill the very King and Lord of heaven. And for this reason, he says, **"the Lord has remembered her iniquities"** <note>original: *recordatus est dominus iniquitatum eius*</note>. That is, He has appointed the day of universal judgment in which her iniquities may be punished. From this it follows: **"Render to her as she herself has rendered to you, and double the double according to her works. In the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give to her torment and mourning."**

<margin>
Matthew 19

Render to her double

Luke 12

Two causes of her damnation.
</margin>

Who are these who are commanded to render to her as she rendered to them, and to double the double according to her works, if not those who will sit with the Lord as He sits to judge on the throne of His majesty? They themselves will sit on judicial seats—namely, the saints and the martyrs of Jesus, with whose blood this harlot was shown above to be drunk. **"Render, therefore,"** he says, **"to her as she herself rendered to you."** That is: condemn her just as she condemned your innocent blood. It was not enough to have said, "as she herself rendered to you," unless he had immediately added, **"and double the double according to her works."** 

For it is clear that while this woman <note>representing Babylon or the worldly power</note> persecuted the saints and martyrs of Jesus, she killed only the body, and after this she has nothing more she can do; but they themselves, in judgment with the same Lord Jesus, have this power: to cast both body and soul into Gehenna <note>the place of final punishment; original: *gehennam*</note>. Well, then, does he say: **"double the double according to her works."** And likewise: **"and in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double."** And he immediately says: **"As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give to her torment and mourning."** For the pride with which she exalted herself, give her mourning; for the luxuries she used inordinately, give her torment. These are the two causes of her damnation: one, because she returned evil to the saints and martyrs of Jesus when she shed their blood; the other, because she overflowed in her luxuries and fornications—which causes were indeed written above and are repeated here in reverse order.

H <note>This "H" is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order for binding.</note>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 18. Following the previous page’s discussion of the "double" punishment Babylon receives, Rupert now focuses on the root cause of her downfall: her internal pride and her false sense of security, contrasting her self-image with the prophetic reality found in the Book of Isaiah.</meta>

482 Rupert’s Commentary, Book <note>The header indicates page 482 of Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on the Apocalypse.</note>

The sum of her guilt is noted, so that the punishment for her sin may be unending: her pride <note>original: *superbia*</note>. For she does not merely sin or commit fornication in any ordinary way, but she glories or glorifies herself in her sins and fornications. Whence it is further added:
**"Because she says in her heart: I sit as a queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall see no mourning. Therefore her plagues shall come in one day: death, and mourning, and famine, and she shall be burned with fire, because God is strong, who has judged her."**
Regarding how and why she says in her heart, "I sit as a queen," etc.

<margin>
Isaiah 47. Babylon, ironically a virgin.
</margin>

Truth <note>a common medieval title for Christ or the Holy Spirit as the source of Scripture</note> long ago confirmed the prophecy that she must therefore endure these plagues. For in the prophet Isaiah it is said to her among other things: **"Come down, sit in the dust, O most heavy virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground, O virgin."** <note>original: *Descende sede in puluere virgo grauissima...*</note> "Most heavy" is said there with irony; for here she is truly pronounced a harlot <note>original: *meretrix*</note>.
Immediately after it is said to her: **"You said: I shall be a lady forever. You did not lay these things to your heart, nor did you remember your end. And now hear these things, you who are delicate and dwell confidently, who say in your heart: I am, and besides me there is no other. I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know barrenness. These two things shall come to you suddenly in one day: barrenness and widowhood, etc."** <note>Rupert is quoting Isaiah 47:7-9 to show the continuity of God's judgment against worldly pride.</note>
Therefore, on account of pride—because this harlot does not just sin in any fashion, but sins by being proud, and in sinning she is proud and exults—she does not consider herself a widow like the City of God <note>referring to the Church, which "mourns" while waiting for Christ</note>, which lives as a pilgrim in this world. Instead, being a harlot, many kings commit fornication with her, as if this were the legitimate marriage of a blessed, powerful, and dominant queen. Because of this, I say, the judgment is just and irreproachable, that these plagues should come upon her: death, mourning, and famine, and that she should be burned with eternal fire. Nor is the sentence doubtful; rather, it must have a certain effect, because **"strong,"** he says, **"is the God who has judged her,"** and once the sentence is brought forth by voice or writing, He is not powerless to fulfill it.

**"And the kings of the earth, who have committed fornication with her and lived in luxury, shall weep and bewail themselves over her, when they see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off..."**

<summary>Rupert explains that Babylon's primary sin is pride, contrasting her self-proclamation as a "queen" with the biblical reality of her status as a harlot. He links the judgment in Revelation 18 to the prophecies against Babylon in Isaiah 47.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 18, moving from the internal pride of Babylon to the external reaction of the world to its sudden downfall. He draws a sophisticated parallel between the "woes" cried out by the kings and merchants and the prophetic scroll described in the Book of Ezekiel.</meta>

### On Apocalypse Chapter 18

...[they will stand] far off for fear of her torment, and they shall say: "Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city, for in one hour your judgment has come."

<margin>The rolled-up book in which there was a song and woe. Ezekiel 2.</margin>
At this point, it is helpful to recall that writing or scroll of which it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: **"And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled-up book, and he spread it before me; it was written within and without: and there were written in it lamentations, and a song, and woe."** <note>Ezekiel 2:9-10. Rupert uses this Old Testament image to explain the structure of divine judgment.</note> For that book is the whole of divinely inspired Scripture, which is spread out before the prophet because it is made intelligible to a faithful man through the opening grace of Christ.

<margin>A song is for the blessed, woe for the damned, lamentation for the penitent.</margin>
In that book are written lamentations, and a song, and woe. Of these three, "song" and "woe" are opposites, while "lamentations" hold a middle place. For the Holy Scriptures promise an eternal song <note>original: *carmen*</note> to the saints and the elect in the world to come. "Woe," however, is for all the impious, such as are denoted in this passage: the kings of the earth who committed fornication with the harlot and lived in luxuries, and the merchants of the earth who became rich from the power of her delights. Furthermore, "lamentations" belong to the penitent, who in the present life lament their sins for a time, so that they might not come to that eternal woe.

This present passage of Scripture demonstrates all these things—namely lamentations, song, and woe—gathered together for those who read studiously. For when it is said: **"Go out from her, my people, so that you do not participate in her crimes, and that you do not receive her plagues,"** repentance is preached to all nations (as has already been said), which is certainly a form of lamenting. 

But "Woe" is expressed here more clearly (as it is their specific lot), when they themselves say: **"Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city, for in one hour your judgment has come."** And again: **"Woe, woe, that great city which was clothed in fine linen, and purple, and scarlet, and was gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls, for in one hour such great riches have been brought to nothing."** And likewise a third time: **"Woe, woe, great city, in which all who have ships in the sea became rich from her prices: for..."**

<summary>Rupert explains the "threefold woe" of Babylon's fall by linking it to Ezekiel’s prophetic scroll, categorizing divine messages into songs for the saved, lamentations for the penitent, and woes for the damned.</summary>
<keywords>Babylon, Ezekiel, Apocalypse, Lamentations, Song, Woe, Judgment, Repentance, Kings of the Earth, Merchants of the Earth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 18. Having previously discussed the "woes" as a form of divine sentence, Rupert now analyzes why the word "woe" is repeated six times and how the destruction of Babylon’s wealth represents the judgment of sins committed through the five physical senses across the six ages of human history.</meta>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...in one hour she is made desolate. A third time "woe" is doubled, and thus "woe" is spoken six times in total. And one and the same cause for saying "woe, woe" is given everywhere, though with a few words changed: "for in one hour your judgment has come," "for in one hour such great riches are stripped away," "for in one hour she is made desolate." For the crimes of all the ages of the world, which are six in number, shall now be avenged upon them all at once; for these people, there is no seventh age, that is, no Sabbath <note>Rupert refers to the common medieval theology of the "Six Ages of the World" corresponding to the six days of creation. The "seventh age" or Sabbath represents eternal rest in God, which the wicked will never reach.</note>. 

And this will be a marvelous and most wretched thing for those to behold who so greatly love this wicked world: because the evil works of so many days or times, and so many ages of the world, shall be judged, and their joys shall perish—replaced by an unending magnitude of torments—in one hour of judgment, one hour of deprivation, and one hour of desolation. Then all those things shall perish at once, in

<margin>All the world’s concupiscence <note>original: *concupiscẽtia*, or intense worldly desire</note> shall perish.</margin>

which the fornicators and lovers of the world lived in luxury with the oft-mentioned harlot. Gold and silver, and precious stones, and pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood <note>original: *lignum tinum*; an aromatic wood used for costly furniture</note>, and every vessel of ivory, and every vessel of precious stone, and of brass, and of iron, and of marble—all of which pertain to the **fornication of the eyes**. 

Next are cinnamon and amomum <note>an ancient spice plant</note>, and other kinds of incense and perfumes, which are surely referred here to the **fornicating sense of smell**. Next are the types of ointment, which look toward luxury <note>The sense of touch or general excess</note>. Then, he says, wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, which (or things similar to them) are referred to the **sense of taste**. 

After many things, there is also brought in the voice of harpers, and musicians, and pipe-players. And the trumpet shall be heard in you no more; these look toward the fifth sense of the body, that is, **hearing**. Therefore, all the instruments of fornication that entice through the five senses of the body are damned; for it is through these senses that every adultery of the soul—which fornicates by turning away from God—is committed. 

The service of beasts of burden and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves <note>original: *mancipiorum*</note>, and the souls of men, are also numbered among the perishing furniture of the world. Even the fruits <note>original: *poma*</note> are expressed by their own name, because they too must perish for their role in inordinate desire...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains that Babylon's "six woes" correspond to the six ages of world history, and he categorizes the city's lost luxuries according to how they tempted the five physical senses into spiritual adultery.</summary>

### On the Apocalypse, Chapter 18

...they should, by saying: "And the fruit of your soul’s desire has departed from you." <note>original: *poma tua desideriũ aīæ*; a reference to Revelation 18:14</note> Nevertheless, among these things are included whatever are the enticements of gluttony or the delicacies of the kitchen, when it is added: "and all things fat and bright have perished from you." Almost all the instruments of pleasure, however many or great they may be, which are drawn in through the five senses of the body—and through which the more noble part of man <note>The "noble part" refers to the soul, which in medieval theology is "imprisoned" or "sickened" by excessive sensory indulgence.</note> grows faint and is taken captive—are expressed by their own names as being about to perish, through the marvelous diligence of the one seeing and writing <note>The "one seeing and writing" refers to St. John the Apostle, the traditional author of Revelation.</note>.

<margin>A wretched spectacle in the final fire of the world.</margin>
Because, evidently, in that hour when this world begins to be consumed by the final fire, it provides a wretched spectacle to all its lovers, where they will see everything they possessed with excessive love perish, not without great sorrow. Therefore, to suggest that the intensity of the pain will be no small thing, he describes the inconsolable misery of those weeping and mourning once, twice, and a third time:

> And the kings of the earth shall weep and mourn over her.
> And again: And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her, for no one buys their merchandise anymore.
> And thereafter: And every shipmaster, and everyone who sails to a place, and sailors, and those who work the seas, stood afar off and cried out, seeing the place of her burning, saying: "What city is like this great city?"
> And they cast, he says, dust upon their heads.

<margin>Not a true repentance of those mourning.</margin>
Dust upon the head signifies the sadness of repentance <note>original: *pœnitudo*; a sorrow for sin or a change of mind</note>. But that repentance is no longer useful or fruitful, because it is far too late. At the same time, it must be known that there is now no reason or wisdom in those repenting. For what kind of repentance, or how rational a manner of it, is there when those weeping and mourning cry out and say: "What city is like this great city?" Even now, they imagine the phantom <note>original: *phantasiām*</note> of transitory glory which they had seen to have been a "great city." Therefore, they do not grieve so much that they allowed themselves harmful pleasures, as they do that these same pleasures are perishing from them beyond recovery. And indeed, if they could [keep] all these perishing fuels of greed, which are here expressed by name alongside their torment...

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 18. On the previous page, Rupert began discussing the mourning of the worldly for the destruction of "Babylon" (the world), explaining how the loss of sensory pleasures causes spiritual despair. He now continues to describe the reactions of different social classes—kings, merchants, and sailors—who watch the destruction from a distance.</meta>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...[they desire] to rescue her from the fire and keep her for themselves. But without a doubt they will not be able to; while things are perishing, the help of those who are likewise perishing will be far away. Hence, as a significant sign of their helplessness, it is said here once, twice, and a third time that "they stood afar off."

> "When," he says, "the kings of the earth see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off for fear of her torments, they shall say: 'Woe, woe!'" <note>original: *væ væ*; Revelation 18:9–10</note>

> Likewise: "And the merchants of these things, who were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning, and saying: 'Woe, woe!'" And a little after: "And every shipmaster and all the sailors stood afar off, and cried out, weeping and mourning, and saying: 'Woe, woe!'" <note>Revelation 18:15, 17–18</note>

All of them—kings as well as sailors or shipmasters, sailors as well as merchants—will "stand afar off," not so much in physical distance as by a failing of the heart and a weakened spirit. For it is evident that at that time the kings will have neither weapons nor armies to fight with, the sailors no oars for rowing, and the merchants no stalls <note>original: *institias*; referring to the places or structures used for trade and packing</note> to gather their bundles. For even the support of pack animals, horses, and carriages will be lacking. 

<margin>A distinction between the simple life and worldly greed.</margin>
Meanwhile, it should be noted that shepherds or countryfolk are not written of as having this weeping and mourning. This is because their duties belong to a simple life, and they serve necessary use rather than superfluous greed. Sailors, however, are rightly not excluded from this sort of weeping and mourning. For they themselves laugh and boast not a little while they row and are carried on a prosperous course through the seas. Anyone who has ever seen ships <note>The original OCR reads *auium* (birds), but the context of *velificantium* (sailing) indicates it should be *nauium* (ships).</note> sailing along favorably, or has heard the <term>celeuma</term> (which is a sailor's song) <note>A rhythmic chant used by ancient and medieval rowers to coordinate their strokes.</note> of wanton sailors, undoubtedly perceives that this is so. 

Nor can these sailors be seen as excusable like the countryfolk or shepherds—with some of whom God spoke from the beginning <note>A reference to the patriarchs and prophets of the Bible, such as Abel, Abraham, or David, who were shepherds and were considered "closer to God" for their simple lifestyle.</note>—for by the strength of the sailors' arms, not only merchant ships but even warships have been driven along, and they have very often stained the sea's waves with the blood of war.

# On Revelation, Chapter 18
### Page 489

...in you any more. And the voice of a millstone shall not be heard in you any more. And the light of a lamp shall not shine in you any more. Here, everything is exactly as it is said, because not only will no crafts of any kind remain—for example, those of planting or building—but even those things which had been planted and built will be entirely taken away.
<margin>1 Corinthians 7</margin>

<margin>Babylon does nothing good for the sake of eternal life, but only for temporal goods.</margin>

To acquire or protect those goods, you held and kept certain laws that did not differ from reason, whether applied externally or internally. You did not observe such things for the sake of the true life, but only so that your princes might trade more securely in the acquisition of gold, silver, estates, and sea-routes, and so that nothing would be lacking for the fulfillment of pleasures.
You have therefore received your reward; for the rest, the damnation that was laid up for you is now owed, and the eternal judgment is now rendered to you.

# On Revelation, Chapter 19
### Page 491

...of the great crowds saying, Alleluia.

<margin>A song of heavenly exultation.</margin>
This is the sound of consolation; this is the song written in the aforementioned book, a song of exultation, your song, O pilgrim citizens of the heavenly fatherland, you who travel as foreigners in this world and lament. While those kings, those merchants, and those pilots and sailors weep and mourn—seeing the vanities and false madnesses in which they trusted perish, and saying, "Woe, woe"—then you shall sing "Alleluia."

<margin>Alleluia.</margin>
For "Alleluia" <note>original: "Alleluia"</note> is a Hebrew word, translated as "Praise the Lord" <note>Rupert correctly identifies the Hebrew *Hallel* (praise) and *Yah* (the Lord).</note>, and many Psalms are titled with this name. In one of them, the inscription is written thus: *Alleluia, of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.* The prophets Haggai and Zechariah foretold that the captivity of the children of Israel by Nebuchadnezzar would be ended, as well as the destruction of the temple; they themselves were present for that return to Jerusalem and the rebuilding of the temple. This serves as a likeness, namely, of all the elect returning to their eternal and heavenly city, Jerusalem, from this earthly pilgrimage where that damned harlot Babylon <note>The "Great Harlot" or "Babylon" represents the worldly system or corrupt church that opposes the "New Jerusalem."</note> inflicted evils upon them.

<margin>The damned say "Woe" three times; the Blessed say "Alleluia" three times.</margin>
> "And so," he says, "after these things I heard as it were the voice of many crowds in heaven, saying: Alleluia."

A marvelous opposition is to be noted here: because those wailing say "Woe, woe" three times regarding that city, these others, on the contrary, say "Alleluia" three times in their rejoicing. For first, he says, "I heard as it were a great voice of many saying Alleluia"; second, he says, "and again they said Alleluia"; and third, "they worshiped God sitting upon the throne, saying: Amen, Alleluia." Not content with this, he repeated again what he had said: "And I heard as it were the voice of a great trumpet, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunders, saying: Alleluia." Why, then, was it said "Alleluia" so often? If you wish to accept the interpretation or the sense of this voice as an equivalent, just as "Woe" was said six times there <note>referring to the sixfold lamentations of the kings, merchants, and sailors in Revelation 18</note>, so also "Alleluia" is said six times here. For after it was first said "Alleluia," there was added: "Praise, and glory, and power belong to our God." Likewise, after it was said "and they worshiped God sitting upon the throne, saying: Amen, Alleluia," there was added: "And a voice went out from the throne, saying: Give praise to our God, all you his servants."

<summary>Rupert explains "Alleluia" as a song of liberation for the "pilgrim citizens" of heaven, drawing a parallel between the return of the Jews from Babylonian exile and the final triumph of the Church. He highlights a symbolic numerical symmetry where the six heavenly "Alleluias" answer the six "Woes" of the worldly city.</summary>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

<margin>
The blessed sing of judgment and mercy. Psalm 100 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 101:1: "I will sing of mercy and justice."</note>

Therefore, just as you heard "woe" six times there, so here you hear "alleluia" <note>original: "alleluia"</note>—that is, praise to God—six times. This is because those to whom the "woe" belongs, succeeding one another through the six ages of the world <note>A common medieval historical framework, dividing time into six periods from Creation to the Second Coming.</note> in those fornications, stored up that woe for themselves. Likewise, these to whom the "alleluia" belongs, succeeding one another through the six ages of the world, exercised themselves in holy virtues for the praise and glory of God. They sing, therefore, and they praise, and praise is beautiful in their mouths. And what do they praise while singing, and what do they sing while praising? Judgment and mercy, upon which the entire subject matter of divine song and praise depends, as the Psalmist says: *I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.* 

And indeed, before the judgment takes place, it is first necessary to sing of mercy, and then of judgment; but after the judgment has been carried out, it will first be to praise the truth of judgment, and then to sing of mercies forever. For now, mercy is offered first, and then judgment is repaid to those who despise mercy; but then, the judgment is first celebrated once in act, and then mercy (as has already been said) is sung for eternity. Therefore, they first praise the judgment when they say:

**"For true and just are His judgments, because He has judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth with her prostitution, and He has avenged the blood of His servants from her hands."**

For two reasons—the same reasons for which we said above that the harlot was condemned—they praise the truth of judgment: one of which is that she corrupted the earth with her prostitution, the other because she shed the blood of the saints. Next, they praise mercy in a most sweet harmony when they say:

**"Because the Lord our God the Almighty has reigned; let us rejoice and exult and give glory to Him, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has prepared herself, and it was granted to her to clothe herself in fine linen, shining and white."**

# On the Apocalypse, Chapter 18
<note>While the header indicates Chapter 18, the commentary focuses on the opening verses of Chapter 19, where the "Alleluia" is first heard in heaven.</note>

### Page 493

From this comes praise and glory; from this comes joy and exultation; from this comes the repeated "Alleluia" <note>original: "alleluia," a Hebrew liturgical call meaning "Praise the Lord"</note>. For while that woman, the harlot and prostitute, is being judged, the Lamb and His wife—another woman, a blessed woman—celebrate their marriage. 
<margin>Song of the blessed.</margin>
Therefore, they say "Alleluia" by singing in accompaniment, because the Lord our God Almighty has reigned. Who is this Lord, or who is this God? It is the Lamb Himself, against whom those fornicating kings fought, and He conquered them; for, he says, "He is the Lord of lords and King of kings." From this let us rejoice and exult, because He has conquered and reigned, and let us—the chosen, the called, and the faithful who are with Him and have conquered with Him—give glory to Him. Whether we are victors or participants in His victory, let us give glory to Him in this, so that we attribute our victory not to ourselves, but entirely to Him, the sole conqueror and sole Almighty.

Neither is it truly only because He conquered and reigned, but because His marriage has come, and His wife has prepared herself. The Father destined her for Him, saying through David in the song of the wedding-feast: 
<margin>Psalm 44 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 45:6-9.</note></margin>
"Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness. The queen stands at your right hand." In what way did she prepare herself? In gilded clothing, surrounded by golden fringes in many-colored variety, of which the first of all is fine linen <term>fine linen (byssinum): a high-quality ancient fabric used for priestly and royal garments</term>, shining and white. For, it says, "the fine linen is the justifications of the saints." 

Furthermore, the first justification, or the beginning of justification, is faith. Just as it was credited to Abraham for righteousness, so also for us who believe, the Apostle says, it will be credited for righteousness. 
<margin>Romans 4.</margin>
<margin>Ephesians 2.</margin>
This was surely given to His wife, because without a doubt, faith is a gift of God.
<margin>The fine linen of the bride and the scarlet of the harlot differ.</margin>
To this shining and white fine linen, the scarlet of that damned harlot was an enemy—hers was not given, but seized; not shining, but hideous; not white, but blood-red. 

That voice of those singing was like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunders—indeed, even like many trumpets. This is because it will be the voice and harmony of many peoples, thundering with a great "thunder of hearts" (that is, of many thundering with great devotion). It is like the trumpeting of many thousands of saints, stirring up not war, but peace and charity toward the Holy Trinity—a charity that always meets and will always meet Him within their hearts.

This is so constant and certain in the mind of every faithful person that there is more room for them to sigh in longing for it than to dispute the truth of the statement. For it is true, and this truth is spoken of now as something ancient, yet it is always to be known as if it were new. "Write, therefore," he says, "because they are blessed who are called to that supper," not of some ordinary calendar day or festival, but the marriage supper of the Lamb. For there, the entire supper is love, where the wife is joined to her Husband—that is, the soul is joined to God—not for an hour, but eternally: because this wedding feast, this love of married life, is eternal life. From this comes that passage in the Psalms: *They shall be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you shall give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure.* <note>Rupert quotes the Vulgate Psalm 35:9, which corresponds to Psalm 36:8 in modern translations. <margin>The words of the angel to John.</margin>
The one who says these things is one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls, who spoke with him above, saying: *Come, I will show you the damnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters,* etc. He shows more than he had promised; for he showed not only the damnation of the harlot, but also the glorification of the blessed woman, the wife of the Lamb, and he allowed the hearing of the heavenly song, which is the "Alleluia" <note>Rupert emphasizes that the angel exceeds the initial "tour" of judgment by revealing the ultimate joy of the Church.</note>. "And these," he says, "are the true words of God": so that we may receive all these things not as the words of any man, or even of an angel, but that we may judge them to be truly the words of God, true and rational, even if we are less able to understand or explain them. Furthermore, how gratefully John received this, and how much he valued demonstrations of this kind, is clear from what he says next.

### CCCXCV
## On Apocalypse Chapter 19

...and [John understood] that God alone ought to be adored by man. Yet, for a little while, due to the ecstasy of mind in which he was, he attended to this very truth less clearly. Nevertheless, he did not wander far from his own sense of judgment. For we read that 
<margin><insert><unclear>Handwritten notes in margin</unclear></insert> Genesis 18</margin>
before him, some of the ancient saints fell prostrate before angels and were not forbidden <note>Rupert refers to instances like Abraham in Genesis 18:2, where bowing to angelic visitors was a mark of profound respect rather than divine worship.</note>. 
<margin>Why the angel did not permit himself to be adored by John.</margin>
Why then did this angel so vehemently forbid him, saying, "See that you do not do it"? Namely, because from the time God was made [man], and took on the true nature of man, and raised that same nature—which had been surrendered to passion and death for the sake of the whole world—and placed it at the right hand of the Father, and gave the Holy Spirit of reconciliation to men, the dignity of human nature has increased above itself. Because humans are now his brothers and friends, their dignity has been 
<margin><insert><unclear>Handwritten notes in margin</unclear></insert></margin>
brought up even to the measure of angelic dignity. Therefore, when he had said, "See that you do not do it," he immediately gave this reason for why he forbade it: "I am your fellow servant and [the fellow servant] of your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus." 
<margin>The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.</margin>
"Therefore," he says, "adore God, whom I also, your fellow servant, adore." And immediately, as if you were asking what he meant by "those who have the testimony of Jesus," or what the "testimony of Jesus" might be, he took care to reveal it at once. "The testimony of Jesus," he says, "is the spirit of prophecy." And who is the spirit of prophecy, if not the Holy Spirit? This clearly is our testimony, as the Apostle says: 
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
"You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry out, 'Abba, Father.'" <note>original: "abba pater." This is a transliteration of the Aramaic/Hebrew word for "Father," used by Paul to denote the intimacy of a child with God.</note> For the Spirit himself bears testimony to our spirit that we are the children of God. Therefore, because the testimony of the faithful of Christ is the Holy Spirit, and he testifies to them not about some small matter, but about the fact that they are children of God, they are rightly warned in the person of John that they should adore no one but the one and only God, while looking back at the dignity of their own condition and the grace they have received. 
<margin>Why he says "spirit of prophecy" rather than "Holy Spirit."</margin>
Since this is so, it could indeed have been rightly said: "For the testimony of Jesus is the Holy Spirit," or "the spirit of adoption of sons which they have received." But for the person of John, he spoke more beautifully: "The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy," because this Apocalypse is a prophecy, as was stated at the beginning...

<summary>Rupert explains that the angel refuses John's worship because, since the Incarnation, human nature has been elevated to the same rank as angels. He identifies the "spirit of prophecy" mentioned in the text as the Holy Spirit, who provides the "testimony" that believers are children of God.</summary>

<margin>
The garment: that is, his flesh sprinkled with blood. Isaiah 63
</margin>
This is the same as if the author were to say: This person, as a man capable of suffering and mortal, has suffered and died; yet as one incapable of suffering and immortal, he is God. For in his passion, his "garment"—that is, his flesh—was sprinkled with his own blood. Whence the prophet <note>Rupert refers here to Isaiah, specifically the famous "Winepress" passage in chapter 63.</note>, greatly wondering, inquires and says: *Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?* <note>original: "de Edom... de Bosra"; Edom and its capital Bozrah were traditional enemies of Israel, often used symbolically in prophecy to represent the world or the site of a great divine judgment.</note> And with him responding: *I, who speak righteousness, and am a champion to save.* The prophet asks: *Why then is your clothing red, and your garments like those of people treading in a winepress?* Why, he asks, did they make your garment red? Why did they shed your blood, if you speak righteousness, if you committed no sins, nor was deceit found in your mouth? Therefore, the garment sprinkled with blood is his innocent flesh, having suffered death and the pouring out of its own blood. 

Furthermore, his name is called the "Word of God"—the Word through which all things were made, and without which nothing was made <note>A reference to the opening of the Gospel of John.</note>—which could not die, and through which even that very flesh, which had died, lived again. Thousands of saints follow the example of his patience and his death. Therefore it says:

**And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in fine linen, white and clean.**

Finally, his "armies" are the martyrs and all the holy people who have struggled in this world in any way for his sake. For because of the very struggles <term>struggles: Rupert uses the word "agones," referring to the athletic or combat-like trials of the faith</term> they endured, they are called "armies." How were they following him? *On white horses*, it says, *clothed in clean fine linen.* "On white horses" means in white bodies, purified by baptism and fittingly adorned with the "justification of good works," which are signified by the fine white and clean linen. Traveling in such a way, they followed him—especially those who put on the purity of life through the sprinkling of their own blood through martyrdom.

### On Chapter 19 of the Apocalypse

<margin>Psalm 2</margin>
...a rod of iron—that is, with inflexible justice <note>Original: *inflexibili iustitia*</note>—just as the Father says to him in the prophet: *You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. This can be understood, in part, in a positive sense, because there is such a thing as a healthy striking and a useful breaking. This occurs while the nations—that is, those from among the Gentiles preordained for life—having heard through the Gospel the threat of future judgment, are shaken with fear and their hearts are "broken" toward repentance. However, all those remaining in unbelief will be struck to their own ruin and broken to their own ruin; they will be like a potter’s vessel, beyond recovery, whose pieces cannot be joined or glued back together. Someone might ask: "But what about the Jews? Does this sword, which so strikes the nations, not touch them?" Hear what follows:

**And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty, and he has written on his robe and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.**

Deuteronomy 32.
Isaiah 5.
</margin>
He who strikes or will strike the nations, and rules them with a rod of iron, now treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. That is, he is already preparing the "crushing" <term>pressura: A Latin term meaning both "tribulation/affliction" and the physical "pressure" of a winepress. Rupert uses this double meaning to link the biblical metaphor to historical suffering.</term> for that people. Already the causes have been stirred up by which the weight and pressure of the Roman Empire would come and weigh upon them, so that it might hem in their multitudes and compress them in a narrow space through the armies of Titus and Vespasian <note>Titus and Vespasian were the Roman commanders (and later Emperors) who led the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, which resulted in the destruction of the Second Temple.</note>. This pressure is surely rightly and most fittingly represented by the winepress. For that nation was, or ought to have been, the vineyard of the Lord; and because, when it should have produced grapes, it produced wild grapes <note>A reference to Isaiah 5:2-4, where Israel is compared to a vineyard that produced bitter fruit.</note>, God himself foretold in the prophet that this evil would happen to them. And because "their vine is of the vine of Sodom," and "their grapes are grapes of gall," God foretold in the "Song of Moses" <note>The "Song of Moses" refers to Deuteronomy 32, specifically verses 32–34.</note> that these evils to be rendered unto them were stored up with him and "sealed among his treasures." In the prophet Isaiah, when he had begun in his own person: *I will sing for my beloved a song...*

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 11

...of my cousin, regarding his vineyard, etc. <note>Rupert is continuing a citation from Isaiah 5, often called the "Song of the Vineyard," where God laments the fruitlessness of Israel.</note> Finally God says: *Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.* And after a few words, he says: *And now, I will show you what I will do to my vineyard. I will take away its hedge, and it shall be plundered. I will break down its wall, and it shall be trodden down,* etc. After these threats he likewise says: *For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his pleasant plant.* David the prophet also, when he had said: *You have brought a vine out of Egypt, you have cast out the nations and planted it,* etc. <margin>Psalm 79</margin> <note>Original: *psal. lxxix.* In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 80.</note> Foreseeing this winepress and this crushing pressure, he said: *The boar from the forest has destroyed it, and a singular wild beast has devoured it.* For by the "boar from the forest" or the "singular wild beast," the Gentile emperor and the Roman army are understood. 

It is fitting, therefore, that where he said: *and he himself shall rule the nations with a rod of iron,* he wished to signify what would happen to the unbelieving Jews. *And he himself,* he says, *treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty,* <note>Quoting Revelation 19:15.</note> as if he were to say: *And the Jews shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led away captive into all nations,* or *And there shall be great distress upon the land, and wrath upon this people.* <note>Rupert is weaving in the language of Luke 21:23-24 to interpret the Apocalypse.</note> 

But why was he not content to have said only "fury" or only "wrath," but instead joined both "fury" and "wrath" together, saying: *the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty*? <margin>The winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God.</margin> <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> <margin>Matthew 27</margin> It is evidently because the "wine" of the Jews—which can be variously called gall and poison, as Moses testified, saying: *Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps*—that poisonous and gall-filled wine of the Jews, I say, who gave the very Lord of the vineyard gall and vinegar to drink while he was hanging on the cross, has earned for them not only fury or only wrath, but fury and wrath together. 

That is, they acquired damnation for themselves not only in the present or only in the future, but in the present and the future simultaneously: so that the Roman army might slaughter and take captive their bodies here in this world, while the devil might possess and hell might torment their souls in the next. Moses expresses both forms of vengeance in one short verse: *A fire,* he says, *is kindled in my fury, and shall burn even to the lowest depths of hell.* With this established, *and he himself treads the winepress...*

<summary>Rupert interprets the "winepress of God's wrath" in Revelation 19 as the historical destruction of Jerusalem and the diaspora of the Jews, arguing that their rejection of Christ resulted in a "two-fold" punishment of physical destruction by Rome and spiritual damnation.</summary>

### On Chapter 19 of the Apocalypse

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 11

...this should be understood according to the variety of the context. For in one sense it signifies the Holy Church or the Catholic faith, while in another it signifies Holy Scripture. Both can be understood from a single verse of the Psalm <margin>Psalm 21 <note>original: "Psalm. xxi." This refers to the Vulgate numbering; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 22:18.</note></margin> where he himself speaks, saying: *They divided my garments among themselves, and for my robe they cast lots.* For the "divided garments" of the Lord signify Holy Scripture, which is often corrupted by heretics; as the Psalmist says elsewhere: <margin>Psalm 10 <note>Modern Psalm 11:3.</note></margin> <margin>John 19</margin> *They have destroyed what you have perfected.* <note>original: "Quæ perfecisti destruxerunt."</note> But his robe which was seamless from the top, and for which they cast lots, designates the Church or the Catholic faith, given to the faithful by divine election, which can be corrupted by no one.

Likewise, his garment is understood to be the Church when the Psalm says again: *Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity, like ointment on the head, which descends onto the beard of Aaron, which descends to the hem of his garment.* <note>Psalm 133:1-2.</note> And the meaning is this: the grace of the Holy Spirit, which dwells fully in Christ our head, first descends from him onto those strong men, the apostles—who are signified by the "beard of Aaron"—and then onto the martyrs and the other children of the Church, who are indeed great, but inferior to the apostles. These are understood to be on the "hem of the garment," because after the apostles, they are the most prominent in the Church, with whose faith and virtues Christ himself is adorned, in the manner of someone who is clothed in a precious garment. <margin>The garment is Holy Scripture</margin>

Furthermore, in this present passage, the "garment" is rightly understood to signify Holy Scripture. Moreover, because the garment is more pleasing and shines most beautifully, and at the same time contains this writing upon his "thigh," it is one and the same Holy Scripture—that scripture which the fathers of his flesh (signified by the "thigh" <note>In biblical allegory, the "thigh" often represents lineage or physical descent.</note>) wrote down. This refers especially to the scripture of the Psalms, which is truly the "scripture of the thigh of Christ," because it is the writing of his father according to the flesh, David. <margin>Psalm 71 <note>Modern Psalm 72:1.</note></margin> Indeed, that he is the "King of kings" is written there in this way: *O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the son of the king.* This verse, to be sure, does not yet proclaim him "King of kings," but only "the king." However, it follows afterward: *And he shall rule from sea to sea, and...*

# On Revelation Chapter 19

...from the river even to the ends of the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents, and all kings shall adore him. <note>original: "Reges Tharſis & inſulæ munera offerent, reges Arabum & Saba dona adducēt..." This is a quote from Psalm 72:8–11 (Psalm 71 in the Vulgate), a passage traditionally read as a prophecy of the Magi and the universal reign of the Messiah.</note> Without any contradiction, a king to whom other kings offer gifts and bring presents—and not only do this but also adore him—is the King of kings. And it is right that men, who are kings, adore this King, who, although he is a man, is also God. This is briefly and magnificently hinted at when it is said in the same place: *His name endures before the sun.* <note>Psalm 72:17.</note> This is the same as if it were said: This king was God before he was born as a man, because he existed before the world was made, of which the sun we see is a living and beautiful part.

Furthermore, the title "Lord of lords" is not as explicitly stated in this passage of Scripture, except where it says: *And he shall rule from sea to sea.* <note>Psalm 72:8.</note> Let us therefore look elsewhere. For in another place, the same father of his flesh <note>The "father of his flesh" refers to King David, from whose lineage Christ descended humanly.</note>—himself a lord of many servants who was called "lord" by public and solemn title (as was the custom due to kings, as you can find readily in the history of his deeds)—this same king and lord, I say, said: <margin>Psalm 110 <note>original: "pſalm. cix." (Vulgate numbering).</note></margin> *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* He, while reigning and ruling himself, called Him his "Lord" just as he called God the Father. Likewise in the same Psalm: *Rule,* it says, *in the midst of your enemies,* <note>Psalm 110:2.</note> many of whom are or were certainly lords, and have ruled or do rule over vast stretches of land; and yet, whether they wish it or not, they cannot escape the dominion of this Lord. 

Therefore, it is true and manifest that he has written on his garment and on his thigh—that is, testified in the Scripture which the ancestors of his flesh wrote down—that he is King of kings and Lord of lords. And indeed, his citizens who hated him could deny him and send a delegation after him, saying: <margin>Luke 19.</margin> *We do not want this man to reign over us,* <note>Luke 19:14, from the Parable of the Ten Minas, often interpreted as the rejection of Christ by his own people.</note> but they cannot destroy or hide this Scripture.

At that time, there were scribes and Pharisees who despised the one calling them. These men, however, who deserved to have a heart free from desires, followed him. What, then, is the meaning of what he says:

> **That you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of the strong, and the flesh of horses, and of those sitting on them, and the flesh of all free and slave, and of small and great.** <note>original: "Ut manducetis carnes regum..." (Revelation 19:18)</note>

<margin>In the calling to the faith, there is no distinction of persons. Acts 10.</margin>
So it is the duty of the apostles, by Gospel authority, to make or hold no distinction among whatever kind of men there may be. This, indeed, is what it means "to eat," according to what was signified to the Apostle Peter. For in an ecstasy, he saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending like a large linen sheet let down by the four corners from heaven to earth, in which were all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth, and the birds of the air. And a voice came to him, saying: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." <note>Acts 10:10-13. Rupert interprets Peter's vision of the "unclean" animals as a command to convert the Gentiles, effectively "consuming" them into the Church.</note> 

Doubtless, those who were signified there by the four-footed and creeping things of the earth and the birds of heaven are more clearly expressed here as men. All are commanded to be admitted to the Christian faith indiscriminately: whether kings, or tribunes <term>tribune: a high-ranking Roman official, used here to represent those in positions of power</term>, or the strong, or the weak, or slaves, or free, or great, or the smallest of the small—whether they be Jews or Greeks.

The sacrament of Christ is not preached to horses but to men, and it is required of them that they mortify <term>mortify: the spiritual practice of "killing off" sinful desires or bodily appetites</term> and entirely abandon the evil habits of carnal works. # On Apocalypse, Chapter 19

<margin>Job 5</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin>
<margin>Job 12</margin>
"With Him is strength and wisdom, and He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived. He leads counselors to a foolish end, and judges to a stupor," etc. <note>original: "Apud ipsum est fortitudo & sapientia..." (Job 12:16-17). Rupert uses these verses to explain how God allowed the Jewish leaders to fall into their own traps.</note> That "deceiver" was the one who prophesied in such a way <note>A reference to Caiaphas's prophecy in John 11:50 that "it is better for one man to die for the people."</note>; and the "deceived" was the foolish people, who, as they were already prone to murder, willingly accepted his prophecy. From this follows:

**Who performed signs in its presence, by which he seduced those who received the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.**

It is true that we do not read that Caiaphas and the other priests and Pharisees of that time performed any "signs" <note>In this context, "signs" (signa) refers to miracles or supernatural wonders.</note>. However, just as all persecutors—those who killed or still kill with a physical sword—are gathered into one body and are called a single "beast," so too all those who deceive with words of falsehood are gathered into one body and are rightly called a single "false prophet." <margin>Exodus 7 and 8</margin> Many of these same deceivers did indeed perform lying signs, such as Jannes and Mambres, who resisted Moses in the presence of Pharaoh. <note>Jannes and Mambres were the Egyptian magicians who, according to tradition and 2 Timothy 3:8, opposed Moses by mimicking his miracles.</note> Therefore, since this discourse concerns those persons who deceived the people into killing the Lord, it is not unfitting to attribute to them the performance of signs "in the presence of the beast"—that is, in service to the beast. For, as has been said, they are one with the whole body of deceivers, some of whom did perform signs; though they did not perform them in every specific act, they did so with a total unity of will. 

Caiaphas, of whom we have already spoken, especially seduced those who received the "mark of the beast"—that is, those who carried out the service <margin>John 19</margin> of Satan by crying out: "Crucify him, crucify him," and "We have no king but Caesar." <note>original: "Crucifige crucifige... nō habemus regē nisi Cęsarem" (John 19:6, 15). Rupert interprets the declaration of loyalty to Caesar over God as the "mark of the beast."</note> By saying this in truth, they received the mark of the beast: namely, an excessive and overly willing profession of loyalty to Caesar against the Lord and against His Christ. Furthermore, by accepting Barabbas, the author of sedition, and rejecting the Prince of Peace—when they had the option to choose whichever of the two they wished—they received the <margin>Barabbas is the mark of the beast</margin> mark of the beast, having been seduced by the aforementioned priests into choosing him. For what did Barabbas represent if not the "mark of the beast"? Ultimately, in his own person, he especially...

R ii

<summary>Rupert argues that the "False Prophet" represents the collective body of religious deceivers, identifying the "mark of the beast" as the Jewish leaders' rejection of Christ in favor of Caesar and Barabbas.</summary>

The great and chief example of the Antichrist was that they were going to receive him who comes in his own name, those very people who did not receive the Son of God, the "blessed one who comes in the name of the Lord." <note>A reference to the triumphal entry into Jerusalem and the Messianic title in Matthew 21:9.</note> For He said: "I have come in my Father's name, and you did not receive me. This is because, from that moment on, however much they may think they worship God, they are convicted of worshiping not God, but the one whom they received (or will receive) after rejecting the Son of God.

> **And these two were cast alive into the pool of fire burning with sulfur; and the rest were killed by the sword of the one sitting upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.**

These two, he says—namely the beast and the false prophet—were cast alive into the pool of burning fire. He strives to make us wonder and to rouse our understanding when he says "alive." For what does "alive" mean, if not "knowing"? <note>Rupert uses an allegorical interpretation where being "alive" represents having full intellectual awareness of one's sins, as opposed to sinning in ignorance.</note> In short, he who knowingly resists the truth descends into hell while "living." But he who serves iniquity while being ignorant of God descends there as if "dead." <margin>Psalm 123</margin> This is the source of that line in the Psalm: "When men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive." <note>original: "Cum exurgerent homines in nos..." (Psalm 124:2-3 in modern numbering). Rupert identifies the "living" here as those who have knowledge but are overwhelmed.</note> Indeed, if the Lord had not been in them, strengthening them by the power of the Holy Spirit—even though they were "alive" and possessed knowledge—they would have denied Christ when conquered by tortures. <margin>The Devil and the Jews well knew that Jesus was the Messiah.</margin> 

And regarding the beast—that is, the devil—it is certain that he knew He was the Christ, yet he himself put it into the hearts of the Jews to kill Him. But regarding the prophet, whom he here calls the "false prophet"—that is, that assembly of malignant priests and Pharisees, concerning whom Caiaphas (as has already been said) prophesied—perhaps someone might doubt whether they knew Him or not? <margin>John 15</margin> But He Himself says, whose word is not to be doubted: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin. But now they have no excuse for their sin." Likewise: "If I had not done among them the works which no one else did, they would not have sin. But now they have both see..." <note>The text breaks off here; it is quoting John 15:22-24, where Jesus argues that the Jewish leaders are guilty because they witnessed his miracles and still rejected him.</note>

<summary>Rupert interprets being "cast alive" into hell as a punishment for those who knowingly and willfully reject the truth of Christ. He argues that the devil and the Jewish leadership (the "False Prophet") were fully aware of Jesus's identity but chose to oppose Him regardless.</summary>

**A**nd this angel is Christ himself, but performing another task, powerfully fulfilling what was begun above. For there, Christ descending from heaven entered the Virgin’s womb to destroy the empire of death and to free those who were being detained in hell. Here likewise, Christ descending from heaven is signified as coming to destroy the dark lordship of the world, to free those who were going toward mute idols in ignorance, just as they were being led. This page transitions into the symbolic meaning of the "abyss" and the "earth," interpreting them as descriptions of wicked humanity, and discusses the temporary cessation of pagan worship before the eventual rise of the Antichrist.</meta>

page 523
### On Apocalypse Chapter 20

<margin>The abyss and the earth represent wicked men.</margin>
...[he was cast] onto the earth. And there, by the name of "the earth," and here by the name of "the abyss," wicked and reprobate men are signified. Those who, by desiring only the earth or earthly things, become the earth itself; and by stirring up evils, they have made themselves a deeper abyss, because the life of their malice is a hidden secret. <note>Rupert uses an allegorical interpretation here: the "abyss" isn't just a location, but a state of the human soul consumed by secret evil.</note> In this way, his power was diminished, and he was, as it were, sent from on high into the abyss, because he is no longer celebrated with public worship in temples—claiming the divine name for himself by robbery as he once did, along with the solemn rite of sacrifices. Instead, only those captive men who remain in wretched slavery serve him in secret; in hidden places, they practice their filth and the traces of ancient sorceries. Therefore, it says:

> And he shut him up, and set a seal upon him, that he should no more deceive the nations.

<margin>Through Christ, the worship of demons ceased.</margin>
That is, so that the deceiving spirit <note>original: *falsator spiritus*</note>—who is not God but the devil—may no longer be celebrated with sacred and sacrilegious sacrifices, and that he might not be adored as he once was as **Saturn** the scythe-bearer, or **Jupiter** the adulterer, or **Venus** the prostitute. It was toward the nefarious worship of such beings that the nations were led, seduced by wretched error. Therefore, the devil shall be held bound (as he is) until the thousand years are finished—until all the times pre-ordained for evangelical liberty are fulfilled. We do not know the length of these times, for God has placed them in his own power.

> After that, he says, he must be loosed for a little time.

The loosing of the **dragon**, or the ancient **serpent**, will be the arrival of the **Antichrist**. For then, in that "son of perdition," the devil will come truly loosed. His persecution against the servants of Christ will be so great and of such a kind that they will not only be forbidden from speaking any word of justice, but will not even dare to confess the name "Christian." And this will not be for long, but for a "little time"—specifically, only for three and a half years. <note>Medieval theologians typically interpreted the "little time" of the Antichrist as 1,260 days, or three and a half years, based on the Book of Daniel and other passages in Revelation.</note> He will have such a short time for the sake of the elect; for as the Lord says:
<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
"Unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved." We have already spoken of this above, where it was written concerning the seventh and final [age]...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book <note>Likely referring to Book 11 or 12 of his "Commentary on the Apocalypse."</note>

<margin>A question concerning God’s will: whether He wills evil.</margin>
...on the head of the sevenfold beast, or the seventh king. And when he comes, it is necessary <note>original: *oportet* — often translated as "it must be" or "it is fated," Rupert explores the theological weight of this necessity.</note> that he remain for a short time. In this passage, the author uses the same word—*oportet*—to describe both him and the others. Therefore, the question is asked: Why is it necessary that he be released for a modicum of time, or that he remain for a short time? For people are accustomed to ventilating questions of this kind, and they become almost suspicious of God's will, thinking that He wills evils to happen, and that they must happen because He Himself (which is a sin even to say) wills iniquity.

<margin>The solution from Paul</margin>
For they say it could not happen in such a way unless God willed it. But indeed, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note>, repelling such an objection of wicked suspicion with an averse mind, says: *O man, who are you to answer back to God?* <note>Romans 9:20</note> Having immediately pushed back the slanderer—who multiplies questions more out of a zeal for contention than for speaking—he turns peacefully to the one who asks with a friendly intention, so that he might not contend, but might deserve to know, at least in some small part, the truth of divine judgment; nor should you doubt that the cause of our evils lies within ourselves.

<margin>Romans 9</margin>
*God,* he says, *willing to show His wrath and to make His power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction, so that He might show the riches of His glory upon the vessels of mercy, which He prepared for glory.* <note>Romans 9:22-23</note> Therefore, when the question is asked regarding that seventh head of malice—that is, the Antichrist—as to why it is necessary for him to be released, let it also be asked of the other heads of the beast: why it was necessary for each of them to remain in their own time.

<margin>Exodus 7</margin>
For example, regarding Pharaoh, of whom the Apostle makes mention because of the adversary speaking against him: *For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth."* <note>Exodus 9:16, quoted in Romans 9:17. Rupert draws a direct parallel between the Pharaoh of the Exodus and the Antichrist of the end times.</note> Just as it is said of this current one <note>The Antichrist.</note> that it is necessary for him to be released, so you may truly say of that one <note>Pharaoh.</note> that it was necessary for him to be raised up. Therefore, let the question be asked of these as well as all the rest, and we shall respond as the Apostle teaches us to respond: namely, that these things must happen because God wills to show His wrath and make His power known; and because He wills this, He therefore sustains the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction. It should be noted, indeed, in what manner...

## On Chapter 19 of the Apocalypse

<margin>
How God endures the wicked
</margin>
...he would have said that what He wills is good—namely, to show His wrath and make His power known. The "evils," however, are those whom He endures: specifically, the "vessels of wrath prepared for destruction" <note>original: *vasa iræ apta in interitum* — a reference to Romans 9:22, where Paul discusses God’s sovereignty over those who reject Him.</note>. Let us take Pharaoh as the example proposed by the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note>, a vessel of wrath prepared for destruction, so that the reason why God wills to show His wrath may become clearer. In what way is it good that He showed His wrath then, or does not cease to show it now? Men who are lovers of pleasure and prone to every vanity—as the children of Israel already were in Egypt—do not understand unless some affliction is present. Indeed, they do not *want* to understand that God, who is good, merciful, and kind, also knows how to be angry, or that He can endure the sight of judgment with severity or the condemnation of His own creature.

<margin>
The fornications of Israel in Egypt. Ezekiel 23
</margin>
At that time, the children of Israel were fornicating <note>In biblical commentary, "fornication" is almost always a metaphor for idolatry—the worship of foreign gods instead of the Creator.</note> with the gods of the Egyptians no less than the Egyptians themselves. Thus, through the prophet Ezekiel, speaking under the guise of the women Oholah and Oholibah <note>original: *Oolla atque Ooliba*. In Ezekiel 23, these sisters represent the kingdoms of Samaria and Jerusalem, respectively.</note> against Samaria and Jerusalem, He says: *Therefore Oholah played the harlot against me, following her lovers the Assyrians; moreover, she did not leave behind her fornications which she had in Egypt.* And after a few verses: *Oholibah multiplied her fornications, remembering the days of her youth, in which she played the harlot in the land of Egypt.* Likewise to her: *And you have sought out,* He says, *the wickedness of your youth, when your breasts were handled in Egypt and the teats of your young womanhood were bruised.* <note>Rupert is quoting the Vulgate translation of Ezekiel 23, which uses graphic physical metaphors to describe the spiritual betrayal of the people.</note>

<margin>
God knows both how to be angry and how to show mercy.
</margin>
Therefore, lest the then-unrefined <note>original: *rudes* — meaning "raw," "uncultivated," or "ignorant."</note> children of Israel remain ignorant that God—though He is a kind and merciful Father—nevertheless possesses a most powerful zeal and will judge with severity, and holds wrath in reserve with which He will punish all sinners, a practical demonstration was sometimes necessary. It was expedient for His wrath to be shown to those whom His goodness desired to be saved. For they could not be saved in any other way unless, knowing the coming wrath through some demonstration, they fled from that wrath to come. It was necessary, therefore, for Pharaoh to be raised up; it was necessary for God to endure that "vessel prepared for destruction"—that impious and proud man—sitting upon the throne of the kingdom, which was surely what it meant for him to be "raised up." <note>A reference to Romans 9:17: "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you."</note>

<summary>Rupert explains that God tolerates the existence of wicked "vessels of wrath" like Pharaoh to demonstrate His power and justice, serving as a necessary warning to the faithful. He uses the graphic metaphors of Ezekiel 23 to illustrate how the Israelites had been corrupted by Egyptian idolatry and needed to witness God's severity to be saved.</summary>

This refers to Revelation 12:4, describing the fall of the rebel angels or the corruption of the faithful.</note> Which can only be rightly said of those who could once have been called "brothers," but "went out from us," who are signified here by Gog, that is, "the covered." <note>Rupert is using a traditional medieval etymology where "Gog" is interpreted to mean "covered" or "roofed," signifying those who hide their malice or are "covered" by the devil.</note> Therefore, they are like the **sand of the sea** because their names are not written in heaven, but are written in the earth, <margin>Jeremiah 17</margin> just as the prophet says: *Lord, all who leave you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth.* <note>original: "Domine omnes qui te relinquunt confudentur, recedentes a te in terra scribentur." (Jeremiah 17:13)</note>

These people "went up," he says, "over the breadth of the earth." Regarding the time of their future—of which he had said: *Satan shall be released, and shall go out, and shall gather*—he suddenly returns to the past tense of the vision, saying: *And they went up, and they surrounded the camp of the saints.* They "went up," therefore—it is implied—in that visionary image. For they are to go up in reality. Their "ascent" is their pride. Indeed, that will be their time to mount up in chariots and on horses, boasting; like locusts they shall leap up and spread out over the breadth of the earth, expanding far and wide, ruling far and wide under such a great prince of the world. Thus ascending, thus acting proudly, they surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city. What he had called the "camp of the saints," he repeated more clearly by saying: "and the beloved city." For the beloved city is the camp of the saints, the camp of peace and of love, firm...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the gathering of Gog and Magog as a spiritual alignment of the wicked and "false Christians" against the Church. He contrasts the "sand of the sea" (those destined for the earth/hell) with the "stars of heaven" (the elect).</summary>

### On Chapter 20 of the Apocalypse, Page 541

...[strengthened] by faith, not by material stone; armed by the Word, not by iron.
The wicked surrounded a camp of this kind, such a city, but they did not break in; they attacked it, but they did not shatter it. They remain outside, and the impious walk in a circle; for even if they harm the body, they do not touch the soul; if they tear the flesh, they do not wound the faith. What happened at last?
**And fire came down from heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the pool of fire and sulfur, where both the beast and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night forever and ever.**
All these things are said by way of <term>anticipation</term> <note>A rhetorical device where the author summarizes the end of an event before describing the process in detail.</note>. For in the following section, he repeats and explains more extensively how these things ought to happen—how the fire is to devour the devil and all those whom he deceived, and how they are to be cast into the pool of fire and sulfur. For he says:

**And I saw a great white throne, and him who sat upon it, from whose sight the earth and the heaven fled away, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the sight of the throne. And books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books, according to their works.**

<margin>The great throne of Christ on the day of judgment. Matthew 25</margin>
Therefore, this seating and all this preparation is that which he who was to sit upon it, looking forward as he was already hastening toward his <term>Passion</term> <note>From the Latin *passio*, referring to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, spoke of in this way: *But when the Son of Man shall come in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the seat of his majesty. And all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them one from another, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,* etc. The **great throne** is that great seat of the highest majesty. Just as that throne is great, so it is also **white** <note>original: "candidus." In Latin, this implies a brilliant, pure, or dazzling whiteness, symbolizing the absolute justice of the judge.</note>, because there is not and will not be anything in that judgment that could be rightly found fault with. He spoke of **the one sitting upon it** without using any name, more magnificently hinting at that person through silence; for he is neither unknown, nor is it permitted to be ignorant of him, and it will be impossible for him not to be recognized then.
