# Commentary of Rupert, Book 12
### Page 532

[...is]: rather, it must be provided for, so that when He who sits upon the throne is seen, the one who is to see Him may have a well-disposed eye prepared.

<margin>Isaiah 26</margin>
For the Prophet speaks against those with malignant eyes concerning this matter: *Lord, let your hand be exalted so that they do not see; let the jealous people see and be confounded, and let fire devour your enemies.* <note>original: "Domine exaltetur manus tua vt non videant, videant & confundantur zelantes populi, & ignis hostes tuos deuoret"; a quote from Isaiah 26:11.</note> For how will the jealous people, how will those with malevolent eyes endure it? For he says that *from his sight the earth and the heaven fled, and no place was found for them.* <note>A reference to Revelation 20:11.</note> How then will the earth or heaven flee? Doubtless, the earth, consumed by a great conflagration, will lose its former appearance, and at the same time earthly works will be dissipated; the works of kings and princes will fall together, and burn together, and there will not remain a stone upon a stone of the cities or fortifications, whichever ones men have built since the time of Cain <note>Cain is traditionally cited in Christian exegesis as the first to build a city, symbolizing earthly, material pride</note>, nor will even the tiniest bit of their dust remain from the fire.

<margin>Genesis 4</margin>
In this way, the fleeing earth will also give back all the blood by which it was corrupted, starting from when the aforementioned Cain killed his brother Abel, and all the bodies of men with which it has been filled from the beginning. For this is what he says:

->And I saw the dead, great and small, standing in the sight of the throne.<-

<margin>Psalm 101</margin>
Furthermore, the heaven will flee in the same way as was predicted by the Psalmist concerning both the earth and the heaven: *In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and all of them shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed.* <note>Quoting Psalm 101:26–27 in the Vulgate numbering (Psalm 102 in modern translations).</note> What is signified here in the singular as "heaven" is the same as what is signified there in the plural as "heavens," namely the <term>aerial heaven: the atmosphere or sky immediately above the earth, distinct from the higher celestial or spiritual realms</term>; for indeed this thicker and more corporeal air is also accustomed to be called "heaven." For this reason, even the birds, which in their flight do not go beyond the lowest air, are nevertheless called "birds of heaven." Although this air is one, there are nevertheless different qualities of air for different places and regions, and therefore it is called both "one heaven" and "many heavens."

<margin>Horace</margin>
Hence one of the pagans <note>original: "ethnicorum"; Rupert refers to the Roman poet Horace</note> says: *They change their sky, not their soul, who cross* <note>original: "Cœlum non animum mutant, qui trãs[currunt mare]"; a famous line from Horace’s Epistles 1.11.27. The catchword "trãs" indicates the start of the next page.</note>

# On Apocalypse Chapter 19 <note>Though the header says Chapter 19, the text continues the commentary on Revelation 20:11–12.</note> Page 533

...run to the sea. Concerning these heavens, there is no doubt that they are destined to perish, clearly being dissolved by excessive heat, when He who sits upon His great throne shall appear. For regarding them, the 
<margin>2 Peter 3</margin>
apostle Peter also says in his epistle: *But the heavens that now are, and the earth, are kept in store by the same word, reserved unto the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.* <note>original: "Cœli autem qui nunc sunt, & terra eodem verbo repositi sunt reseruati in diem iudicii, & perditionis impiorum hominum"; a quote from 2 Peter 3:7.</note>

Wondrous and terrifying will be that flight of the heaven or heavens. For it will not happen in silence, but the breaking apart of those fleeing must be heard terribly, or the flight of those broken apart and tearing themselves asunder, just as an old garment is torn. 
<margin>The crackling of heaven from the power of fire.</margin>
Indeed, the fire will then exercise its just powers not lightly, so that the heavens will crackle not a little. Just as they are now accustomed to crackle at times when the summer heat grows strong (which crackling the natural philosophers <term>physici: those who study the physical world and natural phenomena</term> say is thunder), but it will be a mighty storm, and a mighty fire, which shall burn round about Him as He comes, as one commanded to go forth for the vengeance of the wicked, and to examine the merits of the good and the bad. Furthermore, by the "fleeing earth" sinful men can be rightly understood, and by the "heaven" (that is, the air), the demons, whose power of wandering is in the air, can be rightly understood.

**And no place was found for them.**

We also rightly understand that earth and that heaven here as those who indeed have the will to flee, but no place for hiding can be found from the sight of Him sitting upon the throne—namely, wicked men and malignant spirits, who will not be able to flee the gaze of so great a Judge, nor will they be able to obtain their wish to hide themselves in the clefts of the rocks, and saying to the mountains: *fall upon us*, and to the hills: *cover us from the face of him that sits upon the throne*; but all shall stand before Him, all shall be brought out into the public. <note>This refers to the desperate cries of the lost described in Revelation 6:16.</note> There follows:

**And he saw the dead, great and small, standing in the sight of the throne.**

He said "great and small," which is the same as if he were to say that no one can be hidden from being present there, whether he be great or small. Nor indeed will only their faces appear, but their consciences also; this is what he immediately adds next.

# And the books were opened.

<margin>The Book of Life is the predestination of God.</margin>
For the opening of the books will be the manifestation of consciences. "For we must all," says the apostle, "be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad." <note>original: "Apertio nanque librorum, manifestatio erit conscientiarum. Omnes enim nos (ait apostolus) manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi..."; a reference to 2 Corinthians 5:10.</note>

# And another book was opened, which is the book of life.

This book is the certainty of divine foreknowledge <term>foreknowledge: God's eternal knowledge of all things before they happen in time</term> and of blessed predestination. This book will work greatly toward the truth of the judge: because it is clearly not right for any to be saved except those who are written in this book of life—that is, those who are preordained for life. God had already written their names then, and commanded them to be born when, after our first parents—the male and female—were formed, He blessed them with a gracious blessing, saying:
<margin>Genesis 1 and 3.</margin>
"Increase and multiply." <note>original: "Crescite & multiplicamini"; from Genesis 1:28.</note> For regarding all the others, the cause of their birth was the sin of the first transgression that followed, as the text or the order of the narrative indicates. For to the woman the same God said, once the sin was already committed: "I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions." <note>original: "Multiplicabo ærumnas tuas, & conceptus tuos"; from Genesis 3:16.</note> Therefore (as has been said), this opened book of life will work greatly toward the truth of the judge and simultaneously toward the praise of mercy, when it becomes clear to everyone that none of those who sought destruction for themselves through their own evil works had been preordained. Likewise, none of those who were preordained for life, and who were commanded to be born by that [original] blessing, will be missing from the saved. Nor will a person then appear with the kind of works for which he ought to be condemned, having been saved by the grace of the remaining and persevering power of that same blessing. Hence, congratulating them for the victory, Mercy will say to those who stand on the right hand: "Come, 
<margin>
Congratulation on the victory.
Matthew 25.
Judgment according to works.
</margin>
ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." <note>original: "Veni... benedicti patris mei, percipite regnũ, qđ vobis pręparatũ est a cõstitutione mundi"; from Matthew 25:34.</note> Undoubtedly, as He says this, the victorious blessing of God will be celebrated or commemorated with no small triumph—because among so many thorns and thistles of the curse that followed, it was able to grow and be led to perfection, to the praise of Him who, having been made man for our sake, dissolved the curse and recovered the original blessing.

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 20:12–13. Having established that the "books" are the consciences of men, Rupert now describes the process of judgment based on those records and the physical resurrection of the dead from all places, including the sea.</meta>

<page-num>535</page-num>
<header>On the Apocalypse, Chapter 20, page 535</header>

### And the dead (he says) were judged from those things which were written in the books, according to their works.
<note>original: "Et iudicati sunt (inquit) mortui ex his quæ scripta erant in libris secundum opera ipsorum."</note>

This is so certain that no one is permitted to be ignorant of whose mouth will recite whatever is written in those books. The King himself, sitting upon the throne, asserted that he would recite it in this way—first to those who will be at his right hand: *For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat. I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink,* etc. <note>original: "Esuriui enim, & dedistis mihi manducare. Sitiui, & dedistis mihi potum..." A reference to the Sheep and the Goats in Matthew 25:35.</note> On the other hand, regarding the consciences of those who will be at his left hand, he will pronounce that they did not do all these things, and for that reason he will say: *Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire.* There, no one will be allowed to be absent, no matter where or by what end they were consumed. Whence he also immediately adds:

### And the sea gave up the dead who were in it; and death and hell gave up the dead who were in them.
<note>original: "Et dedit mare mortuos suos, qui in eo erāt: & mors, & infernus dederunt mortuos suos, qui in ipsis erant."</note>

<margin>On the difference between death and hell. Psalm 115.</margin>
The sea, it is understood, gave up the bodies, while death and hell gave up the souls. And indeed, not only the sea, but also the earth shall return all bodies from their graves. But the author is content to have beautifully mentioned only the "sea" here, because it might be more doubted by the unfaithful. To them, while it seems incredible that our bodies can be reformed into a whole from the dust of the earth, it is judged much more impossible to be called back from the sea and all the rivers, if they have been so entirely consumed that not even a tiny bit of dust appears to remain anywhere. Furthermore, "death" and "hell" <term>hell: here translating 'infernus,' referring to the lower world or the state of the damned</term> differ in this: that "hell" is said to belong only to the wicked, but "death" is said to be, and truly is, also for the good. For *precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* <note>original: "preciosa in cōspectu domini mors sanctorum eius"; Psalm 116:15 (115:15 in the Latin Vulgate).</note> Therefore, death and hell gave up their dead. That is, the souls of both the blessed dead, who died in the Lord, and the damned, who were assigned to hell, shall return to their own bodies—wherever those bodies might be, even those which the greed of sea monsters consumed in the depths of the sea.

### And they were judged, every one according to [their] works.
<note>original: "Et iudicatum est de singulis secundum opera."</note>

--- Page 608 ---
<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 20:12–15. Rupert is refining his explanation of the Final Judgment, specifically addressing the "double" nature of the punishment for those not found in the Book of Life.</meta>

<page-num>536</page-num>
<header>Rupert's Commentary, Book 12</header>

...their works, and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.

He had already stated this: that the dead were judged according to their works from those things written in the books. After inserting the detail that the sea gave up its dead who were in it, and death and hell gave up the dead who were in

<margin>The double damnation of the wicked.</margin>
them, only then does he repeat: "And they were judged," he says, "every one according to their works." <note>original: "de singulis secundum opera ipsorum"</note> Indeed, there is a double damnation for the wicked (about whom he immediately adds, "and hell and death were cast into the lake of fire"). For even before they rise with their bodies in that resurrection where the sea returns its dead, the souls of the wicked are judged and tormented in the underworld. And after they have risen, then their souls and bodies together, having been judged, will be tormented forever and ever. Then "hell" and "death"—meaning the wicked people who will stand on the left hand with the devil and his angels—shall be cast into the lake of fire.
**And this, he says, is the second death.**

<margin>The first death is sin; the second death is the eternal punishment of sin.</margin>
This is clearly what he spoke of earlier when he said: *Blessed and holy is he who has part in the first resurrection,* <note>A reference to Revelation 20:6</note> to which he added: *Over these the second death has no power.* Therefore, since the "first resurrection" consists of rising from sins through faith in Christ, the "first death" is rightly understood as sin itself. The "second death," however, is rightly understood as the eternal punishment <note>original: "vindicta," meaning vengeance or legal punishment</note> for sin, regarding which he again adds:
**And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.**

He seems to repeat this for a specific reason: namely, because they are cast into the lake of fire for a twofold cause. That is, both for original sin <term>original sin: the theological concept that all humans inherit a fallen nature from Adam</term>, from which they were not liberated through faith in Christ, and for actual sins <term>actual sins: specific, personal sins committed by an individual during their lifetime</term>, which individuals added to that first transgression during their lives. Therefore, what he had said earlier by way of anticipation: "And the devil who seduced them was cast..."

<summary>Rupert explains the "second death" as the eternal punishment for sin, distinguishing it from the "first death" (sin itself). He argues that the damned face a double judgment: once in the soul before the resurrection, and once in both body and soul after the final judgment.</summary>

**I saw (he says) the holy city, the New Jerusalem.**

<margin>The city of the blessed.</margin>
For it was fitting for the whole assembly of the saints and the elect to be extolled with such venerable praise that he should call it a city: holy by its merits, Jerusalem by its name, and new in its condition. Undoubtedly this is because this city is holy, while that other one which he had seen earlier—the enemy of this one—is both called and is the harlot and the mother of fornications <note>A reference to Babylon the Great from Revelation 17.</note>. This one, by the name Jerusalem, signifies its own true peace and the peace of its God; the other, by the name Babylon, designates its own confusion <note>In medieval exegesis, Jerusalem was etymologically interpreted as "Vision of Peace" and Babylon as "Confusion."</note>. This one is new and persevering in eternal youth; the other, having spent its fleeting youth in fornications and being consumed in a short time, is henceforth wrinkled with eternal old age.

<margin>
The newness of Jerusalem through the grace of double regeneration. Romans 6. Matthew 19.
</margin>
For what is its "newness" if not the double grace of holy regeneration? For now, having been regenerated through the first resurrection—that is, through the baptism of CHRIST—it walks in the newness of life; but then, when that which the present vision describes has come to pass, it will be regenerated through the second resurrection, of which CHRIST himself said: "In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty," etc. <note>Referencing Matthew 19:28, where Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things.</note> Therefore, it will then be truly new in both body and soul. "Such a one I saw," he says, "descending from heaven," and explaining what he had said, he added:

### Prepared by God.

For that holy city does not claim for itself what it is, but remembers that it has received it from God—not by its own merits, but by celestial grace—and it gives eternal thanks. In what way was it prepared by God?

**As a bride (he says) adorned for her husband.**

In every respect, this city is proclaimed to be very different from that great city, the harlot. For that one, sitting in the attire of a harlot upon the scarlet beast full of names of blasphemy, is clearly proven to be a prostitute and a fornicator...

...safe for demons, having committed fornication with kings. But this city is declared modestly adorned for her one husband, her one God, and like a bride—clearly already prepared for entering the wedding—while that adulteress undergoes the deserved punishments of death and hell.

**And I heard a great voice from the throne saying,**
**Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them. And they shall be his people, and God himself with them shall be their God.**

Truly great and delightful is this voice, by which He who sits on the throne demonstrates and commends the holy city and His bride as worthy. For she never commended herself, and therefore it is fitting that her husband, her God, should commend her. On the contrary, that harlot <note>A reference to Babylon, symbolizing worldly corruption and pride.</note> commends herself to her corrupters and those she has corrupted; she magnifies herself in her own heart and with her own mouth among them in her own evils. For on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: **Babylon the great, the mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.** <note>original: "Babylon magna, mater fornicationum & abominationum terræ"</note> Likewise she says in her heart: **I sit as a queen and am no widow, and I shall not see mourning.** <note>original: "Sedeo regina & vidua non sum, & luctum non videbo"</note> But this city does not commend herself; rather her God, her husband, sitting on the throne, commends her with a great voice.

**Behold, he says, the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them.**

<margin>Psalm 103</margin>
"Behold" is an adverb of demonstration; it is a great sign of great congratulation uttered by the mouth of one who is joyful, because as the Psalmist says: **The Lord shall rejoice in his works.** <note>original: "Lætabitur dominus in operibus suis." In the Latin Vulgate used by Rupert, this is Psalm 103; in modern English Bibles, it is Psalm 104:31.</note> For this tabernacle <note>The "tabernacle" refers to the dwelling place of God, here identified as the Church or the assembly of the saints.</note> is the work of the Lord; all its ornaments, both inside and out, are the beautiful works of the Lord, worthy of the proclamations of the Lord who points them out, and worthy of the joy of the Lord’s heart, so that (as has already been said) as the prophet testifies: He may rejoice in them.

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
From the time He formed the first man, took a rib from his side, and built it into a woman, God has not ceased or finished building this tabernacle of His until He completes it and says: **Behold the tabernacle of God.** Furthermore, what he adds, "with men," is the same...

<summary>Rupert contrasts the humility of the New Jerusalem with the pride of Babylon, explaining that God Himself must praise the Holy City because she does not seek her own glory. He links the "building" of this spiritual tabernacle back to the creation of Eve in Genesis, viewing all of salvation history as the construction of God's dwelling place.</summary>

A wondrous assertion of truth. "God," he says, "will wipe away every tear from their eyes." The magnitude of the consolation reserved there for the saints and the chosen of God—who weep in this world—could not be expressed more magnificently. For this kind of expression is drawn from the image of a mother who, unable to endure the weeping of her little child, wipes his eyes and face with her hand and soothes him with kisses. To communicate such great affection for us, the same God says through the prophet among other things: *Their children shall be carried on shoulders, and shall be comforted upon the knees.* <note>original: "Pueri eorū in humeris portabuntur, & super genua consolabuntur"; a reference to Isaiah 66:12</note> And immediately the same Spirit of grace addresses the little ones themselves, saying to them: *As a mother comforts her sons, so will I comfort you, and you shall be comforted in Jerusalem,* etc. <note>original: "Quemadmodum mater consolatur filios suos, ita & ego consolabor vos, & in Hierusalem consolabimini"; Isaiah 66:13</note> However, it would seem pointless for tears to be wiped from the eyes unless the cause of weeping itself were also removed. Rightly, then, it follows and says:

**And death shall be no more.**
<margin>How different the fate of the bride is from the fate of the harlot.</margin>

Under the name of "death," he briefly encompasses all the hardships of mortality. It is as if he were to say: "And that harlot <note>Babylon, representing the corrupt world or the unfaithful city.</note>, whom you saw drunk with the blood of the saints, shall never again be able to drink anything of their blood: since indeed..."

### RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, On the Apocalypse of John the Apostle: Book XII of the Commentaries.

<image-desc>Decorative floral woodcut initial letter S.</image-desc>
We have looked upon the works of the seven spirits of God—what kind of things they have worked with the human race from the beginning until the end of the age—each in its own order, from the first, which is the spirit of wisdom, down to the last of that same order, the spirit of the fear of the Lord. 
<margin>The twofold order of the seven spirits of the Lord</margin>
For as has been said elsewhere, for us who are ascending toward God, the first in order is the spirit of the fear of the Lord, as Scripture testifies when it says: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* <note>Psalm 111:10; Rupert explains that while humans start with "fear" to reach "wisdom," God’s grace descends in the opposite direction.</note> But for the heavenly grace descending to us, another order of these same spirits of the Lord is reckoned by the prophet; for when he speaks of the flower that ascends from the rod proceeding from the root of Jesse, he says:
<margin>Isaiah 11.</margin>
*And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.* <note>Isaiah 11:2-3. The "spirit of piety" is a traditional reading from the Latin Vulgate; many modern English translations based on the Hebrew text omit piety to list six spirits or group them differently.</note> Therefore, seeking out the works of these spirits according to the authority of the Holy Scriptures, we have looked upon and scrutinized, as far as we were able, seven <term>periochas</term> <note>original: "periochas"; refers to the divisions or sections into which Rupert has organized the biblical text.</note>, determining them according to these same spirits. For the writer of this book announced grace and peace to us from these spirits in Christ Jesus, saying at the beginning: *Grace to you from him who is, and who was, and who is to come; and from the seven spirits who are in the sight of his throne; and from Jesus Christ,* etc.
<margin>The argument of the final book</margin>
Now finally, at the conclusion <note>original: "in calce"; literally "at the heel," a common Latin idiom for the end of a work.</note> of this vision or revelation, the entirety of the whole work is shown to this John—the work which Jesus Christ built at such great cost and with so many graces or gifts of his spirits—namely, the holy city Jerusalem, which is the Church of God. This is shown not as she is in this pilgrimage <note>The medieval concept of the "Church Militant" traveling through the world as a temporary exile.</note>, nor as she will stand at the right hand in the final judgment (as was said a little while ago, not without some fear until the fury of the Lord passes, by which those on the left will be sent into eternal fire), but as she will be after the judgment in eternal glory: alone and complete, with all strangers cast out, fully enjoying the vision of God. It begins thus:

<meta>Catchword: And [there] came</meta>

<summary>Rupert of Deutz introduces the final book of his commentary, explaining that his entire analysis has been structured around the Seven Spirits of God. He defines the Church not as a worldly institution, but as the eternal Holy City that will exist after the Final Judgment.</summary>

<header>On Chapter 21 of the Apocalypse</header>

And there came one of the seven angels who had the seven vials full of the seven last plagues, and he spoke with me, saying: "Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." And he took me up in spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, having the glory of God. <note>original: "Et venit unus de septem angelis..." — Revelation 21:9-10</note>

<margin>Christ speaks in the saints. 2 Cor. 13.</margin>
This "one of the seven angels" is Christ himself, who speaks in all those same angels—that is, the holy preachers—just as one of them, the apostle Paul, says: *Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?* <note>original: "An experimentum quaeritis eius qui in me loquitur Christus?" — 2 Corinthians 13:3. Rupert argues that Christ is the primary speaker behind the angelic messengers.</note> This "one" was destined to come to his beloved John and appear to him with his disciples (as you read in the commonly known history of his Assumption) <note>Rupert refers to the *Transitus Mariae* or apocryphal acts of John, which describe John being called to a heavenly banquet at the end of his life.</note> saying to him: "Come, my beloved, to me, because it is time for you to feast in my banquet with your brothers." Therefore, prefiguring this, this one of the seven angels spoke, saying to me: "Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." For he who says these things surely hints that the wedding feast is there, regarding which, as has already been mentioned, he was to say: "it is time for you to feast in my banquet with your brothers." Indeed, the bride is found in the nuptial banquet. But why did he say both: both "bride" and "wife of the Lamb"? Evidently, it is because the marriage of the Lamb and his one and only Church is virginal. Even there, where she will already be a "wife" in the fullness of delight, she will nonetheless remain a "bride," because in that blessed union she will always be a wife with children, yet always a virgin, as the wedding and the bridal festivities remain eternal.

"And he took me up," he said, "in spirit to a great and high mountain."

<margin>The great mountain is Christ</margin>
Truly, he who is transferred to the vision of divinity—which was destined to happen to this man <note>referring to John</note>—is lifted up to a great altitude and the high magnitude of the eternal mountain. For this mountain is Christ, who, like a small stone cut from a mountain <note>A reference to the prophecy in Daniel 2:34-35 regarding the stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth.</note>

M

...without hands. <note>original: "sine manibus" — a reference to Daniel 2:34, the stone "cut out without hands" that became a great mountain.</note> That is, born of a virgin in the humility of our human condition, he grew and became a **great mountain**, and filled the whole world. He grew by ascending above the choirs of angels as the Lord of all things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. "He lifted me up," he says, "to this great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem." Therefore, the city is founded or built upon Christ himself. This is so true that we read how God also spoke of him through the prophet: <margin>Isaiah 28</margin> *Behold, I will place in the foundations of Zion a cornerstone, a precious stone, set in a firm foundation.* <note>original: "Ecce ego mittam in fundamentis Sion lapidem..." — Isaiah 28:16.</note> But in the Gospel, against the scribes and Pharisees, that very Stone uses the testimony of the Psalmist for himself, when he says: <margin>Psalm 118</margin> *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* <note>original: "Lapidem quem reprobaverunt..." — Psalm 118:22 (Vulgate 117), cited by Jesus in Matthew 21:42.</note>

Rightly, therefore, is the city shown atop the mountain, since the Church of Christ is known to be founded upon Christ himself. This is a wondrous construction, with a wondrous placement of the foundation and the stone. For every building and every structure of cities or houses in this world has its foundation at the bottom and its walls rising upward. However, this building or city shown here in the spirit has its highest foundation at the top, <note>Rupert is describing a spiritual "inverted" architecture where the Church "hangs" from Christ in heaven rather than being built up from the earth.</note> from which the entire structure of the walls hangs, as does all the hope and love of the faithful peoples—both of the Jews, who came first, and of the Gentiles, <margin>Why this city is called Jerusalem.</margin> who were built in later. He calls this city "holy" and names it "Jerusalem" because the Church is holy, consecrated by the blood of her Bridegroom, possessing—and destined to possess—the vision of eternal peace. Regarding this, the Holy Spirit sings in the psalm: <margin>Psalm 147</margin> *Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion. For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you, he who has set peace in your borders.* <note>original: "Lauda Hierusalem dominum..." — Psalm 147:12-14.</note> He says of her:

### **Coming down out of heaven from God:**

As he had already stated above. "Coming down," I say, and not "falling," as that angel fell and became the devil and Satan. For to fall is a matter of pride, but to descend is a matter of humility. By always holding itself in this descent of humility, that Jerusalem shall stand for eternity, knowing that what it is, it is not by its own strength.

<summary>Rupert explains that the Church is a mystical city founded on Christ (the mountain), uniquely "hanging" from its foundation in heaven rather than standing on earthly ground. He distinguishes the "descent" of the Church (humility) from the "fall" of the devil (pride).</summary>

Furthermore, this likeness <margin>Christ is the stone, as in 1 Peter 2. For the Church is made like God or Christ not from one thing, but from two: namely, not from faith alone, but from faith joined with the **works of the virtues**. By the jasper, therefore, we understand the beauty of the virtues; by the crystal, we understand the purity of faith, preserved as it was received in baptism.

For childhood is correctly understood through the east; fervent adolescence or youth through the south; mature age through the west; and decrepit old age through the north. > meets them at the fourfold crossroads.

<margin>The Apostles as the twelve foundations.</margin>
The same apostles who are the gates are also themselves the foundations of this city. For the church of God is founded upon their faith; however, it is so in such a way that Christ himself is their foundation. Ultimately, they are called "foundations" because of this one unique foundation, just as the first among them—who is one and the same <note>Rupert refers here to the Apostle Peter.</note>—was called Peter from the "rock" <note>original: "a petra"; a play on the Latin *Petrus* (Peter) and *petra* (rock), referencing Matthew 16:18.</note>, which without doubt is Christ. Therefore, when he had said: *And in those twelve foundations the names of the twelve apostles*, he fittingly added, *and of the Lamb*. For whatever they wrote—by which writings of theirs, as if by foundations, the entire building of the Christian faith and ecclesiastical doctrine is supported—they did not write of themselves, but received it from the fullness of the Lamb, and with their whole intention they clung to and fixed themselves upon his Gospel words. These are the foundations, and these are the gates, about which the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: *His foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob.*

<margin>Psalm 86 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 87:1–2.</note></margin>
For the meaning is this: the "holy mountains," that is the apostles, are the foundations of that glorious city of God through their faith and doctrine; and they are likewise its "gates," because through their preaching and miracles, entrance is made into that Zion. The Lord loves these gates above all the tents of Jacob, that is, more than all those serving as soldiers for Him in the former people <note>Rupert is referring to the Israelites under the Old Covenant.</note>. 

<margin>The Apostles are more excellent than the prophets.</margin>
For although Moses and the other prophets lived holily and justly, and were of immense holiness and faith, nevertheless the dignity of the apostles' merits excels to that degree. They not only lived rightly, but they also saw the Lord himself in His bodily presence (whom the prophets had foretold from afar); they deserved to be refreshed by the inner nourishment of His most rigorous <note>original: "acerbissimae"; while this can mean "bitter," in this context of preaching, it likely refers to the "sharp" or "piercing" demands of the Gospel that lead to spiritual growth.</note> preaching; and, taking up their own cross, they followed in His footsteps, announcing to men everywhere on earth the peace given through His death. Although, however, here in these foundations—

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains that the Apostles are both the "gates" and "foundations" of the New Jerusalem, deriving their authority from Christ, the primary foundation. He argues the Apostles surpass the Old Testament prophets because they witnessed the Incarnation and the Passion directly.</summary>

**And he measured the city with the reed at twelve thousand stadia.** <note>A <term>stadium</term> was an ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet; twelve thousand stadia would be about 1,400 miles.</note>
<gloss>That is <unclear>... by degrees ...</unclear></gloss>
So that you may understand these twelve thousand stadia as divided among four sides, he adds further:
**Its length and width [and height] are equal.** <note>Rupert’s text focuses on the length and width here, though the Biblical verse includes height.</note>
<margin>
How great the circumference of this city is.
</margin>
However, he also adds the height, of which we shall speak shortly. Thus, when you see twelve thousand stadia in the circumference of the city, and the city itself is square, you can easily observe that each of the sides measures three thousand stadia. But how will that which follows stand?
<margin>
To those from whom the apostles were and how it is fortified <unclear>...</unclear> and the area <unclear>...</unclear> made by <unclear>...</unclear> so many more men <unclear>...</unclear>
</margin>
**And he measured its walls at one hundred forty-four cubits,** <note>original: "centum quadraginta quatuor cubitorum"</note> which is far less than three thousand stadia! This saying could be seen as referring to the height of the walls—namely, that the walls stretched up to a height of one hundred forty-four cubits—if he had not said that the length, width, and height of the city are equal. Yet (as we have already said) both the length and the width were three thousand stadia, which far exceeds the quantity of one hundred forty-four cubits. Therefore, this measurement of the wall is something else entirely; its quantity is far different, and far smaller. For one cannot even suspect that when he says, "And he measured its walls at one hundred forty-four cubits," he means any [entire] side of the square city. Instead, where he had said, "And he measured the city at twelve thousand stadia," we must understand the total area of that same city.

<summary>Rupert explores the geometric symbolism of the New Jerusalem, noting that its square shape represents perfect peace and harmony. He grapples with the mathematical discrepancy between the city's massive size (12,000 stadia) and the relatively small measure of its wall (144 cubits).</summary>

--- Page 626 ---
<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Book 12 of Revelation. Following the measurement of the city itself at twelve thousand stadia on the previous page, Rupert now addresses the wall measured at one hundred and forty-four cubits, reconciling the massive difference in scale through spiritual allegory.</meta>

<page-num>554</page-num>

<header>Rupert’s Commentary, Book 12</header>

For the logic of geometric science <note>original: "tricalis [geometricalis] nanque disciplinæ ratio"</note> holds that every square with equal sides multiplies one side by itself, and by that single multiplication fills its own area. Furthermore, this quantity of one hundred and forty-four <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit was an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches.</note> multiplied by itself barely covers anything beyond fifteen <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>. How much less is this than twelve thousand stadia? Therefore, there is (as has already been said) one wall here, and another wall of the city there. How this occurs in man-made cities—where a narrower wall is contained within a larger wall—does not require our demonstration. Finally, one might not build incongruously if, within a city whose circumference is twelve thousand stadia, he were to build a citadel <note>original: "arcem"</note> whose sides were each one hundred and forty-four cubits. We must seek the meaning of the spiritual building, because surely we are compelled to perceive from the very surface of the literal text
<margin>Two ranks of this city</margin>
that another, shorter wall is contained within the larger wall. What then shall we say, except that although it is one city, it is one Church? Yet there are two ranks <note>original: "ordines"</note> of the city: one consists of those who fought bravely while suffering persecutions from without; the other consists of those who finished the course of this present life by working well in the peace of the Church. For the <term>stadia</term> signify the labor of those fighting, while the <term>cubits</term> signify the peace of those working. He measured the city with the reed at twelve thousand stadia; that is, he rewarded that great and strong rank of the holy Church which ran and fought in the stadium <note>Rupert plays on the word "stadium" as both a distance and an arena for athletic/military struggle.</note>, and which shed its blood for that same testimony by testifying to the faith of the Holy Trinity through the four parts of the world. These numbers—namely four and three—are the components of twelve, for four times three, or three times four, are twelve. In this rank, surely, are the apostles and the martyrs of CHRIST. Indeed, the larger wall of this rank contains within it the shorter wall of one hundred and forty-four cubits, because the merits of such great defenders have brought it about that the multitude of the weak, confirmed in the faith of Christ, might attain to a dwelling in that same city by persisting in good works.

<summary>Rupert explains the discrepancy between the city's massive size (12,000 stadia) and its wall's smaller height (144 cubits) by interpreting them as two "ranks" of Christians: the heroic martyrs and the peaceful laborers.</summary>

When he makes a distinction between the wall and the city, saying: "And the structure of the wall was of jasper stone, but the city itself was pure gold," he signifies by the name of the "wall" those faithful of a firmer and more spiritual purpose; but by the designation of the "city"—meaning the streets of the city—he signifies the multitude of a more expansive life <note>original: "laxioris vitæ," referring to those who live in the world rather than in monastic seclusion.</note> and especially of the lay order.
<margin>Pure gold like glass</margin>

Because they frequent holy confession and do not defend their sins, but open them up by confessing, this gold is rightly said to be like "clear glass" <note>Rupert uses the transparency of glass as a metaphor for the honesty of a believer who does not hide their sins from God.</note>. For the beauty or glory of the gates—through which we entered, coming into that city from the four parts of the world—could not be more beautifully or suitably signified than by the name or appearance of pearls.

Indeed, just as a noble woman, adorned with precious pearls, is accustomed to boast before the eyes of men because she is decorated by her husband, so that city, which is the Church, can boast in such princes, such fathers, and such glorious apostles. She is adorned for her spouse, Christ, like a bride. For this reason, the Apostle Paul—being well aware of this, and being surely one of those gates that are always open—speaks to the Corinthians: *For you are our glory, just as we are yours on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ* [2 Corinthians 1:14]. [The vision] showed me a river, and he rightly added **of the water of life.** And because such water illuminates and strengthens by giving life, he appropriately says **bright**, adding **as crystal.** For in crystal there is clarity and firmness at the same time, which are beautiful emblems of that [eternal] life, where our hearts will shine through and our bodies will be made firm by blessed immortality and immortal blessedness. And because the Holy Spirit is said to proceed according to the Gospel tradition of our Lord, as he says:
<margin>John 15</margin>
> When the Comforter <term>Comforter: translated from "paracletus," a title for the Holy Spirit meaning one who consoles or advocates</term> has come, whom I will send to you, the Spirit of Truth, who proceeds from the Father: <note>original: "Cum venerit paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis, spiritum veritatis, qui a patre procedit"</note>
he rightly did not stay silent on this point here. For he says of this river **proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb**: for this is what we profess in the Catholic faith: That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. <note>Rupert is defending the "Filioque" doctrine, the belief that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both God the Father and God the Son.</note> He says:

->In the middle of its street.<-

<margin>Outside the church there is no grace of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
This is spoken appropriately and properly to express the delights of the city: because the Holy Spirit does not flow outside that city, but only **in the middle of the street of the city**, that is, only in the hearts of the elect <term>elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> which have been greatly expanded. And indeed, from the moment Jesus was glorified, this river began to flow toward us, but it has not yet appeared, nor can it be seen here in this present life what it has done for us. The fruit of his entire procession, by which he deigns to come to us, will appear there; this is what he now describes.

## On either side of the river, the tree of life bearing twelve fruits.

This refers to Christ, who chose and sent the twelve apostles. Finally, the fact that Christ was made man and born of a virgin comes from the abundance of this irrigating river: because the Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, and he caused such a tree to rise up for us from the virgin earth of her womb. Likewise, the fact that this tree brought forth **twelve fruits**—that is, that Christ ordained twelve
<margin>Psalm 1</margin>
apostles—comes from the fullness of this river: because he gave the Holy Spirit to them. Therefore we have this in the Psalm:
> And he shall be like a tree that is planted near the running waters, which shall yield its fruit in its season. <note>original: "Et erit tanquam lignum, quod plantatum est secus decursus aquarum, quod fructum suū dabit in tempore suo."</note>

this is what he says here: **every month**. That is, without fail and in eternity. For it will never cease to produce fruit, because the reward of the saints, which comes from Him, will never fail. ### **And the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations,**

<margin>The leaves of the tree are the words of the Gospel</margin>
For the leaves of the tree are the words of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. By receiving these, the nations have acquired for themselves the eternal health of their souls and bodies. ### **And every curse shall be no more.**

This kind of tree and this kind of fruit are said to be on both sides of the river, namely, in the likeness of some visible, delightful river, along whose well-watered banks on this side and that, fruitful growth <note>original: "lingua," literally "tongue," here likely referring to the "language" of nature or the "strips" of land</note> or all manner of green things are seen with great delight.

### **And the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and his servants shall serve him.**

Those who are servants, and who will serve Him, will themselves be the throne of God and of the Lamb in that city. And He Himself will sit in them as **King of kings and Lord of lords**, dwelling in their hearts with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.
<margin>Sweet service in heaven</margin>
That will be a glorious and sweet service, where they remember in their consciences that they are servants of Him by whom, through whom, and in whom they were redeemed. Yet that Lord shows Himself not so much as a master of slaves or a king of servants, but as a Father of children and a Friend of friends. He requires no other service than that of ineffable love—a love that cannot cease from praising and that holds infinite thanksgivings as the highest and most unspeakable delights. For how could they rest from such service?

### On Revelation Chapter 22, Page 567 <note>The Latin header says Chapter 21, but the text comments on Chapter 22:6–8.</note>

It was certainly destined (as we already said at the beginning) to be despised by some, mostly because of its difficulty. Irreverent people are often inclined to despise whatever they read all the more easily when those things are difficult to understand. 

Therefore, just as he said at the beginning: *The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to him to make known to his servants the things which must shortly come to pass* <note>Revelation 1:1</note>; so here also, having first stated: *These words are most faithful and true,* he says: *And the Lord God Almighty of the spirits of the prophets*—that is, the Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets—*has sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly come to pass.* 

Likewise, just as he had spoken there with the intent: *Blessed is he who reads, and they who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things written in it, for the time is near* <note>Revelation 1:3</note>; so he speaks here with the same intent or meaning:

**And behold, I come quickly. Blessed is he who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.** <note>Revelation 22:7</note>

He speaks these things in the person of the Lord Jesus, who, although he seems to delay, will come quickly and fulfill the words of the prophecy of this book. Furthermore, just as he had carefully expressed his own identity once, twice, and a third time at the beginning to commend the book—first saying: *and he signified it, sending by his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God*; and second, saying: *John, to the seven churches which are in Asia*; and thirdly, saying: *I, John, your brother and partner in tribulation,* etc.—so here he clearly expresses his identity as one who has served the Church of Christ well.

<margin>22:8</margin>
**And I, John**—it is understood to mean, "I am he"—**who heard and saw these things.** <note>Revelation 22:8</note>

Therefore, whoever you are that receives the holy prophets, in whom or through whom the Holy Spirit spoke, and receives the Gospel of the Word of God which John wrote, receive this scripture as well. For the Spirit of the prophets sent his angel to show these things to his servants; and he who heard and saw these things is John himself.

From here until the end, all things are spoken in the person of the Lord Jesus, and the prophecy is confirmed from his own mouth, so that no one who wishes to belong to the Lord Jesus would dare to despise it. *Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.* What is said to John alone is also said to every person who understands the mysteries of this book: that they should not seal or close it, but rather open and explain it as much as they can for the building up and instruction of the listeners, because the time is near—that is, what is written in it will quickly be fulfilled. Since this is so, what more remains to be decided or commanded? Therefore, it follows:
**He who harms, let him harm still; and he who is in filth, let him be filthy still. And let the righteous man do justice still, and let the holy man be sanctified still.** <note>Revelation 22:11</note>

Ac si dicat: <note>Translate: "As if he were to say:"</note> Since such great punishments are set aside for the impious, and such great rewards for the pious—as the sequence of this book signifies—the impious man should not doubt that a sufficiency for his merits will be paid back, however much he harms still; and the just and holy man should not doubt that rewards worthy of his merits will be returned, however much he performs justice or is sanctified still. But how do we think this was said: *He who harms, let him harm still; and he who is in filth, let him be filthy still*? Is it because "let him harm" and "let him be filthy" are in the imperative mood <note>The "imperative mood" is a grammatical form used for commands.</note>, that the creature therefore has the impulse to harm or be filthy from the will of the Creator? No

[Page 660]

The Creator wants neither that his creature be harmful nor that it be filthy, but there is a time when He must [stop] caring what that creature does, or how much it becomes defiled, as it is written: <margin>Psalm 9 <note>Original: *Psalm. ix*. In the Vulgate, this is Psalm 9:25; in modern Bibles, it is Psalm 10:4. The verse describes a sinner who, in his pride, does not seek God, but Rupert interprets it here as God ceasing to "seek" the unrepentant sinner as an act of judgment.</note></margin> "According to the multitude of His wrath, He will not seek him." When does this happen? Surely it is when that sinner or filthy person, through the love and defense of his sins and filth, provokes God to anger.

For there are three ways in which a person sins: through ignorance, through weakness, or through pride.

<margin>God assists the one sinning through ignorance.</margin> If a sin is committed through ignorance, and God foresees that this person—whoever they may be—is someone who would be corrected once the truth is known, God assists that ignorance. He does this so that the ignorant and erring person may come to know what is true. 

An example of this is found here: God came to Abimelech by night and said, "Behold, you shall die because of the woman you have taken, for she has a husband." <margin>Genesis 20</margin> When Abimelech replied to this: "Lord, will you kill a nation that is ignorant and just? Did he not say to me, 'She is my sister,' and she herself said, 'He is my brother'? In the simplicity of my heart and the purity of my hands I have done this." God said to him: "I also know that you did this in the simplicity of your heart, and therefore I kept you from sinning against me, and I did not permit you to touch her." <note>This story from Genesis 20 describes King Abimelech taking Abraham's wife Sarah, believing she was Abraham's sister. God intervenes to prevent the sin because Abimelech acted without malice.</note> 

The Apostle [Paul] also obtained mercy for this reason, and was assisted by heavenly compassion, because, as he said, "I did it ignorantly in unbelief." <margin>1 Timothy 1</margin> 

But if someone sins through weakness, such as the person in whose voice the same Apostle speaks: "I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. <margin>Romans 7</margin> But I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind, and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord." <note>Paul describes the internal struggle where a person desires to do good but feels "captured" by their physical impulses or "the flesh."</note> 

God patiently endured the sin of such a person; indeed, He even overlooks it, as Wisdom speaks in praise of His mercy: <margin>Wisdom 11</margin> "You have mercy on all, O Lord, and you hate nothing of those things which you have made, overlooking the sins of men for the sake of repentance." <margin>God hands over the one sinning through pride to shameful desires.</margin> 

Furthermore, if someone sins with pride, God hands him over and leaves him to the desires of his heart in impurity. In such a case, you should not say that it is the Lord's will that the person is harmful or filthy; rather, it is because God was not [dwelling] in that person, and because He is greatly angered by him, and according to...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains that God's decision to "let the filthy be filthy" is a judgment against pride. He contrasts this with God's mercy toward those who sin out of ignorance (like Abimelech) or human weakness (like Paul’s "inner man").</summary>

<keywords>sin, ignorance, weakness, pride, Abimelech, Apostle Paul, mercy, divine judgment, Revelation 22:11, free will</keywords>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 12

[Page 570]

...in the multitude of His wrath, He will not seek <note>original: *non queret*. Rupert is continuing the interpretation of the Psalm verse cited on the previous page, suggesting God eventually stops "seeking" the lost soul as a punishment.</note> him. One must certainly understand that person to be the one of whom it is said here: "He who harms, let him harm still; and he who is in filth, let him be filthy still." This is especially so because He did not say: "He who *harmed*, let him harm still," or "He who *was* in filth, let him be filthy still," but rather: "He who harms," and "He who *is* in filth." This is the same as if He were saying: The one who has a desire for harming, and

<margin>Amos 1 <note>Rupert refers to the repeated refrain in the first chapter of Amos: "For three transgressions... and for four, I will not turn away his punishment."</note></margin>
stubbornly loves his own filth—let no one, after hearing that man defending himself and despising the plagues written in this book, hope for any good from him. For it is written: "For three crimes, and for four, I will not convert him." <note>original: *non conuertam eum*. While modern Bibles translate this as "not revoke the punishment," Rupert uses a version that suggests God will no longer offer the grace of conversion.</note> Because after one has run through three crimes and reached the fourth, there is no longer hope for conversion. The **first crime** is to have dwelt upon the filth of sins in the mind and with pleasure. The **second crime** is to have committed that same filth in action. The **third crime** is to have turned the filth into a habit. The **fourth crime** is to defend that same filth. Therefore, let him who harms, harm; and let him who is in filth, be filthy still: for God no longer cares for him, and he is justly abandoned. This is because he was not merely filthy in a passing way, but he remains in filth by proudly defending his stains. On the other hand, let him who is just and holy—that is, him who holds the good of justice and holiness as his pursuit—continue to perform justice and continue to be sanctified. God, in His providence, ensures that such a person does not depart from this present world before his crown is perfected, and his mansion in the house of his Father <margin>John 14 <note>A reference to John 14:2: "In my Father's house are many mansions."</note></margin> is adorned with the gems and pearls of his merits. Having promised this—that he who harms should harm still, he who is in filth should be filthy, and the just should do justice

<margin>John 14</margin>
still, and the holy be sanctified still—there immediately follows:

> Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according to his works.

<margin>Rewards will not be lacking for both the good and the bad. <note>original: *Non deerunt pręmia & bonis & malis*. The marginal note clarifies that "reward" (*merces*) applies to both the positive payment for the righteous and the "payment" of punishment for the wicked.</note></margin>
Doubtless He speaks in this way as one who is well aware that He possesses great strength and inexhaustible power to punish the harmful and the filthy. However much they have harmed, and however much they have been filthy, they shall receive no less a torture than their [demerits] deserve. Likewise, He is aware of His power to reward the just and the holy, however much justice they have performed, and however much they have been sanctified...

<summary>Rupert explains Revelation 22:11 by defining four stages of sin, concluding that those who defend their wickedness are abandoned by God. Conversely, he encourages the righteous to persevere so their heavenly reward—compared to a mansion adorned with gems—may be completed before death.</summary>

# On Revelation, Chapter 21 <note>Although the header says Chapter 21, the text is actually commenting on Revelation 22:12–15. In many medieval manuscripts and early printed books, these final visions were grouped together under the same heading.</note>

<margin>Luke 12 <note>Rupert alludes to the parable of the faithful and unfaithful servants in Luke 12:45–46.</note></margin>

For He who said, "I am the Alpha and the Omega," explains it by saying, "the first and the last," adding also "the beginning and the end"—namely, the one from whom the beginning of every creature comes, and in whom the rational creature is brought to completion <term>brought to completion: the Latin *consummatur* implies reaching a final goal or perfection</term>. Certainly because the marriage of the Lamb and the holy city Jerusalem (concerning which splendid visions have been shown thus far) is a marriage of holiness, and (as was said above) not...

# Commentary by Rupert, Book 12 <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was a Benedictine abbot and theologian. His commentary on Revelation is one of the most significant of the 12th century.</note>

[Page 572]

...nothing defiled will enter there. Only those are blessed who wash their robes, so that they may have a wedding garment <note>original: *vestem nuptialem*. In medieval theology, this often represented the virtues or the state of grace required for heaven.</note>, and especially that their loins be girded—that is, that they possess the ornament of chastity. This should be done not with the intention of seeking human praise, but for the sake of that expectation: that their power may be in the tree of life <note>original: *ligno vitę*</note>. This means they may truly enjoy the life-giving vision of the supreme divinity, which is entered through the gates of justice, which are the gates of the holy city. Indeed, he spoke of that holy city appropriately in this place, as he was about to add:

<margin>Proverbs 26; 2 Peter 2 <note>Rupert is referencing Proverbs 26:11 and 2 Peter 2:22: "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly."</note></margin>
**Outside are the dogs**, that is, all the foolish who return to their folly just as a dog returns to its vomit; and **sorcerers** <note>original: *venefici*, literally "poisoners." In the medieval world, sorcery and the mixing of harmful drugs or potions were often linked.</note> who destroy human life with poisons; and the **unchaste**, who are ashamed of no filthiness; and **murderers** who are certainly polluted with human blood and are bloody in the eyes of the Lord; and **idol-worshippers**, who surely have no fellowship with him who is the one and only true God; and **everyone who loves and tells a lie**, of which kind heretics are the foremost. All these things are contrary to the holy city, and therefore he says they are "outside"—for him, it is enough to have said "outside" by his command.

### I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you these things in the churches.

<margin>The canonical authority of this book.</margin>
It is as if it were said: "If you seek the authority of this book, I, Jesus, am the author and the giver of this Apocalypse <note>original: *Apocalypsis*, from the Greek word for 'unveiling' or 'revelation.'</note>." This scripture is not from John, nor is it from any man; for John did not receive it from a man, nor did he learn it, but I, who am Jesus, revealed it and sent it through my angel. Just as all scriptures are of divine authority, so also these writings should be testified and recited to you in the churches, and they should be held as the canonical peak <note>original: *canonico apice*, referring to the highest authority of the biblical canon.</note>. Do you ask who I, Jesus, am—I who wish this scripture to be commended by my authority to be testified in the churches?

### I am the root and the offspring of David, the bright and morning star.

<margin>The root and offspring of David.</margin>
It is as if he says: "I am that Jesus, who am both the Lord and the son of David; who, according to my human nature, suffered and was buried, and rose in the morning from the dead." For because he is the Lord, and crea... <note>The text ends mid-word on the catchword 'crea', likely continuing as 'creator' on the following page.</note>

<summary>Rupert explains that the 'dogs' and sinners are excluded from the New Jerusalem, while the faithful who maintain chastity enter. He then affirms that the book of Revelation carries divine authority because it comes directly from Jesus, the descendant of David.</summary>

# On Revelation, Chapter 21 <note>Although the header indicates Chapter 21, the text comments on Chapter 22:16-17. In medieval numbering or specific manuscript traditions, these final sections were sometimes grouped differently.</note>

<margin>Psalm 110 <note>original: *Psalm. cix*. In the Vulgate, this is Psalm 109, but it corresponds to Psalm 110 in modern English Bibles: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand."</note></margin>
...I am the [author or creator] <note>The OCR begins mid-word with *tor*; based on context, this is likely *auctor* (author) or *creator*.</note> of David, just as he himself testifies, speaking in the Spirit: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.* Therefore I am the **root**; and because the son of David was born or made from his seed according to the flesh, therefore I am the **offspring** <note>original: *genus*</note> of David. And indeed now, as long as you, living in this [world], walk by faith, I am the **bright and morning star** for you, ever since I rose from the dead. But then you shall have me as your **sun**, when you enter into such a city as you have heard described, which the brightness of God has illuminated, and which does not need the light of the sun or moon for this very reason: because the brightness of God has illuminated it.

->**And the Spirit and the bride say, "Come." And let him who hears say, "Come." And let him who thirsts come; and let him who desires take the water of life freely.**<-

<margin>The bride speaks outwardly, the Spirit inwardly.</margin>
"I," he says, "have sent [my angel] to testify these things to you in the churches," and with the testimony of these things, the Spirit agrees with the conscience of each of you, and says to each of you: **come**—that is, believe these things which are testified to you here. This the **bride**, which is the Church, says outwardly to the ear of the body, while she conveys the literal sound by reading; this the **Spirit** says inwardly to the ear of the heart, while he suggests the meaning so that one might understand that whatever is said here is reasonable, true, and faithful, and worthy of being heard. Let everyone hear this Spirit—or "the Groom," <note>original: *sponsum*. Rupert notes a textual variation found in some medieval manuscripts.</note> as some manuscripts have it—and the Bride saying, **Come**; that is, let him obey those calling and follow the healthy vocation, so that he may enter the blessedness of such a glorious city. Moreover, the one hearing or obeying should say **come**—that is, let him not be content with his own salvation alone, but let him take care to win over his neighbor by the word of exhortation and be able to bring him along with him. And he who thirsts, who desires to be saved, let him only come: because clearly that river of the **water of life**, which was shown to you, is denied to no one who thirsts, but let him take what he wishes: because a good will alone is sufficient for receiving the water of life, which grace has prepared. It is given to all **freely** <note>original: *gratis*</note>, provided that the seeker or receiver is a person of good will.

**I testify to everyone hearing the words of the prophecy**...

# Rupert's Commentary, Book 11
### Page 658

<margin>
The punishment of heretics for the corruption of the scriptures.
</margin>
...of this book. **If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his share of the tree of life, and from the holy city, and from those things written in this book.** <note>original: *ligno vitæ* (tree of life/wood of life). These verses are from Revelation 22:18-19.</note> This punishment of damnation is undoubtedly for heretics: that their share be taken away from the tree of life—which is Christ—and from the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, and from all the good things written in this book. It is also that the plagues written in this book should be placed upon them. This is because they clearly corrupt the holy scriptures by adding their own opinions or subtracting anything else. They do this out of a desire to build up their own dogma; they would prefer that whatever in the holy scriptures contradicts their views should not remain in any manuscript anywhere. Thus, the author quite firmly defends this scripture as being of divine and canonical authority. He strikes anyone who would corrupt it with the same damnation as heretics, and immediately adds:

**He who gives testimony of these things says:**
**"Yes, I am coming soon."**

<margin>
The authority of this book is divine.
</margin>
The writer could have said here, "Jesus says," but he preferred to say, **"He who gives testimony of these things says."** Here, at the conclusion of the volume, his whole intention is to defend this book as being written by divine authority and the truth of the Holy Spirit. He seeks to protect it from the contempt of all, providing a warning against what was likely to happen: namely, that foolish people might dare to despise this sacred text or judge the literal word as something to be rejected, simply because they do not deserve to grasp its spiritual meaning. **"Yes,"** he says, **"I am coming soon."** What I have said, I say again, and repeating it, I affirm: because I come quickly to render to each according to his works. Truly, this is sweet and desirable to a soul that is diligent—one that loves God rather than this world—and such a soul receives this voice with joy, knowing that the coming of the Lord is near. Therefore, the diligent and chaste bride responds immediately, saying:

# On Apocalypse Chapter 21 <note>original: "Cap. xxi" – though the text discusses the end of Chapter 22</note> Page 673

### Amen, come Lord Jesus

<margin>We ought to desire our redemption through the final coming of Christ.</margin>
In a certain way, he lifts up his head, according to that Gospel saying: **When these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, for your redemption is drawing near.** <note>Luke 21:28</note> Therefore, he says, **Amen**; that is, "may your promise be made true," so that you may come quickly, Lord Jesus. <margin>Psalm 119</margin>
<note>original: "pſal.cxix" – modern Psalm 120:5</note>
**because my stay has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time resident.** Also: **My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?**
<margin>Psalm 41</margin>
<note>original: "pſalm. xli." – modern Psalm 42:2</note>

<margin>Luke 12</margin>

### The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, Amen.

He desires that this not be set apart for a few, but be common to all. This is especially so that, as the Apostle Paul also hoped,
<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin>
we may all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among us through the grace by which we have been redeemed, Amen.

# [The Binding of the Volume]

The manuscript is protected by a sturdy **dark brown, mottled leather** cover, which displays a marbled or speckled appearance. The surface is embellished with <term>blind-tooled<note>A decorative technique where patterns are impressed into the leather using heated metal tools without the use of gold leaf or pigment, resulting in a subtle, recessed design.</note></term> decorations that give the volume a tactile texture.

A rectangular border, consisting of several finely engraved lines, frames the center of the cover. Inside each of the four corners of this frame, the binder has placed a stylized floral stamp, likely a fleur-de-lis or a similar botanical motif.

->**Central Ornament**<-

The center of the cover features a larger, symmetrical <term>ornamental stamp<note>An engraved metal block used to press a complete decorative design into the book's cover.</note></term> containing intricate floral patterns and elegant scrollwork. On the right-hand side, the spine of the volume is visible, characterized by several prominent <term>raised bands<note>Horizontal ridges on the spine of a book where the leather covers the thick cords used to sew the pages together.</note></term>, which are hallmarks of traditional hand-binding.
